News.title: We’re squatters in ‘apocalyptic’ ghost estate – neighbours call us ‘travellers & druggies’… but we’ll never leave
News.content:
SQUATTERS living on an abandoned ghost estate have been branded “travellers and druggies” by locals but vow to never leave.

Victoria Morrall, 39, and David Antram, 61, are living on the “apocalyptic” estate in St Erth, Cornwall.



But their presence has sparked a row among locals who say they have made it an intimidating place to go and called for them to be evicted.

Victoria has been accused of leaving her animals unattended on the estate but has hit back despite her dog being seized by police.



She said the anger of locals is unjustified, accusing them of being out to get her.

Victoria said: “They think we’re gypsies or druggies… and just squatters.”



She lives on the estate with partner David and their two Rottweilers as well as their ponies.

Previously homeless, the couple moved in after leaving their caravan – saying they were conned into renting the place and told it was a “paid security job.”



Locals claimed this week that they hadn’t seen anyone at the estate for days with one dog and three ponies left to wander by the couple.

One local told Cornwall Live: “The squatters have left and abandoned their three horses and a rottweiler.”

The allegedly abandoned animals have been reported to the police and the RSPCA.

It led to both agencies attending and seizing a dog on Saturday with a vet due to arrive and transport the horses in the coming days.

Victoria claims that she was at a funeral however and furiously explained: “The people of St Erth just don’t like us because they think we’re gypsies or druggies and all that lot.



“As far as St Erth is concerned, we’re just squatters.”

She said her and David were in the process of moving off the estate and hadn’t been able to send for their horses yet.

According to Victoria she visits the ghost estate daily and leaves her dog there for “security.”

She said: “The RSPCA have done this by mistake and I am trying to get my dog back, that dog is like my baby.

“The other one is just a puppy and was with me as it wouldn’t do well left but the other we left for security.”



Victoria and her partner have been travelling to and from the estate, sometimes twice a day, from their home in Truro, she claims.

Locals insist that the couple leave their animals there unattended for long periods of time however.

One neighbour described the abandoned development as a “blot” on the area and said there are safety concerns over the squatters living there.

They fumed: “It is really ugly and a real blot on the village. We don’t feel safe having them there at all.

“They have two rottweilers who give a very intimidating feeling. We don’t feel welcome going there at all.



“We just want it gone. It either needs to be returned to a field or have nicer houses built there.”

Victoria claims they have faced a barrage of abuse while living on the estate and had the police called out on a number of occasions.

This included an incident when the couple were both arrested and later released without charge over a firearms and trespass allegations.

Devon and Cornwall Police confirmed they were called to reports of a woman with a suspected firearm on the derelict site on January 24.

It was further reported that a man had been making threats.



The force said units were deployed, including firearms officers, and two air weapons and a machete were seized.

An RSPCA spokesperson said: “An officer attended a property in St Erth on Saturday (August 1) following concerns for a number of animals there.

“Police seized a dog and placed him into our care. We can’t comment any further at this time as enquiries are ongoing.”

A spokesman for Devon and Cornwall Police said: “Police attended Chenhalls Road, St Erth, on the afternoon of Saturday 1 August following a report of a dog and ponies left behind at an unfinished building site.

“An officer assisted with removing a dog which was then passed over to the RSPCA.”



A planning application was first submitted in 2013 for ten homes along with an access road and parking – but it was refused by Cornwall Council.

The local authority ruled it to be “an isolated development in the countryside to the detriment of the rural character of the area”.

However, the applicant – William Trevorrow, of St Ives – appealed and the housing estate was allowed by the Planning Inspectorate in March 2015.

Building started soon afterwards, but the ten houses have never been lived in.

The empty estate has been owned by Barton Bridging Ltd since 2019 when the previous owner went into receivership.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

It has been fenced off and pictures show it has become overgrown and unkempt – with locals branding it a “blot on the village.”

Victoria said they live off-grid in the downstairs of one of the homes, describing the estate as like an “apocalyptic” scene.

News.title: Jon Venables may face public parole hearing as James Bulger’s mum leads new bid for son’s killer to ‘face up to crimes’
News.content:
NOWHERE TO HIDE Jon Venables may face public parole hearing as James Bulger’s mum leads new bid for son’s killer to ‘face up to crimes’

CHILD killer Jon Venables’ parole hearing may be heard in public after James Bulger’s mother launched a fresh bid yesterday.

The brute could finally be made to “face up” to his crimes after brave Denise Fergus made an application to attend the crunch hearing for their two-year-old’s killer.



We previously told how Venables, 43, was hell-bent on keeping any hearing private and had even hired lawyers to shamefully try and keep the public out.

The thug was first released on licence in July 2001 but was recalled to prison in February 2010 after indecent images of children were found on his computer.



He was recalled a second time for the same sick crime in 2017 and has remained in prison since, with parole specialists finding he is still a risk to children.

The Parole Board yesterday confirmed: “The Parole Board has received an application from Denise and Stuart Fergus for the Parole Board hearing in the case of Jon Venables to be heard in public.”



A list of reasons for the application reveals the murdered tot’s mother and her husband, Stuart Fergus, say vile Venables must “face up to his offending by way of a public hearing”.

Their application’s reasons state: “There is significant public interest in the case, and a public hearing could improve public understanding of the parole process.

“They argue that the prisoner should have to face up to his offending by way of a public hearing, especially given that he has committed further serious offences as an adult.

“Public scrutiny would help explain how risk is assessed and managed, supporting confidence in the parole system.



“They consider the prisoner’s further convictions as an adult to be an exceptional feature of the case, adding to the public interest in how the parole review is conducted.”

Denise and Stuart also said that “if this application were granted, they would finally feel listened to and they are prepared for the hearing to take place in public.”

James’s builder dad, Ralph, 59, has previously told The Sun he would also want to be at a public hearing.

Denise and Ralph divorced in 1995. The family were previously told the hearing will not take place until September at the earliest.

Venables and fellow killer Robert Thompson abducted James from the Strand shopping centre in Bootle on February 12, 1993.



They took him to a nearby railway line before torturing and murdering the young boy in one of the most notorious killings in British history.

Both men were detained at Her Majesty’s Pleasure in November 1993, the child equivalent of an indefinite prison sentence.

Thompson was released in June 2001, aged 18, and is not thought to have re-offended since.

Venables, who has a lifetime anonymity order, has previously tried to frustrate the parole process and is actively fighting his victim’s parents’ right to be there.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Parole Board rules mean Venables, who has access to lawyers behind bars, has a week to lodge an objection to the application.



In any public hearing, the killer would likely appear from behind a screen with voice distortion technology used to protect his identity.

News.title: My dad was stabbed in heart by new wife weeks after wedding…now she’s painting herself as victim in sick bid for freedom
News.content:
PHOTOS from her wedding day show Sharon Edwards beaming in a white dress during a glitzy ceremony in Las Vegas – in contrast her husband David was sporting a fresh black eye.

Solicitor David told concerned family and friends he’d accidentally hit himself in the face with the bedside phone in his hotel room – but weeks later he was found stabbed through the heart and his new wife was jailed for murder. Now, while wallowing in prison, she’s still spinning lies in a bid for freedom.



David’s youngest daughter Mahalia, from a previous relationship, was just about to turn seven when the dad-of-four was reported dead at lunchtime on August 23, 2015 at home in Chorley, Lancashire.

Now 18, she has memories of David being physically and verbally abused by her stepmum, including on one occasion when she punched him so hard his glasses snapped in half.

And Mahalia has a collection of photos of her dad with various injuries, including with his arm in a sling, all taken during the couple of years he was with Sharon.



There’s also police bodycam from hours before David was murdered – used in TV broadcasts about the case – in which the dishevelled dad, seen with blood pouring from his head, is called an “idiot” by his new wife.

Tragically, he told the officer at the scene he’d fallen so Sharon was not arrested – allowing her to murder him hours later.

Much to Mahalia’s disgust, she was recently made aware of a page on campaign group Justice For Women last month which paints Sharon as the victim amid numerous appeals to the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC).

On her being jailed for a minimum of 20 years on March 8 2016, the group writes: “The prosecution and media portrayed her as a violent, bullying wife.

“But behind the headlines lies a more complex and troubling story – one of trauma, coercion, and a woman failed by the justice system.”



Using beaming photos of Sharon from the wedding day, it goes on to claim she had previously reported David to police for coercive control, describing him as a “bully” – though there is no publicly available evidence of this.

It claims Sharon had told David she was leaving him, which resulted in an argument before his death, and that in fact he had gone to the kitchen and held a knife to his throat while taunting her, and she does not recall stabbing him.

Mahalia’s brother first spotted the Justice For Women page and told the family about it in July.

She told The Sun: “I was absolutely furious when I first saw it.

“It’s wrong on so many levels… she’s had the audacity to still use my dad’s last name and their wedding photos.



“They show her looking all nice and done up but don’t show my dad with his black eye.”

In a Facebook post, Mahalia said: “Are you f***ing take the p***? How dare this evil dirty scumbag cry domestic violence.”

Mahalia went on to tell The Sun she had since emailed the campaign group to clarify what background checks had been done and what evidence had been seen, and if they can remove the page.



But she says she hasn’t had a response.

“I have no words for it,” she said. She praised organisations like Justice For Women in supporting victims of miscarriage of justice, but added in this case: “I feel like they just need to check the facts and the evidence before they put them up online.”

Sharon has already had at least one application to the CCRC rejected in 2018, according to Women For Justice – before launching another.



In response to the page, Mahalia has been sharing photos and footage of what she claims is evidence against Sharon on Facebook.

This includes coverage by ITV News at the time of her conviction in which police bodycam is used from hours before David’s death, as well as CCTV from a nearby shop the same night in which other customers had to step in to stop Sharon’s aggressive behaviour towards her husband.

The bodycam was recorded by a female police officer who came across David and Sharon arguing in the street.

The officer can be heard saying to Sharon: “What’s going on? I’ve just come round that roundabout and seen you ragging him around.”

Sharon – stood with David up against the wall – laughs and says “We’re drunk”.



She’s told to get into the police car in a bid to separate them, to which Sharon responds “I don’t think so” and the officer tells her: “I do. I’m not asking.”

David, in a timid voice, tells his new wife to listen to the police, to which she angrily responds: “Oh David, seriously?” As she marches down the street she turns back and jibes: “Solicitor or no solicitor…” but is cut off as the officer tries to accost her.

Sharon screams: “Don’t you touch me!”



However, David, who can be seen bleeding from the head, claimed his injuries were the result of a fall and Sharon was not arrested.

As the bodycam concludes, David, seen smoking a cigarette, is told by his wife to breathe before she mumbles “idiot” and he shuffles after her.

The following afternoon, Sharon went on to stab David in the heart. He was found by emergency crews lying on the couple’s bed, the trial heard.

The tragic dad had recently lost his high-paying job as a solicitor. The court heard this was, in part, due to him often arriving dishevelled and sometimes smelling of alcohol and displaying injuries.

When he died, David had approximately 60 external injuries.



DCI Dean Holden said: “Sharon, I think, took this quite badly and I think the perception is that Sharon quite liked being the solicitor’s wife.”

He added “bit by bit she chipped away and almost dismantled” David’s life.

“What was left then was a man without his job, mounting debts, a house that should have been nice but looking somewhat dishevelled and physically David was a different man,” he said.



Sharon’s trial heard she first met David in 2000 when she was giving evidence in court against a previous husband, who she alleged had assaulted her.

David was representing her ex – the pair did not, however, begin a relationship until 2014 after connecting on Facebook.

Mahalia, now a mum-of-one to daughter Isabella, was too young to understand exactly what had happened when her dad died.

She said: “I remember the day that I got told he’d died, I just kept asking my mum, ‘could we go and see him?’

“Obviously, I didn’t know what death meant. I thought he was asleep in the hospital, so I kept asking my mum, ‘Could we go see him?’

“And she just said, ‘We can’t, he’s in Heaven now. He’s never coming back.’

“I was just really confused at the time. I didn’t know what was going on. And then loads of my family members came round looking really sad.”

Mahalia went to the funeral, and can remember the coffin and David’s loved ones crying over it.

She admits, despite the violence she witnessed, she had been close to Sharon as a child, seeing her and David on weekends.



“Sharon seemed to like me – although I think she wanted to replace my mum,” Mahalia says.

Then she began reading up on the case, and what Sharon had done.

“As I got older I started to hate her more,” said Mahalia. “I don’t really think I ever got time to understand what grief was and what I was going through because I was so young.”

She added: “I did expect something like this to happen though because that’s the type of person she is. She’s doing it all to get out of jail.”



As well as learning about the horrors of his murder, Mahalia has also been told about what her dad was like by her family.

“I’ve just heard loads and loads of stories and he seems to have been a very funny man,” she said.

“Obviously, he did make some mistakes in his life.”

Her memories of him are marred by the flashes of abuse against David she recalls, but she cherishes one recollection during a family holiday prior to her mum and dad separating.

“He put my mum’s jeans on and he ran into the room and he was shouting, ‘Oh, you shrunk my jeans, you shrunk my jeans!’



“And then my mum turned around and went, ‘They’re my jeans, David’.”

She added: “I do feel really upset that Isabella will never be able to meet her grandad. He would have absolutely loved her.”

The Sun has approached Justice For Women for comment.

News.title: Inside overcrowded max-security hell jail rife with disease where ‘suitcase killer’ is set to be held over Brit’s death
News.content:
THE Afghan migrant accused of killing a Brit aid worker could spend the next 18 months in a hellish prison with terrorists, rapists and some of Greece’s most hardened criminals.

Professional boxer Sharif Ahmadzai, 26, is expected to be placed in pre-trial detention in maximum security prison Korydallos on the outskirts of Athens.



Elisabeth Ross, 38, was found stuffed in a suitcase in a derelict building in the Kypseli area of the Greek capital on July 18.

Ahmadzai has been charged with homicide with intent, robbery and illegal gun possession and refused to enter a plea during a court hearing on Thursday.





Known to inmates as Colditz after the prisoner of war camp, Korydallos is one of the worst jails in Europe.

Vastly overcrowded, the rat-infested jail has often been singled out by human rights groups.

The European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment described it as an “affront to human dignity”.

They cited horror overcrowding, prisoner violence, severe understaffing, and inadequate healthcare.



As many as eight men can be detained in prison cells that are both dark and dank.

Diseases such as tuberculosis, hepatitis and scabies are said to be rampant – with patients suffering from cancer and kidney problems.

Many are also HIV positive, part of an epidemic sweeping the Greek prison population, Greek reports say.



A law enforcer told The Sun that Ahmadzai could be targeted due to high-profile nature of the case.

Most convicted felons in Korydallos are foreign – with the vast majority imprisoned for drug trafficking.

There have been several high-risk attempts to flee the prison.

One spectacular escape saw a helicopter swoop in to free the brother of Greece’s most wanted robber, who had escaped from behind bars.

The chopper’s pilot later told police the aircraft had been hijacked.



Under Greek law the Afghan can be held in pre-trial detention for up to 18 months.

After two months, he can file his first appeal to be freed pending trial – on condition he wears an ankle bracelet, check in with police and hands over travel documents.

If a hearing does not take place within 18 months, a suspect is automatically freed pending trial.



Court insiders told The Sun that a delay is not likely as UK security services – including the National Crime Agency – had been involved in the probe.

A court official told us: “As there has been so much international attention, the feeling is the trial will not been pushed into the long grass.

“Greek authorities are acutely aware they are being watched. Justice must be served.”

Authorities are awaiting toxicological tests and analysis of vital organ tissue that will determine Elisabeth’s exact cause of death.

Police spokesperson Konstantina Dimoglidou told The Sun earlier this week that the tests would be fast-tracked.



Lack of staff and laboratory space usually meant that such analysis took several months in Greece.

But Dimoglidou said the case was a top priority for authorities.

Ahmadzai’s US-born wife Alaina Hall allegedly reported her husband to cops after she became suspicious he was involved in Elisabeth’s death.



She told cops that she had met Elisabeth through volunteer work in Athens and had last seen her on July 12, after a Bible study meeting, according to Greek news outlet Protothema.

Days later, she heard reports of a body being found stuffed in a suitcase in an abandoned building in Athens.

Later that night, Alaina recalled waking up with a “terrible” feeling.

In the morning she then texted Elisabeth and got two replies which made her suspicious.

Alaina said: “These messages were not in Lisa’s style, both in terms of her level of English and the use of emojis that she never used.”



When she tried calling Elisabeth she didn’t get a reply.

Alaina also told police she had grown suspicious of her husband after she woke to find him missing on the evening of July 15.

When she checked his shared location, she saw he was in Elisabeth’s flat.



Having later confronted him, he told her he had been watching a football match but had gone to Elisabeth’s apartment to use the toilet.

She told police: “I don’t know what to tell you, but all of the above made me feel strange.

“Especially combining the dates, the messages and my husband’s behaviour, I have various thoughts that make me feel uncomfortable.”

Investigating officers also found CCTV footage which allegedly shows him leaving Elizabeth’s apartment with a suitcase and dropping it where her remains were discovered on July 16.

Ahmadzai has told cops he did not kill Elisabeth, saying he found her dead before panicking.



In his testimony, he reportedly said: “I never did harm to anyone. I want you to understand me and believe me. I was just in a panic.”

He is said to have claimed he had visited the house where she was staying and found her lying on the bathroom floor.

Ahmadzai claimed he panicked and fled and then encountered an elderly man near a bus stop and asked what he should do after finding a dead body.

He said he returned to the apartment the following day and placed Elisabeth’s body in a black suitcase, before placing it in the boot of the red Peugeot he drove.

“I found the old man I told you about who gave me the advice. He told me to leave the suitcase with him, and he would take care of it,” he reportedly said.



He admitted to the cops he had taken Elisabeth’s phone and bank cards.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Elisabeth’s devasted family paid tribute on Thursday – describing her as “kind, principled and selfless”.

They said: “Her integrity was absolute, and she dedicated her life to helping others in need. We are in deep pain, and we ask for time and privacy as we come to terms with our loss.”

News.title: The full list of bank holiday dates around the UK in 2027 – including an extra four-day weekend
News.content:
EVERYONE loves a bank holiday, with Brits often looking ahead to see if the next long weekend is on the horizon.

There are still a handful to look forward to before 2026 is finished, but let’s take a look beyond even that and find out when the bank holidays are scheduled for next year.



When are the remaining bank holidays in 2026?

Fortunately, there is still one last long weekend to look forward to this summer while the sunshine remains, allowing plans for a quick holiday getaway to go ahead.

That’s not the case for those who live north of the border, however, as in Scotland, the summer bank holiday took place on Monday, August 3.



For those living in England, Wales, and Northern Ireland, the next bank holiday is set to take place on Monday, August 31.

It may feel as though the summer bank holiday has come later than expected, with an unusually long 14-week gap separating it from the previous spring bank holiday.

But that’s the law, as in these three countries the summer bank holiday must always fall on the final Monday of August.

And because August began on a Saturday this year, the last Monday falls on the 31st – the absolute latest possible date the bank holiday can legally occur.

Past this month’s long weekend, the next bank holidays in England, Wales and Northern Ireland won’t arrive until the festive season.



But Scotland has one more on Monday, November 30 to fit in before then, as Scots take the day off work to celebrate St Andrew’s Day.

Christmas Day and December 28 (Substitute Day) will make up a four-day weekend in December to mark the final two bank holidays of the year.

When are the bank holidays in 2027?

Brits can look forward to double the downtime in 2027, with two four-day weekends on the cards over Easter and the festive period.

For those who are looking to be super prepared and begin planning for next year already, here’s a look at what to expect:

England and Wales bank holidays 2027:

Friday, January 1: New Year’s Day

New Year’s Day Friday, March 26: Good Friday

Good Friday Monday, March 29: Easter Monday

Easter Monday Monday, May 3: Early May bank holiday

Early May bank holiday Monday, May 31: Spring bank holiday

Spring bank holiday Monday, August 30: Summer bank holiday

Summer bank holiday Monday, December 27: Christmas Day (Substitute Day)

Christmas Day (Substitute Day) Tuesday, December 28: Boxing Day (Substitute Day)

Northern Ireland bank holidays 2027:

Friday, January 1: New Year’s Day

New Year’s Day Wednesday, March 17: St Patrick’s Day

St Patrick’s Day Friday, March 26: Good Friday

Good Friday Monday, March 29: Easter Monday

Easter Monday Monday, May 3: Early May bank holiday

Early May bank holiday Monday, May 31: Spring bank holiday

Spring bank holiday Monday, July 12: Battle of the Boyne

Battle of the Boyne Monday, August 30: Summer bank holiday

Summer bank holiday Monday, December 27: Christmas Day (Substitute Day)

Christmas Day (Substitute Day) Tuesday, December 28: Boxing Day (Substitute Day)

Scotland bank holidays 2027:

Friday, January 1: New Year’s Day

New Year’s Day Monday, January 4: 2nd January (Substitute Day)

2nd January (Substitute Day) Friday, March 26: Good Friday

Good Friday Monday, May 3: Early May bank holiday

Early May bank holiday Monday, May 31: Spring bank holiday

Spring bank holiday Monday, August 2: Summer bank holiday

Summer bank holiday Tuesday, November 30: St Andrew’s Day

St Andrew’s Day Monday, December 27: Christmas Day (Substitute Day)

Christmas Day (Substitute Day) Tuesday, December 28: Boxing Day (Substitute Day)

Could more bank holidays be added last minute?

While the official calendar is set well in advance, extra days off can theoretically be added to the schedule at shorter notice.



Under the Banking and Financial Dealings Act 1971, the King has the legal power to declare additional one-off bank holidays across the UK and within individual home nations by Royal Proclamation, acting on the advice of government ministers.

These surprise bonus days are typically reserved for major national events, such as royal weddings, state funerals, coronations, or historic jubilees.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

While there are frequent public campaigns calling for new permanent bank holidays, the government generally resists adding them at the last minute due to the significant economic costs involved for businesses.

As a result, unexpected additions remain a rare occurrence saved strictly for historic national occasions.

News.title: Entire Spanish village for sale for as much as a London terraced house – with its own pool, tennis court and CHURCH
News.content:
VILLAGE LEAVING Entire Spanish village for sale for as much as a London terraced house – with its own pool, tennis court and CHURCH

LOOKING for the perfect getaway this summer?

The keys to an entire Spanish village tucked away in the mountains – with a pool, tennis court, and a church – could be yours for £729,000.



Viana do Bolo, located in the southeast of the Ourense province near Portugal’s northern border, consists of a grand main house, 11 smaller residences, and a chapel.

The properties are fitted with traditional terracotta floors, laid with wooden flooring and a cosy fireplace.



It also has a tennis court and a swimming pool.

Surrounded by nature, it is said that the village is close to the mountain Peña Trevinca and around 30 minutes away from Lake Sanabria.



Asturian Property, which advertises this listing, said that this “whole hamlet” is for sale with “lots of potential.”

In the description, it said that the original price was €1.5 million (£1,290,000) but has now dropped to just over £730,000.



Daniel Garcia, the seller, argued that it is a “great investment for anyone looking to run spiritual events, or for a group of friends or people who want to live a quieter, more eco-friendly lifestyle away from the city.”

García, a trainee firefighter, said that his grandfather had bought the village to keep his family close together.

But he fell ill and died before he could see his plans to renovate all the homes come to life, only finishing three of them.

Mr García said: “After my grandfather passed away, the rest of the houses still needed renovating, and no one wanted to take responsibility for it.”



“After all, it required spending a significant amount of money to renovate the remaining houses, and neither my parents nor my aunts and uncles wanted to take charge of it.”

Daniel Marin is the managing director of the Spanish Property Expert who helps international buyers look for the property of their dreams in Spain.

He told The Sun: “I’ve been in the business for 20 years and I have never heard such a thing.



“But there is always a catch.”

Mr García said that over the last 18 months there has been a rise in interest in the village, especially from Irish buyers in the last few weeks.

The original purpose of the village was to provide accommodation for employees who worked at a local power plant.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

One of its many selling points is its spot near a popular pilgrimage route, the Vía de la Plata Camino, winding from Sevilla to Santiago de Compostela, the religious journey’s final destination.

For more than a thousand years, pilgrims have journeyed to a cathedral in Santiago de Compostela to pay tribute to the buried St James the Apostle.

News.title: Detective who led PC Harper probe is ‘appalled’ that killers could be freed early
News.content:
THE detective who led the probe into PC Harper’s death and put his killers behind bars says he is “appalled” they could be freed early.

Ex-Det Supt Stuart Blaik spoke of his fury at plans to release Albert Bowers and Jessie Cole, who showed “no remorse” for their role in the killing.



Andrew had just wed his wife Lissie, when he was fatally dragged along country roads behind a car driven by Henry Long in August 2019.

Bowers and Cole, then 17, were passengers as PC Harper was pulled for more than a mile after his ankles got caught in a towrope loop.



The pair, who smirked during their trial, got 13 years for manslaughter in 2020, meaning they could soon be freed under the government’s scheme.

And Mr Blaik, who led the Thames Valley Police probe in 2019, said he was “deeply concerned” by the killers’ potential release.



Speaking on BBC Breakfast, he said: “Neither of them showed any remorse during their time in police custody or during their subsequent trial.

“I hope the Government takes account of the strength of public feeling on this issue, which has been both clear and widespread.



“I just really don’t understand why the Early Release Scheme is being used in these sort of circumstances, it just doesn’t feel right.”

Mr Blaik, who left the force in 2023, told how the smirking killers showed “no remorse whatsoever” throughout legal proceedings.

He added: “Their behaviour at the remand hearing and that way that they were reacting to the cameras…

“The fact that they showed absolutely no remorse whatsoever, and then the subsequent trial, that came out again during that process.

‘I don’t understand why something of this nature and seriousness could be part of that early release scheme, it doesn’t make any sense to me.”



Andrew’s furious widow Lissie Harper, 35, spoke of her anger as she described the situation as an “utter betrayal”.

She said: “This is disgusting. I’m beyond appalled and bristling with anger to hear Andrew’s killers are soon to be free.

“The level of disrespect the Government are showing to Andrew and other victims, and their loved ones such as me, is beyond contempt.



“What abhorrent message does this send?

“How dare ministers say the killing of a police officer isn’t enough of a ‘sickening crime’ that deserves the stiffest of punishments.

“Andrew’s killers have shown no remorse. To release them early from their already pitiful sentences is an affront to justice.”

PM Andy Burnham launched an urgent review of Sir Keir Starmer’s early release scheme, which aimed to ease pressure on crowded jails.

But despite raising hopes he could block the move, Mr Burnham decided prisons are too full to exclude manslaughter from the scheme.



Aileen O’Connor, chair of the Thames Valley Police Federation, is now threatening legal action against the decision to free the two killers.

She said the decision was a betrayal of PC Harper’s legacy, as a petition to stop his killers being let out passed 500,000 verified signatures.

Long, the main perpetrator who pleaded guilty, got 16 years and is not eligible for release under the scheme.

Early releases will begin in October.

Mr Burnham said: “I wanted to go even further as I know there will still be concerns about other offenders having their sentence shortened.



“But it’s not possible without the prison system reaching capacity and collapsing, which would put public safety at much greater risk.”

Tiff Lynch, National Chair of the Police Federation of England and Wales, branded the release as “deeply disappointing” and “impossible to justify”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

She said: “The Government has recognised that some offenders are simply too dangerous to benefit from early release, yet those convicted of killing police officers have been left off that list”

“We recently spoke out against the early release of the men responsible for PC Andrew Harper’s death, and officers, their families and the public will be asking why those who murder police officers can still qualify for reduced time behind bars.”

News.title: Taiwan’s president evacuated in dead of night to secret command post in armoured car amid biggest ever China war drills
News.content:
THE president of Taiwan has been practising his escape route amid mounting fears of a possible Chinese invasion.

President William Lai sped off in an armoured vehicle in the dead of night as part of ramped-up military drills on the island nation.



The covert operation forms part of the annual “Han Kuang” exercises – ten days of military drills for soldiers and civilians from August 5 to August 15.

Dramatic footage shows a phalanx of deadly vehicles bristling with soldiers cruise through the streets of Taiwan.



It is the first time President Lai – who came into power in 2024 – has taken part in escape route “Wan Chun” plans.

Hatched during the Cold War, the “Wan Chun” plan plots emergency evacuation for the president in case of an attempted “decapitation” strike from China.



Helicopters swarmed through the skies and missile launchers were erected along the shores as soldiers built barricades.

It comes after 14 Chinese aircrafts and nine warships circled Taiwan on Wednesday, according to authorities.

Beijing has repeatedly threatened to storm the democratically-ruled island which lies southeast of China.

Crazed Xi Jinping regards Taiwan as part of his Communist empire.



Donald Trump revealed in May that Xi asked him directly if America would intervene in the event of a Chinese invasion.



The US President reportedly refused to answer and advised Taiwan not to risk all-out war by demanding independence from China.

He said: “We’re supposed to travel 9,500 miles (15,289km) to fight a war. I’m not looking for that. I want them to cool down. I want China to cool down.

“We’re not looking to have wars, and if you kept it the way it is, I think China’s going to be okay with that.”

Taiwan’s foreign ministry issued a stern response, announcing that “Taiwan is a sovereign and independent democratic nation, and is not subordinate to the People’s Republic of China.”

China’s more than 2 million-strong army dwarfs Taiwan’s estimated 20,000 soldiers.



Despite tensions between Taiwan and the US, the drills have included American techniques for communications and combat.

“The most important new development in this years Han Kuang is the incorporation of American-style military training methods” said William Yang, a senior Northeast Asia analyst for the International Crisis Group.

Why does China want to invade Taiwan? TAIWAN insists it is an independent nation after splitting from mainland China amid civil war in 1949. But China claims Taiwan remains a part of its territory with which it must eventually be reunified – and has not ruled out the use of force to take the island and place it under Beijing’s control. The island, which is roughly 100 miles from the coast of south-east China, sees itself as distinct from the Chinese mainland, with its own constitution and democratically-elected leaders. Taiwan sits in the so-called “first island chain”, which includes a list of US-friendly territories that are crucial to Washington’s foreign policy in the region. This also puts it in an ideal situation to slow a Chinese attack on the West. And with tensions between the two nations high, Taiwan is likely to aid China’s enemy if it means keeping its independence. Taiwan’s economy is another factor in China’s desperation to reclaim the land. If China takes the island, it could be freer to project power in the western Pacific and rival the US, thanks to much of the world’s electronics being made in Taiwan. This would allow Beijing to have control over an industry that drives the global economy. China insists that its intentions are peaceful, but President Xi Jinping has also used threats towards the small island nation.

A key component of the Han Kuang drills, for example, has been the practice of a method called backbriefing where subordinates explain to commanders how they plan to carry out assigned missions.

The US has yet to acknowledge Taiwan as a country but is nonetheless bound by its own laws to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The two nations have been inching closer to a $14 billion arms sales package to Taiwan – but Trump has yet to give his seal of approval.

“Even though Trump and those close to him have flip-flopped on supporting Taiwan, the connection between the two militaries remains strong” claimed Lev Nachman, a political-science professor at National Taiwan University.

News.title: How police let a registered sex offender murder and attack women
News.content:
His first victim was attacked was on a busy Tube in central London.

Levy boarded and positioned himself directly in front of the woman, before leaning his elbow on her. She moved away.

A few minutes later, she felt something touch her, over her clothes, on her vagina. Such was the force Levy used, that she felt like it was an attempt to push his fingers inside her through clothing.

She grabbed Levy's hand and asked what he was doing, but he did not respond.

When other passengers asked if she was alright, Levy protested his innocence.

"What are you talking about - look my hand is covered," he said, pointing to the jumper draped over his arm.

Levy then called her "crazy" and "stupid" and got off the tube at Westminster Station.

The woman got off at the next stop, upset and crying.

She went on to report the assault to BTP. There was CCTV available of Levy, but police did not identify him. He would only be linked to the case two years later, after more women had been attacked.

A year after his first Tube assault, he assaulted three more women in quick succession and was arrested.

After being assaulted herself, the first of those three victims then filmed Levy sexually assaulting a second, unidentified woman, travelling in the same carriage.

The first woman immediately reported what had happened to BTP and provided the footage. Levy assaulted a third woman a week later.

After he had been questioned and had denied the three offences, BTP officers said they did not have enough evidence to charge, and he was released on bail.

The subsequent British Transport Police investigation was full of delays. It was weeks before identity parades were arranged, and BTP did not approach the CPS for six months.

When it did, in May 2025, a CPS team had to scramble to make an emergency charging decision overnight, because BTP had again arrested Levy and wanted him in court the next day. This was highly unusual - BTP had known about the initial offences for six months.

In a statement, BTP Assistant Chief Constable Charlie Doyle said: "It is clear that opportunities to expedite the investigation were missed and we have amended our procedures to address these issues to ensure that repeat offenders are dealt with expeditiously and that linked offences are prioritised more effectively."

News.title: Serial sex offender guilty of murdering two women and raping third
News.content:
Two Met officers are under investigation by the Independent Office of Police Conduct (IOPC) for their decision in August 2024 to downgrade Levy from a high-risk sex offender to a medium-risk.

A police constable had been served with a gross misconduct notice and a detective sergeant with a misconduct notice.

The IOPC said it would be investigating how Levy was managed from his first conviction in September 2021 up to his arrest in September 2025.

"We are examining whether action could or should have been taken to prevent his reoffending, and if all officers involved in his management followed policies, procedures, and training."

The IOPC stressed that the notices indicated the officers' actions were under investigation and did not mean disciplinary proceedings would follow.

The investigation will also consider whether any lessons can be learned or changes introduced at an individual, force-wide or national level.

The British Transport Police (BTP) said that two of its officers have been moved to other roles due to their "incompetence" in handling the case.

BTP Assistant Chief Constable Charlie Doyle said: "It is clear that opportunities to expedite the investigation were missed and we have amended our procedures to address these issues to ensure that repeat offenders are dealt with expeditiously, and that linked offences are prioritised more effectively."

Doyle also said it was possible there are other victims of Levy who are not yet known and encouraged them to come forward.

News.title: Cambridge to review process for hiring senior academics after Jason Arday resignation
News.content:
The University of Cambridge will review its process for appointing senior academics following the resignation of Jason Arday in the midst of a plagiarism row.

The institution said findings from an investigation into the education professor's academic qualifications and appointments would "feed into" a new review on the appointment process for senior academic roles.

The Jesus College fellow has also faced accusations of fabricating or exaggerating elements of his CV. He has defended himself and his work, with attention now turning to Cambridge's handling of concerns and his upcoming memoir.

News of the review comes after a group of academics called for an independent probe into his appointment.

Priyamvada Gopal, professor of postcolonial studies at Cambridge and among those calling for an independent inquiry, said the university was facing "massive reputational damage" over the affair.

"This is reputational damage that has upset colleagues across disciplines, across the political spectrum," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday.

"I've been quite struck by the number of people who are very upset by what has happened. So I don't think it is an option for Cambridge to just sweep this under the carpet and not take any action at all."

Gopal said the university should not be "marking its own homework", adding that the group of academics of which she is a part had suggested a mix of senior academics at Cambridge and elsewhere to conduct an investigation.

Cambridge said on Friday that it was "fully aware of the public commentary and concerns" and would "continue to investigate the circumstances around Jason Arday's appointment and tenure". A spokesperson declined to comment further.

It previously announced an investigation into "new information" about Arday's academic qualifications and appointments on Wednesday, having already said it was looking into allegations of plagiarism.

Jesus College welcomed the appointments review, saying Arday's role as fellow there had been "contingent on his university position".

"We rely on the university to do checks on academic credentials for its appointments," a spokeswoman added.

Accusations of plagiarism in Arday's work were first voiced by Nathan Cofnas - a US researcher whose role at a Cambridge college was terminated after backlash against his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".

He highlighted that plagiarism detection software had found several tracts of Arday's PhD dissertation to be copied verbatim or lightly rephrased from prior academic works by other authors.

Liverpool John Moores University (LJMU), which awarded Arday's PhD, has said it investigated the allegations of plagiarism last year and dismissed them, saying they were likely the result of "honest and reasonable error".

It told the BBC on Friday that its position remains unchanged in light of recent events and that his PhD "still stands".

Cofnas also noted that a retired professor had previously raised concerns about Arday's subsequent academic articles, which led to two journals issuing correction notes, and raised questions about some of his claimed achievements, including extensive marathon running and raising millions for charity.

Several universities at which Arday claimed on his CV to have had academic positions have since denied him having those roles.

The controversy has attracted a range of opinions, including within academia, about whether he had been scrutinised unfairly because of his race.

Arday has admitted errors in his work but denied plagiarism, saying his autism and a lack of adequate supervision early in his academic career may have contributed to those mistakes. He also denied lying about his achievements.

He said his decision to step down should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me", which he has previously said were "racially motivated".

Gopal said universities were "being targeted in particular by a lazy and false division between academic excellence and diversity and equality on campus", which was "really part of culture wars rather than any part of university life".

She and her colleagues found it "unusual" that Arday had been appointed to a "very senior, very prestigious" post early in his career - and that he had been put forward in the media with "frankly a bit of a target on his back".

Gopal also said any investigation should review "whether the university was involved in any way or any level with efforts to deter journalists from reporting on the allegations".

This came after it emerged the Metropolitan Police investigated Times Higher Education (THE) reporter Jack Grove over a complaint of harassment after he contacted Arday concerning allegations of plagiarism last year.

The Telegraph also reported that Arday hired law firm Carter-Ruck to send a letter to THE which implied that the "apparent attack" on Arday might be "racially motivated".

The Met closed the case and Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley apologised for the investigation, telling LBC on Thursday that the complaint should have been "screened out earlier on as not requiring investigation".

News.title: US appeals court halts Trump ballroom project paving way for Supreme Court showdown
News.content:
"Congress has not ceded unfettered authority to the Executive Branch to dramatically redesign, reshape, and reconstruct the White House â the People's âHouse â to fit a particular President's desires," the panel said.

The three-judge panel, in a 2-1 decision, said: "Each President is a temporary tenant, not the owner, of the White House and its Executive Residence."

"The President has no â and claims no â constitutionally assigned authority over that property, which is designed and maintained for the use of all Presidents, current and future, and for the American people," the opinion said.

The administration appealed to the court after a federal judge twice blocked above-ground construction on the ballroom, while still allowing underground work to proceed.

The ruling on Friday upholds that order blocking above-ground construction without congressional approval. The appeals court delayed implementation of its ruling for 14 days to allow the Trump administration to appeal to the Supreme Court.

Construction at the site where the East Wing previously stood was previously ordered to stop, but was allowed to continue in April after a court delayed the ruling while the appeals court considered briefs and heard arguments last month, according to the BBC's US media partner CBS.

The BBC has contacted the White House and Department of Justice for comment.

President Trump has asserted that the new ballroom is needed to "accommodate people for grand parties, State Visits", and has also said that it is "vital for National Security".

He doubled down on the need for the space after an assassination attempt at the White House Correspondents' Association dinner in April.

The three-judge panel on Friday said that its ruling "has nothing at all to do with whether the proposed ballroom is desirable", nor does it weigh in on whether the administration may ultimately construct the ballroom.

"What it does mean is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court's expeditious litigation without securing Congress's authorization, as the Constitution and laws require," the order said.

News.title: Streeting 'sickened' by sex abuse claims at Army college
News.content:
AFC is the largest military training establishment for under-19s in the UK and it receives all the Army's 16-year-old recruits.

North Yorkshire Police told the BBC in a response to a Freedom of Information Act request it had received 16 reports of sexual offences linked to the college in the year to June, including allegations of exposure, voyeurism and sexual assault.

No information was included on whether the reports had led to prosecutions.

A total of 176 complaints of inappropriate sexual behaviour at the college were made between January 2018 and June 2025, according to Ministry of Defence (MoD) data.

The women, whose names have been changed to protect their identities, all attended AFC over the last five years.

One woman, Tilly, told the BBC she was 17 when she was raped at AFC by several fellow soldiers who invited her into their room.

"They started taking my clothes off and then this led to them doing stuff I didn't consent to.

"And then I was rapedâ¦ by multiple junior soldiers, same age as me. It went on for hours. I felt like a piece of meat."

Streeting said he sympathised with the women who had been "badly failed", and praised them for speaking up.

"We have a duty to uphold the very highest standards in uniform and to treat every woman with the dignity and respect she deserves", he added.

Earlier this week, Sarah Atherton, former MP for Wrexham, told the BBC that public confidence in the college could "only be restored through an independent inquiry".

Atherton, who previously served in the Army's Intelligence Corps, led a 2021 government review into the experiences of women in the armed forces.

Emma Lewell MP said: "If this was any other school or residential environment for children, it would have been closed down."

News.title: Record spells with no rain across parts of central and south-east England
News.content:
As the extremely dry spell continues across much of England and Wales, a number of weather stations have smashed their previous longest periods without rain.

It comes after the driest July for England and Wales, external since Met Office records began 190 years ago.

Already Wales and most of England are in drought, with parts of eastern Scotland in significant water scarcity.

Despite some locations receiving rain this week, not enough fell in drought-hit areas to provide any meaningful relief.

These include Wisley in Surrey, which has notched up 51 consecutive dry days and Coningsby in Lincolnshire with 42 days of no rainfall.

News.title: Six-hour train services between London and Stirling running with no toilets after fault
News.content:
A train operator is running services lasting more than five-and-a-half hours despite having no toilets available on board.

The Lumo trains run on the West Coast Main Line, covering the new 417-mile (671km) route between Stirling and London Euston.

Lumo, which is owned by FirstGroup, first warned about a "fault" with the toilets on a service from Stirling to Crewe on Saturday.

Some services have since been stopping for longer at stations such as Preston to allow passengers to get off and use toilets on platforms.

News.title: England footballer Ivan Toney charged with assault at Soho nightclub
News.content:
England footballer Ivan Toney has been charged with assault at a nightclub in central London.

The 30-year-old, who plays for Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli, was charged on 31 July following an incident on Wardour Street in Soho on 6 December.

The former Brentford striker, who started England's 6-4 win over France in the "bronze final" of the World Cup last month, has been charged with assault causing actual bodily harm and is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on 24 September.

A spokesperson for Toney said: "Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court."

After starting his career at Northampton Town, the striker had permanent spells at Newcastle, Peterborough and Brentford before moving to Saudi Arabia in 2024.

He was a surprise selection for England's World Cup squad but apart from the France game, his only other appearance was as a late substitute in the 2-1 semi-final defeat to Argentina.

News.title: Officer who led PC Harper investigation 'appalled' killers could be released early
News.content:
Speaking to BBC Breakfast on Friday, former Det Sup Blaik, who led the Thames Valley Police investigation, pointed to remarks by the judge who sentenced PC Harper's killers. Mr Justice Edis referred to their case of manslaughter as being "very close to a case of murder in its seriousness".

The former officer called for prisoners who were judged to have had a high level of culpability for a manslaughter offence to be excluded from the scheme.

Allowing them to walk free would "undermine" the judicial process and impact police morale, Blaik said, before urging the government to have a "long, hard think" about the case.

The former Det Sup left Thames Valley Police in 2023. This is the first time he has publicly shared his views on the issue.

Streeting said the government is taking the issue "extremely seriously".

"We should never have been put in a position where prisons across the country were so full-to-bursting that any government, let alone this government, had to contemplate the early release of people from serious convictions that have led to being in prison in the first place.

"We're not pretending this is okay."

He pointed to "strong controls" and supervision that will be in place for people released into the community and added that the government is "determined" to build more prison places and is looking carefully into the exemptions under the scheme.

In an earlier statement given exclusively to BBC Breakfast, former Det Sup Blaik said "like many people across the country" he was "deeply concerned and appalled" by the prospect of Bowers and Cole being considered for early release.

He said that because the "death of Andrew was such a serious and tragic case", Bowers and Coles should "not be afforded the opportunity" to be released early.

"Neither of them showed any remorse during their time in police custody or during their subsequent trial.

"I hope the Government takes account of the strength of public feeling on this issue, which has been both clear and widespread," he added.

Under revised plans announced by the government on Monday, prisoners who have committed rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from an early release scheme for England and Wales.

But those guilty of manslaughter may still be eligible.

An average of 150 people a year are sentenced at crown court for manslaughter with an average term of nine years. That means that in any given year there are hundreds of these offenders in jail. If they were all kept in, that would eat into the available spare beds - a number that is declining despite the massive prison-building programme.

If the government were to try to differentiate between different types of manslaughter offenders based on the specific nature of the crime they committed, that could be legally complex to deliver - and may in turn face serious legal challenges from prisoners who find their release dates changed.

Bowers and Cole were sentenced to 13 years for the manslaughter of PC Harper.

They will become eligible for release from prison after serving half of their sentences under the plans, instead of two-thirds.

The driver of the getaway car, Henry Long, was jailed for 16 years for the same offence. But Long will not be eligible.

News.title: Brothers jailed for killing man and injuring his son while racing cars home
News.content:
Following sentencing, Rhys' wife Caroline Jenkins, also known as Carrie, said in a statement she often wondered what difference it would have made to her family's future "if we'd hugged a little tighter and a little longer" when she waved them off that day.

She said, for her son, life "without a dad who was involved in everything you did is a hard adjustment" and it "carried an element of PTSD".

Carrie said Ioan was emotionally and physically scarred by the crash.

"It's impossible to convey the full impact Rhys' death had on us," she said, and there remains a "massive hole left in our lives by his unnecessary death".

Ioan, who broke both arms, and suffered a fractured rib and perforated bowel, said he wished his dad was still here to "watch me grow up and be my dad".

Rhys' youngest son, Gruff, was six when the crash happened.

In his own victim impact statement, he said he was in bed when police arrived to tell his mum what had happened.

After being told his dad had died, he said: "I ran out of the house. I didn't know where I was going. It was the worst feeling of my life."

The court was told Umar Ben Yusaf's car was not directly involved in the crash, but the "competitive" nature of his driving with Abubakr Ben Yusaf contributed significantly.

Judge Timothy Petts said the trauma the Jenkins family had been through in the last 21 months was "difficult for me to summarise".

"You have all been suffering with your own devastating grief but also trying to deal with the practical consequences of Rhys's death and Ioan's injuries.

"It has been an horrendous time for all of you," he told them.

Petts said to Umar and Abubakr Ben Yusaf that he was satisfied they were racing each other.

"Both of you were constantly riding your luck at high speed, completely unnecessarily, and eventually it ran out with appalling consequences.

"Rhys Jenkins never stood a chance because you were so close to him when you lost control. He was driving perfectly properly and did nothing wrong. He had no time to avoid the collision."

Sgt Sara John, from Dyfed-Powys Police's serious collision investigation unit, said: "The sentences passed today cannot undo the tragic loss suffered by Rhys's family."

She added she hoped the outcome "provides them with some closure as they begin to move forward with their lives, which have been changed forever".

"The actions of Abubakr and Umar Yusaf on that day were catastrophic. Their choice to drive in the manner they did shows their utter disregard towards other road users."

News.title: Madonna and Blur producer William Orbit dies aged 69
News.content:
Acclaimed British music producer William Orbit, known for his work with acts including Madonna, Blur, All Saints and U2, has died at the age of 69.

A statement, external released on Friday by Orbit's family and friends "with profound sadness" said he died at home on 23 July. No cause of death was given.

"He will be greatly missed by us and by so many whose lives he touched through his music, friendship and kindness," the statement said.

North London-born Orbit, who real name was William Wainwright, helped to reinvigorate Madonna's career in 1998 with the album Ray of Light, which blended electronic dance music and ambient techno with pop and trip-hop.

It went on to win three Grammy Awards and remains, for many people, the Queen of Pop's greatest record.

News.title: Police make further arrests as Thetford disorder continues
News.content:
Residents who did not want to be named have told the BBC about growing disquiet over the issue of housing.

There is resentment at the perception that asylum seekers are getting free accommodation in an area where young people are struggling to get their own homes.

There are also concerns about the perceived safety of women and girls, specifically around single adult men arriving and living in houses in multiple occupation (HMO).

People explained they had been "kept in the dark" and said they have not been consulted on the issue.

The average cost of housing an asylum seeker for one night in private-rented accommodation is Â£23.25, and Â£144 in a hotel - while subsistence payments range from Â£9.95 to Â£49.18 for each person per week.

Serco, a company which has a contract with the government to find properties that can be used for dispersal accommodation, told the BBC it was not able to comment on the number of asylum seekers or their locations in Thetford for safety reasons.

"We've been working closely with the Home Office and police to ensure that appropriate safeguarding measures are in place," a Serco spokesperson said.

"Such measures are under constant review, and we will continue to monitor the situation.

"We are aware of allegations relating to how address information has been made public and are currently investigating."

News.title: Girl, 11, found dead after search at Midlothian beauty spot
News.content:
An 11-year-old girl has died after being found in the water at a beauty spot in Midlothian.

A major search was launched over reports of concern for the girl in Gore Glen Woodland Park, near Gorebridge, at about 12:40 on Thursday.

The girl's body was found in the park's Gore Water, near Shank Bridge, at about 16:25. She was pronounced dead at the scene.

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "Her death is being treated as unexplained and inquiries are ongoing to establish the full circumstances."

The force said the girl's family was aware.

News.title: Two firms guilty over man killed by falling window
News.content:
Two companies have been found guilty of health and safety breaches after a coach driver was killed by a falling window pane.

Mick Ferris, 53, died when glass weighing 130kg fell 300ft (90m) from a penthouse flat at The Corniche tower block on Albert Embankment in central London in October 2018.

St James Group Ltd and specialist contractors Lindner Prater Ltd were convicted at Inner London Crown Court of "failing to discharge a duty" under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974. The firms will be sentenced on 24 September.

Foster + Partners, the architecture firm behind The Gherkin, and engineering consultants Wintech Ltd were cleared of the same charges.

During the trial, the court heard the "extraordinary" fact that a window panel had already fallen from the same development in August 2017, and the design was not substantially changed as a result.

Prosecuting, Gordon Menzies said: "It's reasonably practicable for clever people to do a simple thing and design a window that doesn't fall out once every year."

News.title: Data breach investigation into Minnie Merriman's medical records
News.content:
NHS Tayside is investigating an alleged data breach into the medical records of a nine-year-old girl at the centre of a murder probe in Arbroath.

Minnie Merriman, from West Yorkshire, died at Ninewells Hospital in Dundee after being found seriously injured at an industrial estate in the town.

Her father has appeared in court charged with her murder.

NHS Tayside said it was "investigating the circumstances" of the alleged breach that happened in a clinical area where staff access patient information.

A spokesperson added: "As a matter of governance, any data protection breach would be recorded and investigated by NHS Tayside and, where appropriate, reported to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO).

"It would not be appropriate for us to comment further on individual staffing matters."

News.title: Divers find 162-year-old Guinness in shipwreck off the English coast
News.content:
How far would you travel for a pint of Guinness? If the answer is to the bottom of the sea, you might be in luck.

There's just one catch - the pint in question is 162 years old.

When Belgian underwater photographer Stefan Panis discovered a bottle buried in a shipwreck off the coast of Dover in 2025, he had no idea what he had found. He just knew something about it had caught his eye.

When Panis and his friend, Eddie Huzzey, surfaced, a quick rinse revealed the familiar Guinness branding. The bottle dates back to 1864.

"We lifted the artefact, and then on the surface a quick rinse revealed 'Guinness'," he said.

Panis, who has been diving for more than 40 years, contacted Guinness to share the discovery.

So far, he has recovered just one bottle, but believes many more remain buried beneath the sand surrounding the wreck and he already has plans to recover more when conditions allow.

News.title: Conor Benn makes surprising comparison between Ryan Garcia and Chris Eubank Jr rivalries
News.content:

Conor Benn has suggested his fight with Ryan Garcia will be more “personal” than his grudge matches with Chris Eubank Jr.

On 12 September, Benn will challenge Garcia for the WBC welterweight title, as the pair headline at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas.

The bout marks Benn’s first time fighting for a world title, and it follows his two domestic duels with Eubank Jr in 2025.

open image in gallery Conor Benn (right) stares down upcoming opponent Ryan Garcia ( Getty )

Benn, 29, suffered his first professional loss when he was outpointed by Eubank Jr in an instant classic last April, before dropping his fellow Briton twice in a decision win in November.

Both fights took place at London’s Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, and they played out three decades after Eubank Sr and Benn’s father Nigel had their own pair of duels.

“Beating Eubank, there will always be something special about that,” Benn told The Ring, “[and] there will always be something special about the first fight.

“I preferred the first fight over the second; it was a fight of the year, and only Eubank could have taken me there. I don’t think any other fighter could have taken me there. You know, it takes two to tango.

“For me, in terms of theatrics and drama and chaos, it was a movie – it was a real-life Creed,” Benn continued, referencing the sequel series to the Rocky films.

Benn then explained how his fight with American star Garcia will be different.

”Winning the world title is for myself, it’s very personal,” he said, “whereas the Eubank fights were for the family name, for family pride. It was for DNA, it was for bragging rights.

“This, for me, is for myself.”

open image in gallery Benn dropped Chris Eubank Jr twice in the final moments of their November rematch ( Getty )

Benn is a natural welterweight, although his fights with Eubank Jr took place at middleweight. He then boxed Regis Prograis this April, also in Tottenham, at a 150lb catchweight. Benn won that contest on points.

He will return to his preferred 147lb when he fights Garcia, who won the WBC title by dropping and outpointed Mario Barrios in May.

That win followed the second pro loss of Garcia’s career, an upset defeat by Rolly Romero in May 2025. Romero dropped Garcia en route to a decision victory in Times Square, New York City, two years after “King Ryan”’s first loss: a stoppage defeat by Gervonta Davis.

President Donald Trump doesn’t have the authority to fast-track his new White House ballroom without Congress’s authority, a divided panel of appellate court judges in Washington, D.C., said Friday.

In the latest blow to Trump’s efforts to build the 90,000-square-foot addition to the White House, two judges on the D.C. Court of Appeals ruled the president must halt construction until he seeks Congress’s approval.

“Each President is a temporary tenant, not the owner, of the White House and its Executive Residence,” the judges wrote.

“We are aware of no instance in American history in which a President unilaterally and using privately collected funds demolished substantial portions of the White House that Congress authorized to be built and American taxpayers paid for. Until now.”

The court will pause the ruling from taking effect for two weeks to give the Trump administration time to appeal to the Supreme Court.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump has rushed the construction of his White House ballroom, claiming its necessary for national security purposes ( AFP/Getty )

Judge Patricia Millet, an Obama appointee, and Judge Brad Garcia, a Biden appointee, ruled in favor of the National Trust for Historic Preservation, the group suing the administration to stop construction of the ballroom.

In doing so, they agreed with a lower court ruling, issued in April, that found Trump overstepped his authority when he demolished the East Wing to make room for the new ballroom.

“This holding has nothing at all to do with whether the proposed ballroom is desirable, or not, as a matter of policy,” the judges wrote. “This ruling does not even necessarily mean that the Defendants may not ultimately construct the ballroom.”

“What it does mean is that the Defendants may not do so during the district court’s expeditious litigation without securing Congress’s authorization, as the Constitution and laws require,” the judges added.

Meanwhile, Judge Neomi Rao, a Trump appointee, said she would have sided with the administration.

The Independent has asked the White House for comment.

open image in gallery Last year, the president demolished the historic East Wing of the White House to make room for his new ballroom – sparking outrage from Democrats and members of the public ( Getty )

Last year, Trump announced he would build the new glamorous ballroom, without using American taxpayer dollars, to serve as an entertaining space for state dinners and events.

But much like Trump’s other D.C. beautification projects, the cost, scale and public understanding of the project have changed over time.

The cost of the ballroom has surged from its original $200 million estimate to $400 million – with some believing it could cost upwards of $600 million. While Trump has said private donations will pay for the ballroom itself, in June the administration transfered more than $300 million from the Secret Service budget to cover security upgrades to the White House.

The administration has continued building the ballroom as legal challenges play out, arguing the ballroom is essential for national security because they are building an underground bunker containing a military complex, a hospital and an emergency operations center.

News.title: Serial sex offender was free to kill two women because of police blunders
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

A "predatory" serial sex attacker was left free to murder two women because police and court blunders saw him released on bail allowing him to prey on other victims.

The Metropolitan Police, British Transport Police (BTP), and Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) are all face serious questions over how Simon Levy was allowed to grope, rape and murder women between February 2023 and August 2025, after he was found guilty of murdering two women and raping a third on Friday.

The timeline of his escalating crimes reveals a string of errors where officials failed to stop a dangerous predator who was already a registered sex offender.

Levy, of Tottenham, north London, was found guilty by a jury at the Old Bailey on Friday for murdering Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, and Sheryl Wilkins, 39, five months apart last year.

The 40-year-old suffocated both women in sexually motivated attacks, with Ms Valencia-Trujillo found in a largely abandoned block of flats on the Aylesbury estate in south-east London, and Ms Wilkins behind a car park wall near Tottenham High Road, north London.

He was also convicted of two counts of rape and assault occasioning grievous bodily harm (GBH) with intent, as well as non-fatal suffocation over a brutal sex attack in January 2025, which the victim survived.

The car park was also where Levy carried out the January rape, which left the victim unconscious with a broken collarbone.

open image in gallery Levy had already been sentenced for 11 counts of sexual assault at an earlier trial ( Metropolitan Police )

The timeline of Levy’s offending reveals successive blunders from the Metropolitan Police, the British Transport Police (BTP) and prosecutors.

Members of the victims’ families burst into tears as the verdict was delivered after the jury deliberated for 13 hours.

Levy was brought into police custody for questioning on September 4 and charged soon after.

Prosecutor Will Martin said his desire to sexually assault women was “on the verge of compulsive or pathological”.

Speaking outside the Old Bailey, Detective Chief Inspector Neil John, from Scotland Yard, said: “Simon Levy is a dangerous and predatory offender. His crimes were calculated, cruel and deeply disturbing.

“Throughout the trial, he has shown complete disregard for the victims and victim-survivor, despite being fully aware of the lasting and devastating impact of his actions.”

Flanked by Ms Wilkins’s two sisters and the daughter of Ms Valencia-Trujillo, he appealed for any more victim-survivors of Levy who have yet to come forward to contact the police.

Ms Valencia-Trujillo’s children described her as a “big character” and “full of life”. She became a grandmother in 2024 and was said to be a “much-loved” member of the community with a love of salsa-dancing.

Mother-of-four, Ms Wilkins’ family said she was a much-loved woman and was missed every day by those who knew her.

open image in gallery Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo ( Metropolitan Police )

Jurors heard that Levy was already a registered sex offender. He sexually assaulted two women in 2018 and was jailed in 2021.

He assaulted a prison officer while in jail in 2022, then once released groped a woman on the Tube in October 2023, three more in October the following year, and beat and raped another in January 2025, before he murdered Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo in March 2025.

He then sexually assaulted six more women on the Tube – one in March, three in April and two in May 2025, before he murdered Sheryl Wilkins in August last year.

open image in gallery Sheryl Wilkins ( Metropolitan Police )

Jurors saw through his claims that all the contact had somehow been accidental on wobbly or crowded trains, or after he became partially sighted in May 2024.

He would grope the young women he had chosen as victims, with some reacting angrily when they realised what had happened.

One called him a pervert and emptied a can of coke over him, while another shouted at him not to touch her.

He was convicted of 10 counts of sexual assault on the Tube, and an 11th at Brixton prison, by a jury at Inner London Crown Court on February 4.

An Old Bailey jury reached verdicts after deliberating for 13 hours.

Levy, who wore sunglasses in court, made no reaction as the verdicts were delivered.

At the time charges were laid, Commander Clair Kelland, who leads the Met’s Public Protection Team, said: “As the lead for public protection at the Met, one of our main priorities is to better protect women and girls.

“The investigation into Simon Levy is one of great complexity. We are working closely with partners across relevant boroughs, including Haringey and Southwark, to encourage reporting and raise awareness of the support we can provide to victim-survivors.

“Whether you are a victim-survivor, or someone with information, we urge you to come forward and speak to us.”

open image in gallery Simon Levy, 40, was arrested on September 4 ( Metropolitan Police )

open image in gallery Levy was found guilty by a jury at the Old Bailey on Friday ( Metropolitan Police )

An Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) spokesperson said: “Our independent investigation began in January following a voluntary conduct referral from the force, relating to alleged failures by two officers in his management following his prison release on licence in February 2023.

“We are investigating the management of Simon Levy from his first conviction in September 2021 up to his arrest in September 2025.

“We are examining whether action could or should have been taken to prevent his reoffending, and if all officers involved in his management followed policies, procedures, and training.

“We are also assessing whether any learning, whether individual, force-wide, or nationally or other changes should be implemented in light of the events under investigation.

“At this stage, we have served a gross misconduct notice on a police constable and a misconduct notice on a detective sergeant, which means that the actions of those officers are under investigation.

“The serving of conduct notices does not necessarily mean disciplinary proceedings will follow.”

People can contact the Metropolitan Police’s incident room directly on 07751 700 330 or anonymously via Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

News.title: Leicestershire prison officer jailed over relationship with ‘Latvian Pablo Escobar’
News.content:
