Sports.title: Injury crisis and a transfer embargo... welcome to life as a manager, Aaron Ramsey! Former Arsenal star excited for new start as Oxford United boss
Sports.content:
Injury crisis and a transfer embargo... welcome to life as a manager, Aaron Ramsey! Former Arsenal star excited for new start as Oxford United boss

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Aaron Ramsey was barely a fortnight into his first managerial role when Oxford United confirmed they had been placed under a transfer embargo for failing to comply with the EFL's new salary rules.

Welcome to the new job, Aaron. You simply can't absorb that sort of rug-pulled-from-under-feet sensation by reading the manuals or attending coaching workshops.

A few days later, Frankie Kent, a centre-half signed on a free from Hearts and the only summer recruit Oxford made before the transfer ban hit, damaged cruciate knee ligaments in training and underwent an operation that will rule him out for most of the season.

Ramsey could have been excused for checking the small print in the contract.

'Absolutely not,' he said at a press briefing on Friday, as he confirmed more injury setbacks with left back Ruben Roosken and South Korea international striker Jeon Jin-woo both ruled out for two to three months. 'We're fully committed, me and my staff. We came here to work with these players and our focus is on them.'

Ramsey says he has not spoken to Mikel Arteta, his friend and former Arsenal teammate, since taking the Oxford job, although they share a similar manner in front of the cameras.

Aaron Ramsey is looking forward to his first managerial role at Oxford United despite the club being placed under a transfer embargo just weeks after his appointment

Oxford have also seen their preparations for the new season hit by a series of injuries

Like Arteta, Ramsey is perfectly polite and yet guarded and brisk. He moves quickly through the room to his seat with a flurry of handshakes, fields the questions without giving much away, smiles, says thanks and disappears with even greater speed.

Perhaps this is the survival mode for modern managers. It hasn't done Arteta any harm.

Ramsey has worked out his own protection techniques having spent 20 of his 35 years amid the glare of expectation.

He was a wonderkid who made his Cardiff debut at 16. He had played in an FA Cup final, joined Arsenal and won his first Wales cap before he was 18.

He was still only 19 when his career was almost ended by a horrific leg break, an impact so painful he revealed this week that he dislocated his jaw screaming.

Ramsey will always have a metal rod in his right leg as a reminder of that day in Stoke, but his recovery and success at Arsenal, winning the FA Cup three times and scoring the winner in the final twice, and 86 international caps, helping Wales reach the last four of Euro 2016, testify to his quiet determination.

'I'm immensely proud of what I achieved, especially since what I had to overcome,' said Ramsey. 'You don't always get the fairytale endings you want but if I look back at my career that's been a fairytale in itself.'

Seven years since leaving Arsenal, however, have been disjointed. A lucrative move to Juventus brought more medals but few plaudits and as he moved into his 30s, he became increasingly plagued by muscle injuries he suspects can probably be traced back to the broken leg.

Ramsey won three FA Cups during his time at Arsenal after recovering from horrific leg break he suffered at 19, which led to him having a metal rod inserted into his right leg

His former team-mate and current Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta had encouraged Ramsey to take his coaching badges early, helping him build towards a career in management

Ramsey had two years back at hometown club Cardiff, which ended with him injured and taking caretaker charge for three matches as they were relegated to League One

A loan to Rangers will be defined by his missed penalty in the shootout of the Europa League final. There was a season in France with Nice, two years back at Cardiff which ended with him injured and in caretaker charge of his hometown club for the last three games as they were relegated to League One.

THREE TIES TO WATCH THIS WEEKEND West Ham v Portsmouth Nine thousand Pompey fans are expected to make the trip to their first game at West Ham since a 4-3 defeat at Upton Park nearly 15 years ago. It could be a record first round crowd for the Carabao Cup with much attention trained on the directors’ box however with David Sullivan expected to attend the game. Sullivan still owns a 38.8 per cent stake in West Ham but stepped down as co-chair in June after historical allegations of sexual misconduct were aired as part of a BBC Panorama investigation. He denies the allegations. Mansfield v Sheffield United Mansfield humbled the Blades in the FA Cup in January. Nigel Clough’s League One team were 4-1 up inside an hour at Bramall Lane. They resisted a fightback to win 4-3, then knocked out Premier League Burnley out before giving champions-to-be Arsenal a scare in the Fifth Round. Can the Stags do it again? Salford v Shrewsbury Salford City will be a little less Manchester United and a little more Dundee United this season after finally relenting to pressure from supporters to revert to their original orange-and-black home colours, 12 years after the Class of 92 takeover changed the colours to red.

And last season in Mexico where he suffered the ordeal of losing his beloved dog Halo from the family ranch before his decision to retire in March.

Little wonder he is relishing this new direction with the chance to sink his teeth into coaching challenges.

'It's something I've been building up to for a few years off the field,' said Ramsey. 'I had a conversation with Arteta when we were playing. He did his coaching badges towards the end of his career and said he wished he'd done it earlier because he started to see the game differently.

'So, it was important for me to take that advice at the time and do my badges in the last years of my career, which I did. And I'm grateful for opportunities I've had to coach in and out at Cardiff U18s in an unofficial role and in and around the Wales camp with Craig Bellamy allowing me to gain experience.

'That confirmed to me the direction I wanted to take. I'm more than ready for this.

'I think one of my strengths as a player was that I didn't get too high or too low. I'm fairly level, consistent in what I want to do and how I handle emotions. I'm calm but confident.'

After four wins in four pre-season friendlies, Oxford's season starts with a Carabao Cup tie at Leyton Orient before a League One opener at home to Milton Keynes Dons.

'I'm very excited to get stuck into the season,' said Ramsey, despite the complications.

Oxford expect to be compliant with the new salary rules and out of the embargo by January at the latest and the new boss swears there is no way he will be tempted to pull his boots on again. Not even if injuries continue to bite.

'Absolutely not,' said Ramsey. 'No, my playing days are firmly finished.'

Sports.title: Two viral sensations have joined South American giants, an Argentina villain now at Chelsea and the Aussie teenager set for a record move - how breakout stars are making the most of their World Cup fame
Sports.content:
Older football fans were wistful heading into the World Cup by suggesting the tournament no longer surprises us with players that people have been previously unaware of.

Gone were the days when an unheralded or young player would emerge from seemingly nowhere, leading to some of the world's biggest clubs falling over themselves in the hope of signing them.

With matches and data so accessible now, it was felt that clubs merely use the World Cup now as confirmation on what they already know about players. It is certainly the case with several of the transfers to have taken place post tournament, with clubs moving for targets they had targeted prior to the World Cup.

Yet the case of Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha has appealed to the romantics, with the veteran landing a move directly off the back of his performances in the United States.

On Sunday, fans of Chilean giants Colo-Colo swarmed around the Arturo Merino Benitez International Airport to greet Vozinha, with their World Cup star having landed to complete a transfer.

Here, Daily Mail Sport takes a look at some of the post-World Cup deals with tournament stars looking to make an impact for new clubs following their impressive showings in North America.

World Cup cult hero Vozinha landed a move to Chilean side Colo-Colo following the tournament

Colo Colo fans waited outside the airport in Santiago on Sunday to welcome the goalkeeper

Vozinha

The 40-year-old goalkeeper finally sealed his post-World Cup move to Colo-Colo on Sunday after touching down in Santiago.

'I'm very happy to be here. And I want to thank the fans for the patience they've shown while waiting for me,' the Cape Verde star told reporters in Chile.

'See you at the Monumental Stadium.'

It completes a fairytale couple of months for the goalkeeper, who was one of the heroes of Cape Verde's surprise run to the last-32, before they were beaten 3-2 by Argentina after extra-time.

As well as keeping a clean sheet against Spain and Saudi Arabia, Vozinha made 18 saves across the tournament and outperformed his xG against by 0.9.

His standout performances were among the highlights of Cape Verde's debut appearance at the World Cup.

At the start of the Spain match in Cape Verde's World Cup opener, he only had 50,000 followers on Instagram, but after making a memorable seven saves, that number dramatically increased, with Vozinha now having 28.6million followers.

Vozinha was named in FIFA's team of the tournament to complete a remarkable rise.

His move to Colo-Colo is the most high-profile of his career, after playing for clubs in his homeland, Moldova, Slovakia, Cyprus and Portugal's second tier.

Vozinha will now look to help Colo-Colo win the league title during his six-month contract, which includes an option of a 12-month extension.

Vozinha was catapulted to fame after his performances against Spain and Argentina

Ismael Saibari

Bayern Munich were keen to stress that their £43million signing of Morocco star Saibari had been part of their long-term planning, rather than a reaction to his World Cup displays.

'We're delighted to have secured the services of Ismael Saibari, one of the most exciting forwards at the World Cup,' said Max Eberl, FC Bayern board member for sport, when Saibari's move was made official on July 1.

'Transfers like this don't happen on the spur of the moment but are the result of long-term planning: the key factor was that we made our position clear to him early on because we were aware of Ismael's skills and were able to show him a clear future with us from the start.

'Ismael Saibari will bring extra quality and unpredictability to our attacking play.'

Saibari had led the line for Morocco at the World Cup, with the versatile attacker scoring in all three of their group stage matches.

He was forced off injured in their last-16 win over Canada, resulting in the 25-year-old having to watch from the stands as Morocco lost to France in the quarter-finals.

Saibari had come into the tournament off the back of being named as the Player of the Year in the Eredivisie, having helped PSV Eindhoven secure a third consecutive title.

The Moroccan has now reported to training with Bayern and will be looking to make an impact in the Bundesliga.

Bayern Munich completed the signing of Moroccan World Cup star Ismael Saibari for £43m

Bayern were keen to stress that Saibari was part of their long-term planning, rather than a reaction to his impressive World Cup displays

Valentin Barco

Chelsea's signing of Barco was confirmed after the World Cup, but was agreed long before it.

Daily Mail Sport reported back in May that the Blues had agreed to sign the former Brighton full back from their sister club Strasbourg – a 13th deal between the two BlueCo clubs.

Barco, who had been playing as a midfielder in Ligue 1, had earned a call-up to Argentina's World Cup squad off the back of his performances last season.

The 22-year-old had limited involvement for Argentina on their path to the World Cup final, featuring for just 19 minutes in a group stage match against Jordan.

That still did not stop Barco making an impact on the pitch, with the Argentina hitting the headlines when he clashed with Jude Bellingham after England's semi-final defeat at the World Cup.

Barco infuriated the Three Lions after he sprinted across the pitch when Enzo Fernandez equalised late on in the clash.

He ran right in front of several England players and appeared to taunt them, before John Stones reacted by giving him a shove. Barco later also came onto the pitch in the aftermath of Lautaro Martinez's winning goal.

There were also reports that the new Chelsea star had been winding up the England bench for the entirety of the 90 minutes.

In response to his antics, Bellingham gave the 22-year-old a slap on the back of the head after the full-time whistle as Argentina's players celebrated, causing a scuffle on the pitch.

The reception Barco receives from English crowds this season will be interesting, while Chelsea fans will be hoping he can make an impact on the field of play.

Chelsea confirmed the signing of World Cup villain Valentin Barco on a seven-year deal

Barco's provocative celebrations irked England's Jude Bellingham after their semi-final clash

Bellingham slapped Barco on the back of the head following his overzealous celebrations

Johan Manzambi

'I am very, very happy and I am excited to play with this club,' Manzambi said after sealing his move from Freiburg to Aston Villa.

'It's a very big club in England, and they're playing in the Champions League. I've already played against Aston Villa, and for me, it was the perfect plan.

'I hope I can play the same as in the World Cup and with Freiburg.

'I'm sure that with the team, the coach and the staff that I can do the same.'

Manzambi opted for the move to Villa Park over Newcastle, despite the Magpies having a £49million bid accepted and had verbal agreement on terms with the 20-year-old.

The Swiss international had been one of the breakout stars of the World Cup, having initially begun the tournament as an impact substitute before forcing his way into a starting role.

Manzambi scored three goals and provided two assists until his tournament was cruelly ended by a knee injury.

While Manzambi played higher up the pitch for Switzerland, Aston Villa highlighted how he operated in a more deep-lying role for Freiburg. The midfielder had impressed Aston Villa during their preparations for the Europa League Final, even though Freiburg were beaten 3-0 by Unai Emery’s side in May.

Manzambi will be a central player in Aston Villa's revamped team this summer, with Morgan Rogers and Youri Tielemans having left the club and Amadou Onana out for a prolonged period with a knee injury.

Johan Manzambi began the World Cup on the bench before becoming a breakout star

The Swiss midfielder, who snubbed Newcastle, will be a key part of Aston Villa's new look midfield

Tim Payne

Like Vozinha, Payne was catapulted to fame at the World Cup where the New Zealander became a viral sensation.

Argentine content creator called Valen Scarsini, known as 'El Scarso', set out to find a player at the 48-team tournament in the US, Mexico and Canada who was unheralded and unknown for most fans.

He then wanted to see just how far his mission to make the player famous could go.

Payne ended up being his pick because the Wellington Phoenix centre-back only had 5,000 followers on Instagram.

Scarsini's bizarre campaign led to Payne's follower count exploding, with the 32-year-old now boasting over 5.6million followers.

The interest of a South American audience to Payne and New Zealand's World Cup campaign carried on, with the defender landing himself a transfer as a result.

Club Olimpia, Paraguay's biggest club, signed Payne ahead of the All Whites' first match of the tournament, reportedly paying £430,000 to Wellington Phoenix for his signature.

'Club Olimpia is one of the biggest clubs in South America, with an incredible history, passionate supporters and ambitions that match its stature, and I am looking forward to rising to that challenge,' Payne said when confirming his move.

'For our family, this is something really special. My son, growing up speaking Spanish like his mum did, immersing ourselves in her culture and her family's world is what makes this so much more than just a football move.'

Payne had also made the point of thanking Scarsini and his followers for their role in his life-changing move.

Payne made his debut for Olimpia on Sunday and marked it with a goal, curling a superb effort into the top corner from the edge of the box.

New Zealand's Tim Payne became a viral sensation after an Argentina influencer encouraged fans to follow him on Instagram, taking his followers from 5,000 to over 5.4million

⚽️¡QUÉ GOLAZO! Tim Payne debutó con la camiseta franjeada y en pocos minutos marcó este golazo.



📺Tigo Sports



▶️Viví el #ClausuraAPF2026 en https://t.co/pGNhXoLRh7 pic.twitter.com/zmObqWdI5i — Tigo Sports (@TigoSportsPY) August 2, 2026

Payne secured a move to Paraguyan side Olimpia after his profile was raised and marked his debut for the club with a superb goal on Sunday

Lucas Herrington

Herrington saw his World Cup end in heartbreaking fashion after sending a penalty over the crossbar in Australia's shootout defeat by Egypt in the last-32.

The 18-year-old was quickly offered support by Sweden great Zlatan Ibrahimovic, who praised his courage in stepping up to take the penalty at such a young age.

'Penalty is like lottery. You score, you become a hero, you don't score, sadly you become zero,' Ibrahimovic said.

'I just want to reach out to Herrington. You're 18 years old, you're young, this is just the beginning of your career.

'You stepping up there, you showed a lot of courage, not everybody will do that. My friend, you're the best. Don't listen to the rest. Listen, Herrington, if you want to reach out, I'm here.'

Exactly one month on and Herrington is closing in on a move from Colorado Rapids to the Premier League, with the teenager set to become the most expensive Australian player in history at around £17million.

Lucas Herrington suffered heartbreak after missing his penalty in Australia's shootout loss to Egypt

The teenage Australian defender is now expected to complete a move to Hull City

Herrington, who earned praise for his composed performances at the World Cup, is expected to seal a move to newly promoted Hull City, with their owner Acun Ilicali confirming their interest to the BBC on Saturday.

Asked if Herrington was someone Hull were looking at, Ilicali said: 'Yes.

'He's (got) very big potential. Very young boy. I think (a) future star. We are very close, very close.'

Asked when he thought a decision might be made on Herrington, Ilicali said: 'One week.'

Sports.title: Inside Jake Paul's plot to overthrow the UFC: How influencer plans to recruit Dana White's biggest stars... and hand an olive branch to Ronda Rousey
Sports.content:
Inside Jake Paul's plot to overthrow the UFC: How influencer plans to recruit Dana White's biggest stars... and hand an olive branch to Ronda Rousey

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Jake Paul has never been shy about declaring war on the establishment.

He has spent years accusing Dana White of underpaying fighters, publicly challenged the UFC president on everything from athlete welfare to revenue sharing and repeatedly insisted there is room for a genuine rival in mixed martial arts.

Now, he believes he finally has one.

This week, Most Valuable Promotions (MVP) completed a landmark merger with the Professional Fighters League (PFL), creating a combat sports company that combines boxing, MMA and entertainment under one banner.

The PFL name will gradually disappear over the coming months before being retired completely in January 2027, when the organization officially becomes MVP MMA. The combined company boasts almost 400 athletes worldwide, blending PFL's roster with MVP's rapidly growing boxing stable.

It is the biggest structural shake-up in MMA since the UFC cemented its dominance more than a decade ago.

Jake Paul (pictured above) has never been shy about declaring war on the establishment

He has spent years accusing Dana White of underpaying fighters, publicly challenged the UFC president on everything from athlete welfare to revenue sharing

Nobody inside MVP is pretending Dana White's empire is about to crumble overnight. But behind the scenes, the ambition is crystal clear.

'We know we're not going to overtake the UFC in the near future,' MVP co-founder Nakisa Bidarian said. 'This is a long term plan and over time we can close in on their position and create a Nike-versus-Adidas dynamic, or a Pepsi-versus-Coke dynamic, over the next seven to 10 years.

'We started this company five years ago and have been pioneers in boxing and in changing the way people consume content. We delivered the first live professional sporting event on Netflix.

'When we decided to enter MMA, we always said that if it proved successful, we would do more. Now, we the advantage of world-class infrastructure, elite fighters and the leadership of John Martin as CEO of the overall platform. We are not here to mess around.'

The merger instantly transforms MVP from a boxing promoter into a genuine multi-sport combat sports company.

Former PFL chief executive John Martin now oversees the wider business as CEO, while Jake Paul and Bidarian remain on the board, with Bidarian continuing to lead MVP Boxing alongside the promotion's blockbuster events.

Yet while the structure has changed, the philosophy has not.

From day one, Jake Paul has built his business around one message: fighters deserve more money. That message now sits at the heart of MVP's long-term strategy.

Daily Mail Sport sat down with Nakisa Bidarian to talk about how he and Paul are looking to reshape the economics of MMA

'The focus has always been to give at least 50 per cent of revenue back to the athletes,' Bidarian explained. 'If you look at traditional stick-and-ball sports that operate with those kinds of revenue-sharing models, they've created enormous enterprise value.

'When athletes receive a fair share, they're more invested, more committed, the product improves, and there's greater alignment across the sport.'

The comments represent another direct challenge to the UFC's long-standing business model, where fighter pay has remained one of the sport's most fiercely debated issues.

But simply paying athletes more is only one part of the plan. MVP believes it can also create stars in a way its rivals cannot.

'It's about branding, storytelling, exposure, engagement and producing content 24/7,' Bidarian said. 'It's about presenting our athletes for what they are - some of the best fighters in the world.

'Nobody does that better than MVP and Jake Paul. Our first MVP MMA event was a tremendous success and this merger turbocharges our ability to build on that momentum.'

The next battle will be fought in free agency.

MVP knows it cannot approach contracted UFC fighters, but once those deals expire, the landscape changes.

Bidarian believes PFL star Dakota Ditcheva has what it takes to become a global super star

'In MMA, just like in boxing, if a fighter is under contract you can't interfere with that,' Bidarian said. 'You have to wait until they become free agents.

'For example, the 155-pound champion Usman, who fought on Friday night, has just completed the final fight of his contract. I'm sure the UFC will try to re-sign him.

'But whenever a fighter comes out of contract with the UFC, of course we'll take a look. If they're the right fit for us, and we're the right fit for them, we'd love to make that partnership happen.'

The ambition stretches well beyond signing one or two marquee names.

'Our goal is to become the Pepsi to their Coke, the Adidas to their Nike, and eventually make this a genuine two-horse race,' Bidarian said. 'Sometimes we'll be ahead, sometimes they'll be ahead.

'But make no mistake, there's a real opportunity for a fighter-first platform. Very quickly, we're going to establish ourselves as the leading alternative.

'And in seven to 10 years' time, MVP will be the culturally relevant, empowerment-driven brand that Gen Z, Gen Alpha and even Gen Beta are focused on.'

One major advantage MVP believes it holds is flexibility.

Former UFC heavyweight champion Francis Ngannou remains central to the company's plans

Unlike publicly listed companies, Bidarian insists remaining privately owned allows the organization to pursue aggressive deals without shareholders dictating every financial decision.

'We intend to remain a private company for the foreseeable future because it provides us with a level of financial flexibility that public companies simply cannot match,' he said.

'In many ways, I would love for the UFC to announce tomorrow that they were increasing fighter pay to 50 per cent of revenue. But they can't. Doing so would significantly impact their margins, lower their enterprise value and ultimately affect the wealth of their owners.

'We have the freedom to be more aggressive in how we structure agreements and attract the best talent in the world.'

The roster itself is expected to evolve rapidly. Former UFC heavyweight champion Francis Ngannou remains central to the company's plans.

'That's absolutely what we want,' Bidarian said. 'Francis and I have spoken several times. He's excited to get back competing. He already has a relationship with the PFL, so it's just a case of making sure everyone is aligned on how we move forward. But yes, absolutely, Francis Ngannou is going to be part of what we're building.'

Women's MMA will also become a cornerstone of the new promotion.

Bidarian revealed he has already spoken to former UFC superstar Ronda Rousey about the future of the sport.

MVP already enjoys a close relationship with Matchroom through their recent boxing alliance, and Bidarian believes the partnership could eventually stretch beyond the squared circle

'Ronda Rousey is the most dominant female combat sports star in history in terms of popularity,' he said. 'She'd be more than welcome to be involved in MVP MMA in whatever role she wants. I spoke to her yesterday and listened to her thoughts on what we need to do.'

He also believes the promotion already possesses its next crossover superstar.

'Women's MMA will be a major focus for us. We have Dakota Ditcheva, who I believe is the most marketable female MMA fighter in the world.

'She's still young, undefeated, an outstanding striker and has enormous potential. We're excited to build around that.'

There may even be opportunities for crossover with boxing.

MVP already enjoys a close relationship with Matchroom through their recent boxing alliance, and Bidarian believes the partnership could eventually stretch beyond the squared circle and into their 'talent agency'.

'Listen, if Matchroom's talent from their talent agency become free agents, of course we'll have those discussions. We have a great working relationship with Eddie and Matchroom.

'The two MMA athletes they announced - Tom Aspinall and Ian Machado Garry - are both under UFC contracts, so there are no discussions to be had there for the moment but should they become available that's different.

Bidarian revealed he has already spoken to former UFC superstar Ronda Rousey (winning her contest with Gina Carano above) about the future of the sport

'I do think there's a huge long-term opportunity for Matchroom and MVP as combined entities. That's not today, and probably not three years from now. But when you think about Eddie's position in men's boxing, what we've built in women's boxing, and what we're going to build in MMA, I think there's a very clear path to what's possible over the next five to 10 years.'

For now, the UFC remains comfortably on top.

Dana White has already dismissed the merger between MVP and PFL, joking that it combines 'two organizations that struggle to sell tickets', while TKO president Mark Shapiro has taken a more measured stance, welcoming legitimate competition.

But inside MVP, nobody is looking for a quick knockout.

Instead, Jake Paul and Nakisa Bidarian are preparing for a long fight – one they believe could eventually reshape the economics of MMA.

They are not promising to replace the UFC.

They are trying to become something the sport has never truly had before: a genuine alternative.

Sports.title: Top football executive linked with replacing Gianni Infantino reports FIFA president to Ethics Committee - following failed plan to sell the World Cup, overturning of Florian Balogun's suspension and award of Peace Prize to President Trump
Sports.content:
Norwegian FA president Lise Klaveness will report Gianni Infantino to FIFA's Ethics Committee as European football intensifies pressure on the FIFA president.

UEFA have already pledged to boycott FIFA tournaments so long as Infantino remains FIFA president.

And the head of the Norwegian FA, Klaveness - who has been mooted as a potential successor to Infantino - endorsed that position after their monthly board meeting. Former FIFA president Sepp Blatter is among those advocating for Klaveness to succeed Infantino.

The 45-year-old former lawyer will also submit a complaint to the FIFA Ethics Committee, which has the power to impose bans from football.

The complaint will not only challenge the proposed sale of a £3.1billion stake in the World Cup to private investors, but also the decision to award an ad hoc FIFA Peace Prize to President Donald Trump and the suspension of Florian Balogun's red card at the World Cup following alleged political pressure from Trump.

‘The board believes that we do not have confidence in Gianni Infantino. We did not have that in the last election and we do not have it now,’ Klaveness said.

‘There is no going back for Gianni Infantino. The international football community is very divided, and we must unite now.

Lise Klaveness has long been an opponent of Gianni Infantino

Klaveness spoke to reporters on Friday to explain the decisions taken at the Norwegian FA's monthly board meeting

Europe have upped the pressure on Infantino, with UEFA vowing to boycott FIFA competitions so long as he remains in post

‘We will ask the FIFA president to resign now. There is no doubt about it: there is a deep crisis in international football cooperation.

‘Irreversible transgressions have occurred,’ she added on the decision to complain to the ethics committee.

‘We have reached a situation where extraordinary measures are needed to create lasting change.’

UEFA are leading the charge to dethrone Infantino as FIFA president. However, the Swiss football administrator appears to retain support from Africa, South America and Asia - which is enough to fend off any leadership challenge.

Meanwhile, Mexico have broken ranks from CONCACAF's opposition to Infantino, reaffirming their confidence in the FIFA leadership.

UEFA's current refusal to play in FIFA competitions will cause the governing body significant commercial problems, potentially prompting Infantino to reconsider his position at the top of world football.

But the FIFA president has shown no sign of relenting thus far after being supported by the governing body's hierarchy on Wednesday.

Sports.title: Inside the new-look Birmingham City: How Blues' recruitment has been supercharged, their transfer wishlist, the coaching talents taking centre stage and why Chris Davies is shaking things up at rebranded HQ
Sports.content:
For the first time in many years, there is a welcome air of calm around Birmingham City on the eve of a new campaign.

Life has rarely been dull for Blues supporters in recent seasons. They have watched their club wobble on the edge of oblivion. They have witnessed Jude Bellingham, Wayne Rooney and Tom Brady at close quarters and marvelled at US owners’ Knighthead’s £2-3billion investment plans, including a 62,000-seat stadium.

Blues’ American owners have developed a rivalry with their counterparts at Wrexham that brought David Beckham to St Andrew’s when the teams met in September 2024.

They bought Jay Stansfield for £15million in League One and showcased a six-part Amazon Prime documentary a year ago.

This summer has allowed Blues finally to pause for breath. Although there will be more signings, so far they have spent less than £5million. The training ground looks different, so too the style of play. The approach to recruitment feels more measured.

Ahead of Saturday’s Carabao Cup tie at Swansea, Daily Mail Sport visited Blues’ base in rural Warwickshire to see how they are shaping up.

After a rollercoaster few seasons at St Andrew's, Birmingham City look set for a year of stability and solid progression

But ambitions remain high under the stewardship of Tom Wagner (left) and Tom Brady

What are the goals?

Promotion to the top flight remains the focus – but perhaps with a little more realism attached. When boss Chris Davies pointed out a year ago how few teams were able to bounce straight from League One to the Premier League in consecutive seasons, it did not fit the script.

When Birmingham won promotion from the third tier, there was a two-year plan to reach the summit – and ideally, it would happen instantly.

Though nobody will say it publicly, Daily Mail Sport understands that senior figures at Blues realise that it might not be quite that easy. There is an acceptance that promotion might take longer than the initial two-year forecast, though the expanded six-team play-offs should play into the hands of clubs like Blues.

Last season Davies stuck to his high-possession game and though it yielded excellent home form, Birmingham struggled on the road, winning only five times in the league and losing 13. Expect a more flexible style this term with Blues playing a more direct game, especially away from St Andrew’s.

This switch dates back to New Year’s Day, when Birmingham lost 3-0 at Watford and Davies saw a lack of strength – in body and mind. Like the Premier League, the Championship’s athletic demands have grown dramatically and, in some fixtures, Blues felt they were being physically outmatched.

In came Jhon Solis, August Priske, Carlos Vicente and Ibrahim Osman in January. The first three are expected to be key figures this term after having six months to adapt while Blues remain keen to re-sign Osman from Brighton.

Blues have added set-piece coach Scott Fry, whose input helped Lincoln score 30 set-piece goals in League One in 2024-25. After a spell at Rangers, he was snapped up by Blues and in the recent friendly against Barcelona, Fry took centre stage in the technical area at every restart.

Blues are keen to re-sign Ibrahim Osman after taking him on loan from Brighton last season

‘It seems to be calmer than it was last year,’ says Davies. ‘That’s not to say we lack ambition, but I think that calmness bodes well.

‘We know what we’re walking into – the players do, I do. We’ve got that continuity and it’s the best way to approach it.

‘There was a lot there last year, because of winning League One the previous season and I felt we deserved to finish higher than 10th – but it was a creditable finish. We went through the ups and downs and emerged stronger, so I’m hopeful and excited.’

What could happen before the window closes?

Davies feels Blues are well set at the back and in goal but the club are keen to improve the squad in midfield and attacking positions.

Following Craig Gardner’s departure as director of football in June, Blues are a little more methodical in their approach to recruitment and will rely heavily on data. Joe Carnall and Micky Moore are running the department as Blues consider a long-term replacement for Gardner. Keep an eye on the experienced Mike Rigg, currently working as technical director in the Blues academy and another who follows data closely.

Here, though, Davies sounds a note of caution. He has watched with interest as Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck have joined Chelsea this summer, while James Milner retired at the end of last season aged 40.

‘Football has gone "data, data, data" but it doesn’t measure character, personality type or leadership skills,’ said Davies. ‘There’s a very human side to it.

‘I worked with Jordan Henderson at Liverpool – he’s 36 now but he’s gone to a massive club like Chelsea and went to the World Cup. That’s because of his personality and leadership skills.

‘I am happy with what we have here,' says boss Chris Davies. 'We don’t have a team of mercenaries here for the money'

‘You have your ups and downs in the Championship. Someone could be outstanding on the data and you think, "Wow, he’s too good for this level". But what is he like when you lose three games in a week, or he’s not starting? Will he help the team?’

‘I am happy with what we have here. We don’t have a team of mercenaries here for the money. These players want to win games for this club. I’d rather have a worse player on paper but I know he’s committed, than someone who’s a better player but you’re not quite sure (about his character).’

How might the season go?

At heart, Davies is a coach. He has never been one of those managers to watch from the sidelines and leave sessions to others.

Before becoming Blues boss, Davies was right-hand man to Brendan Rodgers and Ange Postecoglou and loves to be – as the modern football buzz phrase has it – on the grass.

In recent times, though, Davies’ assistant Ben Petty is thought to have taken a more prominent role in sessions, allowing Davies to take a wider view of life at the Elite Performance and Innovation Centre (EPIC), Blues’ base near the picturesque town of Henley-in-Arden.

Visiting EPIC ahead of the Swansea fixture, the change was noticeable. Bare walls told the story of an imminent rebrand and there were fewer motivational quotations emblazoned on various surfaces.

NFL superstar Brady remains an influence behind the scenes and the logo of his performance and fitness company, TBRx, was still visible, although not as prominent as 12 months ago. Yet TBRx staff will continue to manage players’ recovery, which means reporting to EPIC the day after every game. No Sundays off for Blues players.

Much is made of the rivalry between Birmingham’s Americans and those at Wrexham – Hollywood superstar Ryan Reynolds and fellow actor Rob McElhenney. Blues leaned into that last season but this term, it may be a little different. It will be intriguing to take the temperature when the teams meet in north Wales on August 28.

Birmingham have a natural leader in defender Christoph Klarer but Davies is keen to share the responsibility around his dressing room

Davies is also keen for his players to take greater responsibility. In Christoph Klarer, they have a natural leader as skipper but he cannot do it alone. So during pre-season, Davies asked players to split into small groups to discuss certain topics – sometimes tactical, others technical or mental – and report their findings to the squad.

‘If it’s just me explaining things to them, it’s like you’re preaching all the time,’ Davies argued. ‘When the players speak, nuggets come from it that I find really useful. We did it during pre-season in Portugal. They have to have a voice.’

As well as Klarer, Blues have a natural leader at the top of the club. Chairman Tom Wagner has been absent from St Andrew’s since suffering a stroke in February. In an update last week, Knighthead wrote that they ‘expect to see (Wagner) at a match in the near future.’ That would be hugely welcome news across the club and fanbase.

Sports.title: Roy Keane and Micah Richards dress up as traditional Victorian gentlemen, perform pigskin keepy-uppies and enjoy a day out at the terraces as they turn back the clock for Sky Bet's new 'Game's Back' advert
Sports.content:
See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Roy Keane and Micah Richards have embraced football's roots by dressing as Victorian gentlemen for Sky Bet's latest 'Game's Back' campaign.

Revisiting football's earliest days ahead of the new Premier League season, the popular Sky Sports punditry duo donned period costumes as they took in the action from the terraces and showed off their keepy-uppy skills with a traditional pigskin ball.

Sky Bet's new advert, which officially launched on August 7, plays on the familiar 'game's gone' phrase often used by supporters looking back nostalgically at how the sport has changed over the years, from players refusing to celebrate against former clubs to the introduction of VAR.

The advert begins with Keane and Richard sitting on the sofa watching modern-day football, before the Manchester United legend complains that the 'game's gone' over a five-minute VAR decision.

The punditry duo then take a trip through different eras of football to discover that supporters were always questioning how the game was evolving.

Transported first to 1965, the pair complained about the introduction of the substitutions law before heading further back in time to 1891 to learn how fans moaned when nets were first attached to goalposts.

Popular punditry duo Roy Keane and Micah Richards have embraced football's roots by dressing as Victorian gentlemen for Sky Bet's latest 'Game's Back' campaign

Richards and Keane also showed off their keepy-uppy skills with a traditional pigskin ball

In one light-hearted moment, Richards shushes his famously fiery punditry partner while the pair watch on from the stands, poking fun at Keane's well-known habit of questioning changes in the modern game.

Sky Bet also shared behind-the-scenes footage of Keane and Richards shooting the advert, which showed off the duo's chemistry.

Keane said: 'One thing about football history is that people have always questioned changes to the game, but it's funny looking back at some of the things we'd never want to lose now.

'We had good fun bringing those moments to life.'

Richards added: 'Football fans love a debate and that's never going to change'.

'Game's Gone is a phrase that has engrained itself in football culture and beyond,' said Harry Phillips, Sky Bet Marketing Director.

'Yet even though we all love to moan about the game, it's never been more universally popular and when push comes to shove, it's the incredible moments of football culture, both on and off the pitch that keeps us coming back.

Sky Bet's new campaign plays on the familiar 'the game's gone' phrase often used by supporters looking back nostalgically at how the sport has changed over the years

'We believe football always has and always will create moments no fan can resist. And at Sky Bet, we champion those iconic moments of football and fandom by giving our customers more ways to get in on the action.'

The new Premier League season kicks off with champions Arsenal hosting newly-promoted Coventry City on Friday, August 21.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Wilson key for Wales, NI aim for big upset while history beckons for ROI
Sports.content:
Sky Sports assesses Thursday's 2026 World Cup play-off semi-finals as Wales host Bosnia-Herzegovina, Northern Ireland go to four-time winners Italy and the Republic of Ireland face Czech Republic in Prague.

Thursday 7.45pm: Wales vs Bosnia-Herzegovina (winner will play Italy or Northern Ireland)

Harry Wilson is not the new Gareth Bale, but he's doing the job of Bale at his best, especially for Wales.

Fans have long been excited about Wilson's natural talent, but are now seeing his influence in the Premier League on a weekly basis for Fulham. This season, he has 10 goals and six assists for club, while for country, his stats are even better with five goals and two assists in his last five games.

If Wilson starts running the show, his confidence will feed to the other players and to the home crowd, and Wales will be very difficult to stop on their own patch.

Which World Cup group would Wales be in? If Wales qualify for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Craig Bellamy wanted to create an identity for Wales when he took over as head coach. It's now clear: he wants front-foot football coupled with intensity and energy.

Bellamy doesn't always see that in international football as he finds it slower at times compared with club football, but his Wales side will not be ponderous. You could see during the qualification campaign that Wales' intensity in winning the ball back very quickly and holding possession grew. Now it's about consistently doing it.

Apart from consistency in play, there needs to be consistency in selection. Much is always made about the 'spine' of a good team, from the goalkeeper to the glory hunter! Leeds United provide a fair chunk of Wales' spine with 'keeper Karl Darlow on form and in receipt of the No.1 keeper's jersey. Joe Rodon is the rock at centre-back that success relies upon, while team-mate Ethan Ampadu's versatility means he can link anywhere between defence and midfield. Throw in one of the in-form Premier League stars, Harry Wilson, and a strong spine can take a team a long way.

Ask Bellamy if he has thought about preparing for the play-off final against either Italy or Northern Ireland and you'll get glared at. It's Bosnia, Bosnia and Bosnia. He won't entertain anything beyond Bosnia until the game is over. It's a danger, a banana skin he wants to avoid. Thinking too far ahead isn't good on this occasion.

Geraint Hughes

Thursday 7.45pm: Italy vs Northern Ireland (winner will play Wales or Bosnia-Herzegovina)

On paper, perhaps in reality, it's David vs Goliath.

Northern Ireland enjoy David vs Goliath. Once upon a time it was David (Healy) vs England and David (Healy) vs Spain.

For smaller nations there is comfort in being the underdog. A loss would be met without a major backlash, a win makes you a hero. That's how Michael O'Neill's side will approach Thursday's assignment in Bergamo against Italy.

Which World Cup group would Northern Ireland be in? If Northern Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group B with Canada, Switzerland and Qatar.

Conor Bradley and Daniel Ballard are out. Between them they represent 50 per cent of the Northern Ireland players currently plying their trade in the Premier League.

The pair's absence is as much a blow to Northern Ireland's attacking prospects as it is defensively. Ballard represents their best aerial threat from set-pieces, Bradley their most dynamic player on the ball.

And yet for some reason that only football can explain, hope remains. The four-time World Cup winners are heavy favourites but far from the Azzurri powerhouse of old.

If Northern Ireland have it their way, it's unlikely to be a pretty spectacle. But can they frustrate their hosts? 0-0 at half-time? Pounce on the sense of angst that will exist among the home support?

To call it a free hit would be to downplay the importance of the game. But Northern Ireland are free from the weight of expectation.

Daring to dream of a result that becomes instant folklore.

Michael Morrow

Thursday 7.45pm: Czech Republic vs Republic of Ireland (winner will play Denmark or North Macedonia)

Image: Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson and captain Seamus Coleman spoke to the media in Prague

History beckons for the Republic of Ireland here in Prague.

Make no mistake, this will be the biggest game to date for a lot of these Irish players as they attempt to take another step to this summer's World Cup but they must get past Czech Republic to do so.

Which World Cup group would Republic of Ireland be in? If the Republic of Ireland qualified for the World Cup they would be in Group A with co-hosts Mexico, South Africa and South Korea.

Still coming off the euphoria of the incredible back-to-back wins against Portugal and Hungary last November, this is an Irish team full of confidence.

Having spoken to a few people around the Czech Republic team, those results have been noted and they are particularly worried about Irish striker Troy Parrott, who scored five goals in those two games in November - including the 96th-minute winner against Hungary.

Head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson spoke ahead of this game about one of the key aspects is visually and mentally being ready for the challenge ahead of them, he seemed as calm and confident as usual.

However his key selection dilemma is does he bring back the experienced, tried and tested players such as Seamus Coleman, Robbie Brady and Chiedoze Ogbene - all three have had limited game-time this season for a variety of injuries.

Coleman and Brady especially are the only two players in the squad who were part of Ireland's last team in a major tournament which was in 2016 - their experience could prove vital.

Image: Can Troy Parrott recreate his Irish heroics in Prague on Thursday?

Their opponents are in a state of flux.

Czech Republic have a new head coach who takes charge of his first game on Thursday, with West Ham's Tomas Soucek also being stripped of the captaincy after November's internationals having caused shockwaves in the local media - Wolves' Ladislav Krejci has replaced him.

The pressure feels like it's all on the home side which could play into Ireland's advantage as they look to take another step to qualify for this summer's World Cup - their first since 2002.

Danyal Khan
