What Empresas CMPC does. Empresas CMPC S.A. engages in the production and sale of pulp and wood products in Chile and internationally. It operates through Pulp, Biopackaging, and Softys segments. The Pulp segment produces and markets pulp, forestry, and lumber products to the industrial pulp mills, remanufactured products, and plywood plants. This segment also offers sawn…

CMPC: stable sales did not protect profit

CMPC’s first-half sales were almost unchanged at US$3.733 billion, but adjusted EBITDA fell 14% to US$525 million and the margin narrowed by 2.3 percentage points to 14.1%. Net income dropped from US$131 million to US$33 million. In the second quarter alone, net income was US$9 million, down 89% from US$81 million a year earlier.

Part of the fall reflects an unusually demanding base. The sale of TENSA added US$46 million to first-half 2025 EBITDA. CMPC also estimated a US$40 million first-half impact from higher Brent-linked logistics and production costs after mitigation and hedging. Foreign-exchange results deteriorated by US$32 million, although a US$38 million tax benefit partly softened the decline.

The portfolio was not uniformly weak. Softys, CMPC’s tissue and personal-care business, increased first-half sales 10% to US$1.728 billion as volumes recovered in Brazil and Mexico. That gain offset declines in pulp and Biopackaging revenue, but not enough to preserve consolidated margins.

Cencosud’s digital growth meets a profit shock

Cencosud reported second-quarter revenue of CLP 4.095 trillion (about US$4.44 billion), down 1.8% year on year. Adjusted EBITDA fell 15.8% to CLP 307.9 billion (about US$334 million), and the reported margin contracted from 8.8% to 7.5%. The company recorded a quarterly net loss of CLP 18.1 billion (about US$19.6 million), reversing a profit of CLP 103.0 billion (about US$111.7 million) a year earlier.

For the first half, profit attributable to controlling shareholders fell 79.6% to CLP 39.8 billion (about US$44.4 million). Excluding Argentina’s IAS 29 hyperinflation and currency-accounting adjustments, second-quarter net income was positive at CLP 21.5 billion (about US$23.3 million) but still fell 84.2%. Cencosud attributed the pressure partly to the non-cash inflation effect of UF-denominated debt on non-operating results.

Operating indicators were more resilient than the bottom line. Online sales rose 14.6% and generated 8.9 million transactions. Active loyalty customers reached 31 million, Prime subscribers increased 31.3%, and private-label penetration rose to 18.9%. Cencosud opened the first three Don Salva hard-discount stores and maintained its plan for about 40 locations by year-end.

What investors should take from the split

Santander’s result shows how an inflation-linked balance sheet can benefit when UF variation rises and credit costs remain controlled. CMPC’s figures show the opposite sensitivity: stable sales can still produce a sharp earnings fall when logistics costs, currency effects and one-off comparison items move against the company. Cencosud sits between them, with improving digital engagement but weaker reported profitability.

For international investors, the immediate lesson is sector selection. Santander’s upgraded guidance rests on profitability already delivered in the first half. CMPC must defend margins while energy and freight remain volatile. Cencosud must prove that its transformation spending, discount format and larger loyalty ecosystem can translate customer activity into earnings.

What to watch next

The next checkpoints are Santander’s ability to keep ROAE above 24% as inflation normalizes, CMPC’s pulp pricing and Brent-linked cost exposure, and Cencosud’s second-half margin recovery. For the retailer, the pace and economics of the Don Salva rollout will matter more than store-count headlines alone. For all three, Chile’s inflation path, consumer demand and exchange rate will continue to affect reported numbers in different ways.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much did Santander Chile earn in the second quarter of 2026? Santander Chile earned CLP 383 billion, about US$416 million. Profit rose 40.0% from the previous quarter and 40.4% from a year earlier. Why did Santander Chile’s profitability rise? Higher UF inflation increased readjustment income, while lower loan-loss provisions and cost control also helped. Quarterly ROAE reached 31.5%. How did CMPC perform in the first half of 2026? CMPC reported US$3.733 billion in sales, US$525 million in adjusted EBITDA and US$33 million in net income. Net income fell 74% year on year. Why did Cencosud’s first-half profit fall? Weaker operating profit and non-operating pressure, including the inflation effect of UF-denominated debt, reduced earnings. Profit attributable to controlling shareholders fell 79.6%. What is the main investor takeaway? Chile’s corporate cycle is highly sector-specific: inflation supported bank earnings, while cost, currency and accounting effects weighed on forestry and retail profits.

01 The session in one read

Brazilian stocks retreated on Thursday, with the Ibovespa losing 1.23% to close at 175,546 points. The decline was broad, touching commodity giants, big banks and recent market favourites, and it came just a day after local yields adjusted to the central bank’s decision to lower the Selic rate to 14%.

The real, however, wrote its own script. Brazil’s currency strengthened 0.20% to 5.1104 per US dollar, putting more distance between itself and the 52-week high of 5.5901 reached during an earlier bout of fiscal nerves.

The backdrop was a mixed global session—the S&P 500 slipped a tiny 0.18% while the Dow dropped 0.85%—but the local story was overwhelmingly about individual company reports. Petrobras delivered a blowout profit of R$52.4 billion for the second quarter, a 97% leap from a year earlier, while Bradesco posted its tenth straight quarter of rising earnings.

Yet good news on the earnings front was not enough to hold up the broad tape. Miner Vale fell 1.7%, Smartfit tumbled 7.8%, and even large private banks such as Bradesco and Itaú saw their shares decline despite reporting improved return on equity and contained loan delinquencies.

Assessment — A consolidation under the earnings microscope MEDIUM The breadth of the decline was notable, with large banks and commodity names sliding alongside a few high-flying growth stocks. The one clear positive was the real’s stability, suggesting that foreign capital is not yet fleeing despite lower local rates. The next stretch will be dictated by whether US payrolls data on Friday tilts the global rate outlook, and whether the flood of local quarterly reports—from Itaú to WEG—can offer a steadier handhold for the index after it ran into resistance well below its 2026 high.

03 Why it moved — rate-cut hangover meets earnings traffic

The central bank’s decision to lower the Selic by a quarter-point to 14%—the fourth straight reduction—is now fully absorbed, and the initial relief rally that greeted the move has faded. What is left is a market trying to gauge how much further the easing can run, and how quickly it will feed into company margins and consumer spending.

Earnings reports provided the session’s main flashpoints. Petrobras delivered a 97% profit leap to R$52.4 billion, powered by higher crude prices and rising production. But the shares managed only a modest 0.5% gain on heavy turnover, suggesting that a good chunk of the good news was already in the price.

Bradesco’s numbers were widely described as reassuring: net income climbed 16.2% from a year earlier to R$7.1 billion and return on equity—a gauge of how profitably a bank deploys shareholder capital—rose to 16.2% from 14.6%. Yet Bradesco’s preferred shares fell 1.9%, and Itaú Unibanco’s shed 1.3%.

That sell-the-news reaction in financials, combined with Vale’s 1.7% drift lower on softer iron-ore sentiment, was more than the index could absorb. The overall tone was not panic—it was a re-pricing of expectations now that the rate path feels clearer.

Among the few gainers, C&A Modas and TIM Brasil each rose 1.1%, while Petrobras preferred shares edged 0.5% higher on the session’s heaviest volume of R$384 million. The market’s cross-listed foreign trackers also saw heavy selling—MercadoLibre’s Brazil-listed certificate (MELI34) slumped 5.1%, mirroring the tech giant’s New York slide rather than a local Brazil story.

06 The technical picture

The Ibovespa’s 1.23% decline left the index sitting on a cluster of recent lows near 175,500, a level that has acted as a floor several times since early July. The 52-week high of 198,657, reached in February, now looks distant, and the market is trading 11.6% below that peak.

The 180,000 mark, a round number that also coincides with a minor resistance level formed in late June, is the immediate upside barrier. On the downside, the 173,000-174,000 zone is the next obvious support band—a break below that would open the door to a test of the 170,000 handle, which the index has not seen since May.

What is the Ibovespa?

The Ibovespa is Brazil’s main stock index, tracking the largest and most-traded companies listed on the B3 exchange in São Paulo.

Why did the Brazilian real strengthen if stocks fell?

The real firmed to 5.1104 because Brazil still offers high interest rates compared with developed markets, attracting carry-trade flows even as the Selic was cut.

What does the Selic cut mean for Brazilian stocks?

A lower Selic rate of 14% can help company earnings by reducing borrowing costs and boosting consumer spending, but it also reduces the appeal of Brazilian fixed-income for foreign investors.

Why did Petrobras shares rise only 0.5% after such strong profits?

Markets often ‘price in’ expected good news ahead of an earnings release. The 97% profit jump partly reflected higher oil prices, which were already known, so the share price reaction was muted.

03 Why it moved — Banxico holds, Wall Street hesitates

The August 6 session had two pulses: a cautious global beat and a steady local drum. On Wall Street, the Dow fell 0.85% and the S&P 500 shed 0.18%, with traders citing nervousness over a rebound in oil prices and uncertainty ahead of Friday’s US jobs report. Crude-tracking funds jumped more than 3% on the day. That filtered directly into Mexico through the heavyweight stocks that foreign funds trade most.

At the same time, Banxico removed any doubt about its near-term intentions. The five-member board voted unanimously to keep the key interest rate on hold for a second consecutive meeting. The accompanying statement showed policymakers believe inflation will not sustainably reach the 3% target until the fourth quarter of 2027—pushed back from the second quarter previously projected—making any cut before year-end a distant prospect.

That high-rate backdrop is a double-edged sword for Mexican equities. It keeps the peso attractive for carry traders—investors who borrow in low-yielding currencies to buy higher-yielding ones—but it also raises borrowing costs for Mexican companies. The result was an uneven session: globally exposed names such as Cemex and Grupo México fell, while domestic retailer Walmex and the regulated airport operators gained. Bottler and convenience-store group Femsa was the notable exception among consumer names, dropping 2.3%.

The split between global and domestic exposure told the session’s real story. Cemex, Mexico’s globally diversified cement producer, fell 1.9% on the heaviest share volume of the blue chips. Traders treat Cemex as a proxy for worldwide construction demand, so its decline reflected the broader unease about economic growth. Grupo México, the copper and infrastructure group, shed 1.3% as commodity nerves spread.

Retailer Walmex, by contrast, added 0.7%. It is a classic defensive name—people still buy groceries when the economy cools. Femsa, the vast bottling and convenience-store conglomerate that owns OXXO, was the exception, dropping 2.3%. The airports were the brightest spot: Grupo Aeroportuario del Pacífico (GAP) gained 2.2%, and Grupo Aeroportuario del Sureste (ASUR) rose 1.5%, extending a run of strength for Mexico’s tourist-facing infrastructure stocks.

06 The technical picture

The IPC at 66,396 points is stuck in a well-defined range. The index is 7.3% below its 52-week closing high of 71,601, but it sits roughly 14% above the 52-week closing low of 58,070 points. Chart watchers often focus on the 65,000 level as a psychological floor—breaks below that have been brief and quickly bought in recent months.

For the peso, the technical story is one of quiet strength. USD/MXN at 17.22 is about 0.55% above the 17.13 low of its 52-week range, which marks the peso’s firmest close of the past year. A concerted push down through that 17.13 level would signal a new leg of peso appreciation, but that would likely require a clear catalyst, such as a surprisingly weak US jobs print on Friday or a sudden dollar sell-off.

01 The session in one read

Chile’s equity market came alive on Thursday as the S&P IPSA added 1.05% to 11,275, its strongest single-session advance in recent weeks. Every pocket of strength pointed back to lithium: SQM-B, the local listing of the world’s second-biggest lithium miner, surged 3.7% and dominated both the turnover table and the mood.

That bright commodity pulse came alongside a slightly firmer peso. The Chilean currency strengthened to 913.86 per dollar, a gentle rise that sat comfortably with the equity rally as risk appetite firmed across the board.

Retail and banking names chimed in too. Falabella and Cencosud, two of the country’s most recognisable consumer brands, rose 0.9% and 2.0% respectively, while bank BCI produced the eye-catching 5.6% jump that lifted the financial sector. The breadth gave the rally a credible feel, even though copper—Chile’s traditional anchor—was not the main driver.

Globally, trading was mixed with US benchmarks edging slightly lower, but Santiago brushed off that caution. Local investors were busy pricing in what looked like a repricing of lithium demand prospects, a theme that has quietly tightened lithium carbonate prices in China and brought bargain-hunters back to Santiago’s flagship resource stock.

Assessment — Lithium spark, not a macro shift MEDIUM Today’s rally was concentrated rather than systemic. The IPSA’s 1.05% gain rests heavily on SQM-B’s 3.7% lithium-powered leap, with a strong second layer from a retail block. With the peso firming alongside equities, the market chose to focus on the brightening revenue picture for exporters. The volume—$26 million in SQM-B alone—was serious, but the concentration of the gains suggests this was a stock-specific catalyst rather than a whole-economy re-rating. The variable to watch now is whether Chile’s trade balance data on Friday reinforces the commodity optimism or exposes cracks that the equity rally has so far ignored.

03 Why it moved — lithium’s heavy footprint

The day’s central narrative belonged to lithium, not copper. SQM-B, the B-series shares of Sociedad Química y Minera de Chile, climbed 3.7% on turnover of $26 million—a figure that alone accounted for a substantial share of the broader market’s volume. Behind the move lay tightening physical lithium carbonate prices in China, the main processing hub for battery materials.

Copper, Chile’s more familiar macroeconomic heartbeat, traded in a quieter corridor and offered no sudden jolt. But lithium’s specific supply-demand arithmetic—limited near-term capacity expansions, robust electric-vehicle battery demand—has given SQM an upward bias that the market has learned to follow.

At home, the Banco Central de Chile’s latest business perceptions report, published earlier this week, suggested that most firms were holding staffing levels steady rather than cutting, though hiring intentions had softened compared with earlier in the year. The mix of cautious labour market data and still-stable demand gave consumer-facing stocks like Falabella and Cencosud room to advance without triggering immediate inflation anxiety.

A separate government announcement about forming a working group to promote service exports—specifically wealth management and investment administration for non-resident clients—added a subtle pro-business undertone to the session, even if the immediate stock-market impact was limited to sentiment.

The index remains inside a gentle ascending channel that has been in place since the June lows. With volatility gauges subdued and the VIX—Wall Street’s fear gauge—dipping a further 4.17% to 15.15, the external environment is not yet flashing the kind of stress that typically reverses a steady grind higher in risk assets.

World.title: Milei Clears Brazil-Argentina Naval Exercise Despite Rift
World.content:
Argentina · DEFENCE

Key Facts —The authorization. President Javier Milei’s Decree 717/2026 permits Brazilian naval personnel and equipment to enter Argentina from 10 to 24 August for the bilateral Fraterno XXXIX exercise. —The exercise. The drills run from 13 to 24 August at Puerto Belgrano and Mar del Plata naval bases and in Argentine waters between them. —The mission. Fraterno trains the two navies in combined naval, air-naval and amphibious operations, including antisubmarine warfare. —The legal route. Milei used an emergency decree because Congress had not considered the annual bill authorizing foreign-force entries and Argentine deployments abroad. —The Brazilian force. Annex I lists Tamandaré- and Niteroi-class frigates, the submarine-rescue vessel Guillobel and a Riachuelo-class submarine, carrying about 450 personnel between them, plus staff officers and specialists. —The cost. Argentina budgets ARS1.309 billion (about US$875,000) for the operation from existing Argentine Navy funds. —The contrast. Reuters reported, citing a Brazilian government source, that Brazil had reduced its representation in Buenos Aires to chargé d’affaires level after Milei again insulted President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

Milei approved a Brazil-Argentina naval exercise for August, keeping Fraterno XXXIX on schedule despite a sharp deterioration in diplomatic relations.

Milei Clears Brazil-Argentina Naval Exercise Despite Rift. (Photo: Internet reproduction)

What Milei authorized

Decree 717/2026, signed on 5 August and published the following day, authorizes Brazilian naval personnel and assets to enter Argentine territory from 10 to 24 August. Fraterno XXXIX itself is scheduled for 13–24 August at the Puerto Belgrano and Mar del Plata naval bases and across the Argentine exclusive economic zone between them.

Annex I lists a Tamandaré-class frigate with about 135 personnel, a Niteroi-class frigate with about 200, the submarine-rescue vessel Guillobel with about 80 and a Riachuelo-class submarine with about 35, plus Brazilian staff officers and specialists. It puts Argentina’s operating cost at ARS1.309 billion (about US$875,000), financed from the Argentine Navy’s budget.

Why Fraterno matters to both navies

Argentina and Brazil have conducted Fraterno annually since 1978. The exercise is designed to standardize planning and command procedures while improving interoperability in naval, air-naval and amphibious operations. Argentina’s decree specifically identifies antisubmarine warfare as a reason for participating.

The Argentine government argued that withdrawal would significantly weaken training for high-complexity tactical operations with Brazil. That language frames participation less as a diplomatic gesture than as a practical requirement for maintaining combined naval skills.

An emergency decree fills Congress’s gap

Under Argentina’s constitutional framework, Congress authorizes the entry of foreign troops and the deployment of national forces abroad. The executive had submitted a bill covering the combined-exercise program from 1 September 2025 through 31 August 2026, but lawmakers had not acted on it.

With the first Brazilian arrivals due on 10 August, Milei’s cabinet used a decree of necessity and urgency. The same instrument also authorizes Argentine participation in Viekaren XXVI with Chile and in Siforex XIV and Unitas LXVII in Peru. The decree must now be reviewed by Congress’s Permanent Bicameral Commission under Argentina’s DNU procedure.

Military links survive the diplomatic freeze

The timing gives the exercise political significance. Reuters reported, citing a Brazilian government source, that Brazil told Argentina relations would be handled at chargé d’affaires level and that Ambassador Julio Bitelli would not return to Buenos Aires for now. The move followed Milei’s renewed attacks on Lula during an Argentine television interview.

Argentina’s foreign minister, Pablo Quirno, said Buenos Aires would not answer with a reciprocal diplomatic measure. Milei and Lula have not held a formal bilateral meeting since the Argentine president took office in December 2023. Yet the decision to proceed with Fraterno shows that professional military channels can remain functional even when presidential diplomacy is nearly frozen.

Why this matters for Latin America

Brazil and Argentina share long South Atlantic coastlines. Their naval cooperation supports shared procedures in waters carrying regional trade and helps prevent a personal political conflict from spreading into every layer of the bilateral relationship.

For governments and companies watching regional risk, the distinction matters. Diplomatic downgrades can slow political coordination, but they do not automatically dissolve technical arrangements built over decades. Fraterno XXXIX is a test of whether that institutional insulation still holds under unusually hostile rhetoric.

What to watch next

The immediate test is whether the authorized Brazilian personnel and equipment begin entering on 10 August and the full exercise starts on 13 August as planned. Beyond the drills, watch the bicameral commission’s review of the emergency decree and whether Brazil keeps its embassy at the lower level after Fraterno ends. Any operational reduction or cancellation would signal that the political rupture is beginning to affect defense cooperation.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Fraterno XXXIX? It is the 2026 edition of an annual Argentina–Brazil naval exercise held since 1978 to improve combined planning, interoperability and tactical training. When and where will the exercise take place? Brazilian personnel and equipment are authorized to enter Argentina from 10 to 24 August. The drills run from 13 to 24 August around Puerto Belgrano, Mar del Plata and the Argentine waters between them. Why did Milei use an emergency decree? Congress had not considered the annual bill authorizing foreign forces to enter Argentina and Argentine forces to deploy abroad before the exercise dates. Has Brazil broken diplomatic relations with Argentina? No. Reuters reported, citing a Brazilian government source, that Brazil downgraded its representation in Buenos Aires to chargé d’affaires level and that Ambassador Julio Bitelli would not return for now. What will the two navies practise? The decree identifies naval, air-naval and amphibious operations, standardized command procedures and antisubmarine warfare training.

01 The session in one read

The Buenos Aires stock market fell for a second straight day on Thursday, with the Merval index—Argentina’s benchmark equity gauge—shedding 1.76% to settle at 3,100,732 points. The drop came alongside a modest but psychologically significant softening of the peso, which closed at 1,499.50 per US dollar, the weakest level of its 52-week trading range.

Trading was coloured by a sharp rise in Argentina’s country-risk premium, a measure that tracks the extra return investors demand to hold the nation’s bonds compared to US Treasuries. The JPMorgan-compiled index jumped more than 4% to 446 basis points, putting it firmly back on traders’ radar screens.

The catalyst was a sobering presentation by Santiago Bausili, president of the Banco Central de la República Argentina (BCRA), the country’s central bank. Bausili told journalists that the rise in bank delinquency was a ‘slow digestion’ that would take nine months to work through, and he categorically ruled out a government bailout for indebted households.

His message—that the adjustment is shifting from prices to the real economy—rattled banking stocks. Yet the session was not uniformly negative: YPF, the state-controlled oil company, rallied 2% after announcing the successful sale of two mature oil fields in Mendoza province, raising US$405 million to refocus on its high-growth Vaca Muerta shale operations.

Assessment — Reform trade faces a patience test MEDIUM The Milei administration’s economic programme is built on fiscal austerity, tight money, and a sacrifice of short-term consumption for long-term stability. Central bank chief Santiago Bausili reinforced that blueprint this week, rejecting any reduction in reserve requirements and describing the clean-up of bad loans as a nine-month ‘slow digestion’. That discipline is positive for long-term bondholders but creates friction for banks and consumers in the immediate term. The variable to watch is whether country risk stabilises below 450 basis points or continues its recent drift higher, which would signal that the market is losing patience with the pace of microeconomic recovery.

03 Why it moved — BCRA’s tough-love message jars with the market

Thursday’s decline was driven mostly by a repricing of Argentina’s financial stocks after BCRA president Bausili’s monetary-policy presentation. He explicitly rejected calls to lower reserve requirements on banks—a measure that would have freed up cash for lending—and said the priority remained accumulating central-bank reserves to anchor the peso.

Bausili also dismissed the idea of a ‘Plan Platita’, a colloquial Argentine term for a populist cash-splash ahead of elections. His language was clinical: the state would not intervene between banks and their delinquent borrowers. For a market that has grown accustomed to thinking the Milei administration has political pressures under control, the remarks were a sharp reminder that the real economy is still absorbing the shock of austerity.

Local media reported that Argentine households hold roughly US$7 billion in idle dollar deposits that cannot easily be lent out under the current regulatory framework. With bad loans rising, the banks are caught between restrictive rules and a central bank that is unwilling to ease. Grupo Financiero Galicia fell 3.5%, making it one of the session’s biggest drags by turnover, while Banco Macro also came under pressure.

A separate survey from the BCRA showed that private economists now expect July inflation at 2%, with a break below that threshold in the months ahead—good news on the surface. But the same survey pencilled in only modest GDP growth, and traders are increasingly focused on the lagged effect of the tight-money policy on corporate earnings.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Merval?

The Merval is Argentina’s benchmark stock index. It tracks the largest companies trading on the Buenos Aires stock exchange, weighted by market value and trading volume.

Why did country risk jump?

Country risk rose after the central bank president said there would be no state bailout for households struggling with bank loans, and that the clean-up of bad debt would take nine months. Investors interpreted the message as a sign that economic pain will linger.

What is a CEDEAR?

A CEDEAR is an Argentine depositary receipt—a peso- or dollar-denominated certificate that tracks a foreign stock and trades on the Buenos Aires exchange. MELI, for example, is a CEDEAR that follows the US-listed shares of MercadoLibre.

Why did YPF rise when everything else fell?

YPF confirmed it raised US$405 million selling two mature oil fields in Mendoza province. The deal is part of a strategy to exit older conventional assets and redirect capital to the high-growth Vaca Muerta shale formation.

01 The session in one read

Colombia’s COLCAP index — the basket of the country’s most liquid shares on the Bolsa de Valores de Colombia — added 0.24% on Thursday to close at 2,350.44. The gain was modest but directionally consistent with a session where buyers edged in cautiously, cheered by a firm crude market and a currency that outran every major Latin American peer.

The real action was in the foreign-exchange market. The Colombian peso strengthened 0.72% to 3,180.94 per US dollar, a standout move in a region where the Brazilian real and Mexican peso barely budged. At that level, the peso sits just 1% above its 52-week strongest point of 3,122, a sign that offshore funds are warming to local short-term paper.

Underpinning the mood, global crude prices held above recent troughs even as Gran Tierra Energy announced a full exit from Colombia and Ecuador. The US$1.33 billion sale to France’s Maurel & Prom is the eighth such departure, yet the market treated it as an isolated corporate story rather than a systemic warning, at least for now.

Trading on the equity side was thin. Turnover in Bogotá was too thin for any single line to set the tone, even on the most active names. Among the domestic blue chips that normally dominate — Ecopetrol, Bancolombia, ISA — the session was a holding pattern, with no name swinging more than a fraction of a per cent.

Assessment — Stable but unconvincing MEDIUM The combination of a rising peso and a barely positive COLCAP paints a picture of a market supported by external tailwinds rather than domestic conviction. The currency’s strength suggests foreign capital is creeping back into local TES bonds after their post-election yield spike, but equity volumes remain too low to signal genuine confidence in Colombian risk. The variable to watch is whether oil can hold its recent floor into next week’s local inflation data — a print above expectations would quickly test the peso’s newfound composure.

03 Why it moved — crude floor meets local exit

Oil is Colombia’s macroeconomic centre of gravity — it funds a significant slice of the government’s external revenue and shapes the peso’s fortunes. On Thursday, global benchmarks were stable enough to keep sellers at bay, even as headlines confirmed that Gran Tierra Energy had agreed to sell all its Colombian and Ecuadorian assets to Maurel & Prom for US$1.33 billion.

Gran Tierra’s departure makes it the eighth international oil company to leave Colombian territory in recent years, adding to a list that already includes heavyweights who have scaled back or exited over regulatory and security concerns. The local media covered the deal extensively, framing it as further evidence that the energy sector’s profile in the country is shrinking.

Yet the equity market’s response was notably composed. Ecopetrol, the state-controlled oil producer that is the single largest weight in the COLCAP, did not stage a dramatic move in either direction. That calm suggests investors had already priced in a gradual thinning of the foreign upstream presence and are now looking instead at the global crude curve for their next cue.

On the currency side, the peso’s rally drew additional support from a domestic bond market that has stabilised sharply since the presidential election. Local one-year TES yields have fallen by 123 basis points from their mid-May peak of 13.9%, according to La República, a powerful signal that institutional money is returning to Colombian fixed income. That bid for pesos to buy bonds almost certainly spilled over into the foreign-exchange market.

At the other end of the spectrum, Brazil’s Ibovespa dropped 1.23%, making it the region’s weakest performer, while Mexico’s IPC slipped 0.19%. The divergence within Latin America was stark — Pacific-facing markets caught a bid related to commodity stability, while Brazil continued to wrestle with its own domestic interest-rate narrative.

06 The technical picture

With the COLCAP at 2,350.44, the benchmark is slowly clawing its way off deeply oversold levels from earlier in the year. The next psychologically important hurdle is 2,400 — a level that, if broken on meaningful volume, would signal the first credible reversal in months.

On the currency chart, the dollar-peso pair’s break below 3,200 is technically significant. The pair is now approaching the 52-week low of 3,122, and a move through that floor would open the door to a rapid retracement toward the 3,000 handle, a level not seen since the early part of the decade.

Traders should note, however, that both the COLCAP advance and the peso rally are occurring on thin participation. A true trend change would require confirmation from local pension funds and foreign institutional desks, which have largely sat out the equity market in recent months.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the COLCAP?

It is Colombia’s main stock-market index, tracking the most liquid and valuable companies listed on the Bolsa de Valores de Colombia, including Ecopetrol, Bancolombia and ISA.

Why did the Colombian peso strengthen so much?

A combination of falling local bond yields — which attract foreign money into peso-denominated debt — and steady crude oil prices gave the currency a strong bid on August 6.

Was the Gran Tierra sale a big deal for the market?

Yes and no. It marks the eighth foreign oil-company exit from Colombia, which is worrying long-term. But on the day, crude prices held firm and Ecopetrol shares were steady, so the market treated it as old news.

Why does this report use New York listings?

Colombia’s three largest listed companies also trade in New York as ADRs, and those closes are publicly verifiable where individual Bogotá prints are not. The ADRs move with both the share price and the peso, so a 0.72% currency gain lifts them independently of any change in the business.

04 Copom and the macro backdrop

The central bank’s decision to cut the Selic to 14.00% was broadly anticipated, yet the post-meeting statement offered a dovish surprise by downplaying service-sector inflation risks. Fiscal friction remains a low hum rather than a roar. A fresh law criminalising deepfake content involving minors has grabbed political attention, while a queue of 32 provisional measures awaits congressional votes, covering everything from import taxes to export credit lines.

World.title: Is Costa Rica Losing Its Tourism Edge in Central America?
World.content:
Imagine that the seven nations of Central America are participants in a race. The race has no finish line. Instead it’s an ongoing competition to be the tourism king of the region. Until lately it hadn’t really been competitive. Costa Rica was a Ferrari surrounded by Ford Pintos. Most of our neighbors had too many internal problems– El Salvador was run by gangs, Guatemala hit a peak of over 6,000 murders a year, Nicaragua was-and is- run by aging dictators, Honduras and Belize lacked tourist infrastructure and Panama, with the canal and international banking, was indifferent.

We have been the tourism giant in the region for three decades for good reason. Combine amazing nature, a multitude of tour options, housing that runs the gamut from simple cheap cabinas to 5-star luxury, and a class of local workers that understand good customer service and you have the winning recipe to bring in visitors and keep them coming back.

Don’t be fooled by the ‘Tico Time’ label; in my twenty years in various branches of tourism here I found the vast majority of Ticos to be pros, punctual, knowledgeable in their field and appreciative of the opportunity tourism provides. And the ones who lack professionalism usually get weeded out quickly.

Costa Rica remains the top dog, but a quick glance in the rear view mirror shows some of our neighbors gaining ground. Both El Salvador and Panama reported record numbers the first half of this year. Guatemala just announced a “Sustainable Tourism Master Plan”. Nicaragua, despite being Central America’s worst dictatorship, has shown an uptick in visitors the past few years.

One obvious advantage all of these places have over Costa Rica is the cost of a vacation. I recently ate at a restaurant in Manuel Antonio. A standard cheeseburger with fries came to over $18 (in colons) with service charge and tax included. This outrageous overpricing extends to other services throughout the tourist reliant areas of the country. The abysmal exchange rate has turned Costa Rica into a destination out of reach for many who would have come here in years past when travelers got more bang for their buck.

And Costa Rica does not have the market cornered on natural beauty. The first time I flew into Guatemala City at dusk, the fiery sunset highlighted the volcanic ranges ringing the city, I felt like I was flying into Shangri-La. Add Lake Atitlan and the ancient Mayan city at Tikal, and you have a place waiting to be explored.

Panama, while not reliant on tourism, offers miles of coastline, great offshore fishing, the canal and the glittering city of Panama itself. Honduras and Nicaragua are also making strides, with Roatan in Honduras in particular being a great drawing card.

And now El Salvador has entered the conversation as it has experienced a massive tourism boom in 2026, hitting record numbers driven by major security improvements, surf infrastructure, and global events. While their tourism revenue numbers are only about half of Costa Rica’s, they are marketing the country as a safe destination with surfing, fishing, historical tours and more.

As for Costa Rica, we are seeing a shift in strategy. Visitors ready to spend more money and not concerned with the exchange rate and the comparatively high prices are being targeted in marketing campaigns. Raw numbers are not as important as the per capita budget of visitors.

The budget traveler, the backpacker, the camping on the beach surfer are still welcome, but may find our much cheaper neighbors more appealing. The present day Central America tourism pie is big enough to share. We can only hope that Costa Rica doesn’t price itself out of reach for not only tourists on a budget, but locals as well.

World.title: Cincinnati Open Opens This Weekend With Practices, Fan Events and New Attractions
World.content:
The Cincinnati Open will begin welcoming fans Saturday, August 8, several days before the first official matches are played, as one of the biggest tournaments on the North American tennis calendar opens with a full weekend of player practices, fan activities and special events.



The two-day Community Weekend at the Lindner Family Tennis Center in Mason, Ohio, will give fans an early look at players preparing for the ATP and WTA 1000 tournament before qualifying begins Tuesday. The opening weekend is part of the tournament’s continued expansion beyond traditional match days, with organizers placing greater emphasis on player access, practices and activities around the grounds.



For tennis fans, the biggest draw may simply be the chance to watch some of the world’s top players practice from much closer than is normally possible during tournament competition.

Players Take to the Practice Courts

Saturday’s Kids Day will run from 10 a.m. until 4 p.m. and include open player practices, tennis drills, autograph sessions, a scavenger hunt, live music and other activities throughout the grounds. Unlike a normal tournament day, when attention is divided between matches taking place across multiple courts, the opening weekend gives spectators an opportunity to follow players through their final training sessions before competition begins.



That could provide an early look at how some of Cincinnati’s leading contenders are adjusting to the hard courts and summer conditions in Ohio. The tournament field includes many of the biggest names in men’s and women’s tennis, along with a sizable Latin American contingent.

Brazil’s João Fonseca and Argentina’s Francisco Cerúndolo are among the leading Latin American men entered, while Colombia’s Camila Osorio headlines the region’s representation on the women’s side. Practice schedules can change and are normally finalized closer to the sessions, meaning fans hoping to see a particular player will need to monitor tournament updates throughout the weekend.

Red Bull BassLine Makes U.S. Debut

Saturday evening will feature a different version of professional tennis when Red Bull BassLine makes its United States debut on Grandstand Court. The exhibition runs from 7 p.m. to 10 p.m. and combines a quick-fire knockout format with music from a live on-court DJ.



Rather than playing traditional full matches, players compete in shorter contests designed to create a faster and more informal atmosphere than a regular ATP or WTA match. The event has previously been staged in Europe and Australia, with Cincinnati becoming its first U.S. location.



It will be separately ticketed from the daytime Community Weekend activities, although a BassLine ticket also provides access to the tournament grounds earlier Saturday.

Cincinnati Open 5K Starts Sunday

Sunday will begin at 8 a.m. with another first for the tournament: the inaugural Cincinnati Open 5K. The run will take participants through the tournament’s 40-acre grounds before finishing with a post-race gathering. After the race, All Access Sunday will run from 10 a.m. until 4 p.m. and include additional player practices, meet-and-greets, autograph sessions, live entertainment and a Center Court photo opportunity.



The tournament will also feature adaptive tennis activities during the weekend. Fans who want another day focused primarily on training rather than matches will have one final opportunity Monday, August 10, when the grounds reopen from 10 a.m. until 4 p.m. for player practices.

Competitive Tennis Begins Tuesday

The atmosphere will change Tuesday morning when qualifying officially begins. Gates are scheduled to open at 9 a.m. on August 11, with the first qualifying matches beginning at 10:30 a.m. The second day of qualifying follows Wednesday before the men’s and women’s main draws begin Thursday, August 13.

The tournament then continues through August 23, when both singles champions are scheduled to be crowned. Cincinnati occupies an important position on the tennis calendar because it is one of the final major tournaments before the US Open in New York. Players use the event not only to compete for significant ATP and WTA ranking points but also to test their games against elite competition under North American hard-court conditions.

That makes the practice sessions and early rounds particularly useful indicators of player form heading toward the year’s final Grand Slam.

Cincinnati Builds on Record 2025 Tournament

The opening weekend follows a record-setting year for the Cincinnati Open. More than 285,000 people attended the tournament in 2025 following a major redevelopment of the Lindner Family Tennis Center. The venue now includes 31 outdoor courts and an expanded campus designed to accommodate the tournament’s larger ATP and WTA fields.



The Cincinnati Open was subsequently named the 1000-level Tournament of the Year by both the ATP and WTA. This year’s tournament extends the experience even further by opening the grounds before qualifying begins, turning what was traditionally preparation time for players into several days of public access.

For fans, it also means the Cincinnati Open effectively begins before the first official point is played. The Tico Times will be there to provide on-site coverage and photography from Mason beginning August 13, following the tournament’s leading storylines and Latin American players as the field moves toward the US Open.

World.title: Cincinnati Open 2026 Guide: Dates, Players and What to Know
World.content:
The Cincinnati Open returns to Mason, Ohio, this August with one of the strongest combined men’s and women’s fields of the North American hard-court season. The tournament begins with public events and player practices on August 8 before qualifying starts August 11. Main-draw competition begins August 13, with the men’s and women’s singles champions scheduled to be crowned August 23.

Played at the Lindner Family Tennis Center outside Cincinnati, the tournament brings ATP and WTA competition together at the same venue. Both sides carry 1000-level status, placing Cincinnati among the most important events outside the four Grand Slam tournaments.

It also represents one of the final major tests before the US Open, giving players an opportunity to adjust to North American hard courts, earn significant ranking points and build momentum before traveling to New York.

When Does the Cincinnati Open Begin?

The 2026 Cincinnati Open officially opens with Community Weekend on August 8 and 9. The two-day program includes player practices, autograph opportunities, children’s activities, entertainment and the tournament’s inaugural 5K race. A fast-paced Red Bull BassLine exhibition is also scheduled for Saturday evening.

Fans will have another opportunity to watch open practices on Monday, August 10, before competitive matches begin. Qualifying will take place August 11 and 12. The men’s and women’s qualifying draws will each feature 48 players, with 12 men and 12 women advancing into the main tournament.

Main-draw play begins Thursday, August 13. Day sessions are scheduled to start at 11 a.m., with night sessions beginning at 7 p.m. during the early rounds. The singles finals will both be played Sunday, August 23.

Which Players Are Expected to Compete?

World No. 1 Jannik Sinner leads the men’s field and will attempt to regain the Cincinnati title he won in 2024. The Italian is joined by several of the sport’s biggest names, including Alexander Zverev, Novak Djokovic, Daniil Medvedev, Ben Shelton, Taylor Fritz, Alex de Minaur and Frances Tiafoe.

Defending champion Carlos Alcaraz will not compete. The Spaniard withdrew on August 4 as he continues to recover from a wrist injury. The withdrawal removes one of the tournament’s leading attractions, but the men’s field remains deep. Cincinnati has also awarded main-draw wild cards to Stan Wawrinka, Grigor Dimitrov, Jack Draper and Gael Monfils.

Wawrinka and Monfils are both competing in their final ATP seasons, adding another storyline to the opening rounds. Dimitrov won the Cincinnati title in 2017, while Draper has already established himself as a dangerous opponent on hard courts. The women’s tournament is led by Aryna Sabalenka, Iga Swiatek, Coco Gauff and Jessica Pegula.

Other prominent entries include Madison Keys, Elena Rybakina, Naomi Osaka, Mirra Andreeva, Linda Noskova and Jasmine Paolini.One of the tournament’s biggest attractions will come in doubles, where Serena and Venus Williams have received a wild card to compete together. It will be their first Cincinnati Open appearance as a team.

Venus Williams has also been awarded a singles wild card. Other women’s wild-card recipients include Sloane Stephens, Taylor Townsend, Caroline Dolehide and Lois Boisson. Player entries remain subject to change until the draws are finalized.

Latin American Players to Follow

The men’s field includes a sizable Latin American presence, led by Brazilian João Fonseca and Argentina’s Francisco Cerúndolo. Fonseca has quickly become one of the region’s most closely followed young players. His aggressive baseline game and growing international profile should make his matches among the most anticipated of the early rounds.

Cerúndolo arrives as Argentina’s highest-ranked entrant and one of the region’s strongest candidates to make a deep run. Argentina will also be represented by Sebastián Báez, Juan Manuel Cerúndolo, Tomás Martín Etcheverry, Mariano Navone, Román Andrés Burruchaga, Thiago Tirante and Camilo Ugo Carabelli.

Peruvian Ignacio Buse, Chilean Alejandro Tabilo and Paraguayan Adolfo Daniel Vallejo are also listed in the men’s field. On the women’s side, Colombia’s Camila Osorio will be the leading Latin American player in the main draw. Additional players from the region could join her through qualifying.

The strength of the Latin American contingent gives fans throughout the region several players to follow beyond the tournament’s established global stars.

Why Cincinnati Matters Before the US Open

The Cincinnati Open is more than another stop on the summer tennis calendar. Its position immediately before the US Open makes it an important measure of player form. The conditions in Ohio can be hot and humid, and the hard courts reward players who can control points quickly while remaining physically strong through long matches.

A strong week in Cincinnati can change expectations entering New York. It can also expose injury concerns, fatigue or tactical weaknesses at the most important stage of the season. The expanded men’s and women’s singles draws provide additional opportunities for emerging players, qualifiers and lower-ranked entrants to face the sport’s biggest names.

For established contenders, however, Cincinnati is about more than preparation. An ATP or WTA 1000 title carries considerable ranking value and is one of the most prestigious trophies available outside the Grand Slams.

A Transformed Tournament Venue

The Lindner Family Tennis Center completed a $260 million redevelopment before the 2025 tournament. The project expanded and modernized the grounds, adding new courts, improved stadiums, park-style landscaping, additional shade, upgraded fan areas and a new player clubhouse.

The transformation helped the Cincinnati Open earn both the ATP Masters 1000 and WTA 1000 Tournament of the Year awards following the 2025 event. The venue now has 31 outdoor tennis courts, giving spectators more opportunities to watch matches and practices at close range.

When Will the Draw Be Released?

The qualifying and main draws are expected closer to the beginning of competition. Once the draws are published, fans will know each player’s potential route through the tournament, possible early-round matchups and where the leading Latin American players have been placed.

The daily order of play will then determine match times and court assignments. The Tico Times will provide on-site coverage and photography from the Cincinnati Open beginning August 13, with particular attention to Latin American players, major tournament storylines and the final preparations for the US Open.

World.title: Costa Rica Protest to Defend Judiciary Amid Government Clash
World.content:
Judicial employees, university representatives and civil society groups are preparing demonstrations across Costa Rica today as the dispute between President Laura Fernández’s government and the Judiciary grows increasingly confrontational. The main gathering is scheduled to begin at 4 p.m. at Plaza de la Democracia in downtown San José.

Organizers have described the event as a peaceful demonstration in defense of judicial independence, democratic institutions and Costa Rica’s system of checks and balances. The protest is expected to continue until approximately 8 p.m. and will include speeches, cultural presentations and activities organized by unions and civic groups. Participation is open to the public.

The National Council of University Rectors (Conare), has also called on university communities and the public to participate. Its march will leave the Fuente de la Hispanidad in Montes de Oca at 3:30 p.m. before continuing toward Plaza de la Democracia. Similar gatherings have been announced outside judicial buildings in other areas of the country. Confirmed locations include Nicoya and Liberia, while calls have also circulated for demonstrations in Puntarenas, San Carlos and other judicial districts.

Eight unions and professional organizations representing judicial employees are among the groups supporting the San José protest. They include the Judicial Workers’ Union, or Sitrajud; the Public Defense Union, Sindepu; the National Association of Criminal Investigators, ANIC; and the Costa Rican Judges Association, Acojud.

The National Association of Judicial Employees, Anejud; the National Association of Judicial Professionals, Anprojud; the Association of Accounting and Finance Professionals of the Judiciary, Asprotcofi; and the National Front of Struggle, FNL, are also involved. The demonstrations follow several weeks of escalating tension over government spending cuts and a Constitutional Chamber ruling involving substitute Supreme Court justices.

The dispute intensified after the Constitutional Chamber (Sala IV), issued a ruling on July 30. In a 4-3 decision, the court overturned the Legislative Assembly’s attempt to return a list of candidates for substitute justices to the Supreme Court. The ruling also temporarily extended appointments that had expired on December 16, 2025.

The court said the temporary measure was needed to prevent disruptions in urgent cases while lawmakers complete the appointment process. Substitute justices are required when permanent members of the Constitutional Chamber cannot participate in a case because of conflicts of interest, illness or other legal restrictions.

Fernández responded by accusing part of the Judiciary of carrying out a “coup d’état” against the Legislative Assembly, which has the constitutional authority to appoint Supreme Court justices. The Constitutional Chamber rejected that characterization and said its decision fell within its legal authority to protect access to constitutional justice and prevent the court from becoming unable to handle important cases.

On August 3, Legislative Assembly President Yara Jiménez and ruling-party lawmakers filed a criminal complaint against the four justices who supported the majority decision: Fernando Cruz Castro, Paul Rueda Leal, Ingrid Hess Herrera and Jorge Araya García. Fernández, several Cabinet ministers and supporters of the governing Pueblo Soberano party accompanied the lawmakers to the Supreme Court.

The complaint accuses the justices of suspected prevaricato, a criminal offense involving a judge or public official who knowingly issues a decision contrary to the law or bases it on false facts. The judicial dispute comes alongside growing concern over spending reductions ordered by the Ministry of Finance, which is headed by former president Rodrigo Chaves. Chaves also serves as minister of the Presidency in the Fernández administration.

Judicial authorities say three government budget actions during the past two months have reduced funds available to the courts, the Public Prosecutor’s Office and the Judicial Investigation Police, known as the OIJ. The Judiciary has said one of the measures reduced its operating budget for the second half of 2026 by approximately 42%.

Officials have warned that the reductions could affect fuel, expert reports, criminal investigations, court proceedings and the execution of search warrants. Those warnings come as Costa Rica continues to confront organized crime, drug trafficking and high homicide levels. Fernández and Chaves have rejected allegations that their administration intends to close, control or dismantle the Judiciary.

Both have argued that spending reductions are required because of the government’s fiscal position and that the judicial system needs significant reforms. The government says the changes are intended to reduce spending, eliminate privileges and make the courts more efficient. Judicial leaders and protest organizers argue that the measures could weaken one of the country’s most important democratic institutions.

World.title: Three minors charged with murder of 18-year-old Ewart Hernandez Jr.
World.content:
Three minors charged with murder of 18-year-old Ewart Hernandez Jr.

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have formally arrested and charged three male minors in connection with the murder of 18-year-old Ewart Josiah Hernandez Jr.

Police say that on Thursday, August 6, two 17-year-olds and a 15-year-old were jointly charged with Murder in relation to Hernandez’s killing, which occurred in Belize City on Monday, August 3.

Hernandez was reportedly on a motorcycle in the Swift Hall parking lot at around 1:15 p.m. when he was approached by two males. One of the men allegedly produced a firearm and fired a single shot, striking Hernandez. He was rushed to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where he was pronounced dead at 1:32 p.m.

Investigators recovered an expended shell casing from the scene, and police said surveillance footage from cameras in the area assisted investigators in pursuing suspects. Police had initially detained persons for questioning as the investigation progressed.

Police had also said that Hernandez was not known to them and that no motive had been established for the killing.

World.title: Department of Environment investigating fish kill in Belize River Valley, public urged to avoid untreated river water
World.content:
Department of Environment investigating fish kill in Belize River Valley, public urged to avoid untreated river water

By Zoila Palma: The Department of the Environment (DOE) is investigating a fish kill reported in the Belize River Valley and has issued a public advisory warning residents not to consume fish or other aquatic resources from affected areas while the investigation continues.

The Ministry of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management said the DOE received reports on August 4 of numerous dead fish floating along sections of the Belize River, prompting a multi-agency response.

According to the department, a joint assessment was launched involving Belize Water Services Limited (BWS), the Ministry of Health and Wellness, the National Emergency Management Organization (NEMO), the Fisheries Department, the Ministry of Infrastructure Development and Housing (MIDH), and other relevant agencies.

The release stated that “the Department is actively responding to the ongoing fish kill issue reported in the Belize River Valley area.”

DOE said the exercise included “water quality monitoring and sampling, as well as assessments of land-clearing activities, potential wastewater discharge sources, and other factors that may have contributed to impacts on the aquatic environment.”

As investigations continue, the DOE is advising residents to take precautionary measures.

The department warned the public “not to consume fish or other aquatic resources from the affected areas and not to drink untreated river water or use untreated river water for cooking or food preparation.” It also advised against using untreated river water for livestock or pets until further notice.

The department emphasized that the advisory applies only to untreated water taken directly from the river and does not affect the public water supply.

The release noted that “BWS has confirmed that the water currently being supplied from its Water Treatment Plant remains safe for consumption and meets the required potable water quality standards. There has been no disruption to the continuity of the water supply.”

DOE noted that technical assessments are ongoing to determine the cause of the fish kill and pledged to keep the public informed as new information becomes available.

The DOE also reminded the public that the release of untreated wastewater, or treated effluent that fails to meet environmental standards, is prohibited under Belize’s Environmental Protection Regulations and constitutes an offence.

World.title: The case for Allan Pollard, measured the way a city should measure a mayor
World.content:
The case for Allan Pollard, measured the way a city should measure a mayor

By Horace Palacio:

The People’s United Party will soon ask its Belize City delegates a single question. Who should carry its banner for mayor in 2027, Councillor Allan Pollard Jr. or Deputy Mayor Eluide Miller?

Today I am going to answer that question openly, and make the case for Pollard. But I will make it the way this column has always insisted arguments be made, on the record, with respect for both men, and by a standard bigger than either of them.

Because before we compare two candidates, remember what the prize actually is. Belize City is not a title. It is the largest, hardest job in municipal government in this country. Flooding that swallows streets. Drains that fail. Garbage that piles. Traffic that strangles. Crime that shadows whole neighborhoods. Whoever wins this convention inherits all of it. So the question for delegates is not who do you like. It is who is readiest, this March, for that load.

Measure the two men by that standard, and the case builds itself on four pillars.

Pillar one. The record. Allan Pollard has served the people of Belize City as an elected councillor for eight years, across three terms, including service as deputy mayor. Eluide Miller, a capable young man, has served two. That is not an insult to Miller. It is arithmetic. Pollard has sat through four times the budgets, four times the floods, four times the hard seasons of that council. He has already held the deputy’s chair Miller holds now, and then kept serving. The city’s problems are too old and too heavy for the top job to double as a classroom. Experience is not everything, but in a crisis city, it is not nothing either. It is the difference between learning the machine and driving it.

Pillar two. Character, tested in the dark. Here is the part of Pollard’s story that tells you more than any manifesto. In 2023, he wanted this same candidacy. The party asked him to step aside for unity’s sake. He swallowed his ambition and did it. Reports say the Prime Minister personally assured him his patience would be honored this cycle. Now, let me be precise about why this matters, because it is not the reason some think. I have written before that no seat in Belize should be awarded by turn, only by merit, and I stand by every word. Pollard does not deserve the candidacy because he waited. He deserves consideration because of what the waiting revealed. A man who can put the team above his own ambition, keep working for three more years without sulking, and return stronger, has shown you his character under the hardest test politics offers, the test of being told no. Most politicians fail that test loudly. Pollard passed it quietly. That is the temperament you want holding a city’s purse and pressure.

Pillar three. Whose hands hold him. Look carefully at the two campaign launches, because launches are confessions. Miller announced flanked by seven fellow councillors, the establishment closing ranks, with the outgoing mayor reportedly grooming him as successor. Pollard arrived with no councillors at all, just a crowd of ordinary city people, family, friends, supporters he did not have to summon. One candidacy was born in the council chamber. The other was born on the street. And a mayor, understand, does not answer to the chamber. He answers to the street. Give me the candidate the people carry over the candidate the machine crowns, every single time. It is also worth noting what Pollard said about that machine, that he wants the door open to new faces, talented people, older, younger, business people, and that whoever the delegates elect to the slate gets his full backing. That is a builder’s posture, not a boss’s.

Pillar four. The money question. There is a figure floating around this race, two hundred dollars per delegate, the whispered price of convention support. I wrote months ago that free is the most expensive thing in Belize, that every bought vote is a purchase the politician later recoups from the public. So hear what Pollard put on the record when the figure was raised. He does not pay for delegates. His relationships with them were built over years of showing up, and, in his words, that is something money cannot buy. A candidate who refuses to buy his way in owes nothing on his way up. That single stance, publicly planted, is worth more to this city than any promise on any flyer. And let me be crystal clear in fairness, no evidence before me says Miller pays for delegates, and I make no such claim. I simply issue the challenge this column must issue. Mr. Miller, plant the same flag, publicly, and let this be the first convention in memory where both camps swear off the wallet and compete on the work.

Now, the fairness Miller is owed, because this endorsement will not be built on his burial.

Eluide Miller has done something in this race that deserves genuine applause. When party heavyweights reportedly leaned on him to step aside and clear the path, he refused, and insisted the delegates decide. That is democratic spine, and it is exactly what I have preached in these pages, conventions over coronations, always. Both camps, let us be honest, have maneuvered behind the scenes in this contest, which is precisely why the convention itself is the clean answer. Miller is young, described even by neutrals in the party as energetic and creative, and if he loses this race well, his future in city politics is real. The party leader himself says both men have talent, and he is right.

But talent is the entry fee, not the verdict. The verdict comes from the standard we set at the start. Which man, this March, is readiest for the hardest municipal job in Belize?

Eight years against two. A deputy mayor’s chair already held, then exceeded. Ambition tested by sacrifice and passed. A campaign carried by the street rather than crowned by the chamber. And a public refusal to purchase what should only be earned. On the record before the delegates, that is Allan Pollard’s case, and it is a strong one.

So to the delegates who will file into that convention, I close with this. You hold a privilege thousands of city residents wish they held. Do not sell it, to anyone. Do not lend it to pressure, from anyone. Weigh the records, question both men hard, and choose the readiest hands.

Weighed that way, honestly and without malice, my case is made.

The city’s next chapter should be written by the man who spent eight years learning to hold the pen.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: Prime Minister meets with stakeholders in sugar industry to discuss mealybug infestation
World.content:
Prime Minister meets with stakeholders in sugar industry to discuss mealybug infestation

By Zoila Palma: Today, Prime Minister John Briceno met with stakeholders in the sugar industry to discuss the mealybug infestation.

In addition, the PM also received updates on two important initiatives —CRESAP and the Building the Adaptive Capacity of Sugarcane Farmers in Northern Belize (BAC-SuF) Project.

The PM explained that financed by the Green Climate Fund and implemented by the Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre (5Cs), BAC-SuF is helping to strengthen the resilience of our sugarcane farmers and safeguard the future of this vital industry.

World.title: Cabinet Approves Amendments to Cybercrime Bill to safeguard freedom of expression
World.content:
Cabinet Approves Amendments to Cybercrime Bill to safeguard freedom of expression

By Zoila Palma: Cabinet has approved amendments to the Cybercrime Bill aimed at clarifying the scope of offences while ensuring the legislation aligns with constitutional protections for freedom of expression.

According to the Cabinet statement, the changes are intended to preserve the Government’s ability to prosecute serious forms of technology-facilitated abuse, including malicious deepfakes, online impersonation, extortion, threats, and targeted harassment.

At the same time, the amendments seek to safeguard freedom of expression, political debate, journalism, satire, and public accountability.

As part of this safeguard, the cabinet release notes that the DPP’s written consent will be required before the prosecution of an offence can occur.

This latest revision comes after concerns were raised by media organizations, civil society groups, and members of the public that earlier provisions of the Cybercrime Bill could have had unintended consequences for free speech and press freedom.

World.title: Cabinet approves US $8 million loan from Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) for efficiency of wage bill
World.content:
Cabinet approves US $8 million loan from Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) for efficiency of wage bill

By Zoila Palma: During Cabinet’s meeting on July 28th and August 4th, 2026, the Government of Belize approved entering into a loan agreement with the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) for US$8 million.

According to the cabinet release, the loan will be used to “improve the efficiency of the Central Government’s wage bill and to increase the efficacy of strategic public employment”.

The funding is expected to help improve the allocation of public resources, promote more efficient staffing across government ministries and departments, and support efforts to modernize public sector management.

The project carries a total value of US$9 million, or roughly BZ$18 million, made up of the US$8 million in IDB financing and US$1 million in local counterpart funding, and is to be implemented over a five-year disbursement period.

World.title: Cabinet approves 20.9 million dollar investment in electric buses and charging infrastructure
World.content:
Cabinet approves 20.9 million dollar investment in electric buses and charging infrastructure

By Zoila Palma: During Cabinet’s session on July 28th and August 4th, 2026, the Government of Belize approved the change of its planned investment in the National Bus Company (NBC) from “terminals to electric buses and related charging infrastructure with a value of approximately BZ$20.9 million”.

The decision will require a revised Public Transportation Investment Bill to reflect this change.

The revision will include a proposed long-term lease agreement under which the Government would lease the bus terminals to the NBC.

The move forms part of the Government’s efforts to modernize Belize’s public transportation system through the introduction of electric buses and supporting infrastructure.

World.title: Youth Shadow Mayor Begins Leadership Journey at Belize City Hall
World.content:
Youth Shadow Mayor Begins Leadership Journey at Belize City Hall

By Zoila Palma: Youth Shadow Mayor Caitlin Aragon officially began her leadership experience with the Belize City Council after being welcomed by Mayor Bernard Wagner during an introductory visit to City Hall.

As part of the visit, Aragon toured the Office of the Mayor and learned about the daily responsibilities of the Mayor’s Office and the Belize City Council’s role in serving residents and guiding the city’s development.

The initiative provides mentorship and hands-on exposure to local government, giving the Youth Shadow Mayor valuable insight into leadership and public service

World.title: Card, Douglas win silver in 100m at World U20 Championships
World.content:
Jamaica's Shanoya Douglas parades with the Jamaican flag after winning the silver medal in the women's 100m on Thursday's second day of the 2026 World Athletics Under 20 championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon. Douglas, the world leader was beaten by American Maria Maxwell. (Photos: Paul Reid)

OREGON, USA — Jamaica’s Gary Card and Shanoya Douglas won silver medals in the men and women’s 100m on Thursday night at the World Athletics Under-20 Championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon.

It was the first medals for Jamaica at the championships, putting them in ninth position on the medals tables.

Americans Tate Taylor and Mia Maxwell delighted the home fans by winning the double, only the second time athletes from the same country had taken both gold medals at the same under-20 championships after Americans Noah Lyles and Candace Hill achieved the feat in 2016 in Bydgoszcz, Poland.

Card got off to a fast start but was chased and caught by Tate who passed him to win in a personal best 9.94 seconds (0.1m/s), the Jamaican second in 10.05 seconds. South Africa’s Marko Ferreira took the bronze with 10.16 seconds.

Maxwell got the edge over Douglas at the start and held off the Jamaican to the tape, running 11.14 seconds (-0.1m/s). Douglas finished second in 11.17 seconds with Italy’s Kelly Ann Maevane Doualla Edimo third in 11.27 seconds. Theianna-Lee Terrelonge was sixth in 11.37 seconds

It was the first time in 10 years an American won the women’s 100m and snapped the four-championships winning streak by the Jamaicans – Briana Williams in 2018, Tina Clayton in 2021 and 2022 and Alana Reid in 2024.

Also on Thursday, thrower Able Mills failed to record a legal throw in both the women’s discus and shot put finals that were held within two hours of each other.

Mills had thrown distances close to her lifetime bests to qualify for both finals but failed to make a legal mark in either.

Jamaica also failed to qualify any runner in the 400m finals set for Friday afternoon, all four failing to get past their semifinals.

Jabari Matheson who was running his fourth 400m race in two days, placed sixth in his semi-final in 47.29 seconds, the first time he failed to go under the 47.00 second mark at the championships.

Jason Pitter failed to get up to his high standards, and was sixth in his semi-final in 46.50 seconds after he advanced on time from the first round.

Daniellia Dixon was fifth in her semi-final in 53.77 seconds and Shameika McLean, who had run three times since the start of the championships, just failed to get into the final after placing fourth in her semis in 54.24 seconds.

-Paul A Reid

World.title: Celebrating 64!
World.content:
Thousands of Jamaicans packed the National Stadium in St Andrew on Thursday as the country marked 64 years of Independence with the signature Grand Gala event celebrated under the theme ‘United in Celebrating Resilience’. The Grand Gala, held annually by the Ministry of Culture, Gender, Entertainment, and Sport through the Jamaica Cultural Development Commission, is the grand finale of Jamaica’s Emancipation and Independence season. Portfolio minister Olivia Grange said that the event, which had more than 1,800 participants, would present Jamaica’s story, diversity, achievements, and creative power on the nation’s largest cultural stage.
