World.title: Berlin clubs struggle as drink sales dry up and costs rise
World.content:
Berlin's clubs are still drawing crowds, but shorter nights, fewer alcohol sales and rising costs have changed their business model. Door fees, rather than bar takings, are increasingly their real financial lifeline.

Berlin's world-famous club scene has remained in high demand, but venues are increasingly struggling to turn packed dancefloors into sustainable businesses.

A major survey released on Friday found that club revenue has shifted dramatically away from drinks and toward admission fees.

What's happened to Berlin's clubs?

The shift reflects changing nightlife habits since 2017, when around 60% of revenue came from food and drink sales and just 21% from entry fees.

Today, ticket sales account for 59% of revenue, while food and drink generate just 20%.

"People are planning their club nights more consciously, staying for shorter periods, and drinking less,” according to the report, the first comprehensive study of the sector since 2019.

Some 73% of respondents said alcohol consumption was falling, while 60% reported rising demand for non-alcoholic drinks and 57% said guests were staying for shorter periods.

At the same time, costs are rising.

Staff costs were cited as a major burden by 64% of respondents, operating costs by 62%, customers' declining purchasing power by 60%, and rents and leases by 54%.

Some 85% of the clubs polled said financial pressure was already changing their event programs.

Is running a Berlin club lucrative?

Demand remains strong, with 83% of clubs and event organizers reporting occupancy rates of at least 50% and around a third exceeding 75%.

But fewer venues are making enough money to cover their costs.

Club closures in Berlin: The end of an era? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In 2017, 79% were at least breaking even. By 2025, that figure had dropped to 61%.

Some 39% ended the year in the red, compared with 21% in 2017.

The number of smaller operators has also risen sharply. Some 45% now generate less than €100,000 ($115,595) in annual revenue, compared with 16% in 2017.

Long-term insecurity remains another major problem. Only 8% of operators own their venues, while 31% have rental or lease agreements lasting less than five years.

How are clubs adapting?

Some 23% of respondents said they were considering closing their business within the next 12 months. Since 2020, at least 24 club and cultural venues have closed, but around 25 new ones have opened.

Many venues have already adapted to the pressure.

Some 67% have increased drink prices, 47% have raised admission charges and 39% have expanded private rentals.

The Club Commission is calling for publicly owned buildings to be opened up for nightlife, more reliable long-term funding, formal recognition of clubs as cultural venues and better working conditions.

World.title: Eco wins: Hungary goes solar, marmots go viral and Rome gets an upgrade
World.content:
From Hungary's accidental solar revolution to marmot crowdfunding and a long-overdue upgrade for Rome's big snake, good news comes in strange packages this week.

Hungary's former leader Viktor Orban called European Union climate policy a "utopian fantasy" and effectively banned wind turbines. And yet the country has quietly become Europe's solar leader, with 25% of its electricity now being being generated from the renewable energy source, ahead of sunnier countries like Spain, and Greece.

The boom was driven not by climate concern but by self-sufficiency politics and cheap subsidies. Now a 450-megawatt park, just east of Budapest, is due online by September 2026. It's set to power around 106,000 households.



Marmot researchers find a new way to fund their science

When US federal funding dried up, researchers from UCLA and the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory got creative. They launched OnlyMarms: a free platform posting videos of yellow-bellied marmots eating, digging and scampering in the wild, where fans can donate to support the science.

The team has tracked individually marked marmots in Colorado since 1962, building six decades of data on family lives, social behavior and responses to environmental change — and say studying marmot hibernation could even hold clues about human aging.

Rome's 'big snake' gets a cooler future

Corviale, a kilometer-long brutalist housing complex outside Rome nicknamed "the big snake," was completed in the 1980s and has since fallen into decay. With summers in some parts of Italy's now averaging around 30 degrees Celsius (86 Fahrenheit), life inside has become tough for its more than 4,000 residents.

But upgrades are coming: a new library doubling as a cooling shelter, more trees and energy efficiency improvements, all aimed at helping Corviale stay cool as temperatures keep rising.

Senegalese designer turns discarded textiles into sustainable fashion

Berlin-based designer Mame Khady Badji transforms discarded clothing into bold garments inspired by her Senegalese heritage, combining traditional Ndiakhass techniques with contemporary streetwear. Her creations have drawn musicians, performers and creatives — and recently appeared at Berlin Fashion Week 2026.

After moving to Germany in 2017, Badji built her label with support from Berlin's textile community. Now she's pursuing an ambitious goal: proving that recycled fashion can be both culturally rooted and commercially viable.

World.title: Thailand: Several killed in school shooting north of Bangkok
World.content:
The shooting incident took place at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School in ​the ‌Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi, just north of the capital city of Bangkok. Several people were killed in the attack.

Several people were killed and others injured in a shooting at a high school in Thailand's Nonthaburi province, north of the capital city of Bangkok, local authorities said.

Students, teachers and other workers were evacuated from school as authorities deployed police officers, rescue workers and emergency doctors to the scene.

Boy accused of killing grandparents before school shooting

According to the police, the suspected gunman, who is a 14-year-old student at the school, is thought to have first fatally shot his grandparents with his grandfather's handgun. The suspect lived with his grandparents, and police found them dead behind a locked door as they began to investigate the shooting.

Authorities later revised down the total death toll. Having initially said that the suspect killed six people, including students, at the school, police later said he killed two teachers and three other adults who were staff at the school.

Officials said the suspect then took his own life at the site, in the Nonthaburi province bordering Bangkok.

A nearby hospital later said more than 20 people were wounded, with 10 of them in a critical condition Image: Peerapon Boonyakiat/ZUMA/IMAGO

Bangyai Hospital, about 5 kilometers (roughly 3 miles) from the school, said 23 people were wounded, of whom 10 were in critical condition, with most suffering gunshot wounds. Earlier reports gave conflicting casualty numbers.

Thailand's Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul expressed his condolences and stated that he had instructed relevant officials to assist those affected.

"It's such a terrible incident. It should never have happened," he told reporters.

Later, Anutin said that the teenage suspect in the deadly school shooting was "under stress" and there was preliminary evidence of him planning the attack ahead of time. The prime minister also told reporters that he would discuss gun control with the country's police chief.

Students, teachers and other staff members had to hurriedly leave the site Image: Chalinee Thirasupa/REUTERS

Students express shock

The incident took place at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School in ​the ‌Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi.

"I didn't think it was a gun at first," an 18-year-old student told Reuters, adding that he initially thought it could be firecrackers. "There were many shots: bang bang bang. Then it went quiet. ​Then it started again."

"I was afraid that I would die, and I was scared that I wouldn't be able to pursue my dreams," said Pawarisa Maylissa, a grade 12 student who hopes to attend medical school. "I heard many gunshots very loudly because it seemed the suspect was on the floor directly above us. I could even hear bullets hitting the floor."

According to district authorities, the Debsirin Nonthaburi School had an enrollment of around 3,100 students and 147 teachers in the 2025 academic year.

Belongings left behind by evacuated students at Debsirin Nonthaburi School, following the shooting incident at the school Image: Peerapon Boonyakiat/ZUMA/IMAGO

School shootings in Thailand

Thailand has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in the region. It is estimated that around 10 million firearms are in circulation, or about one for every seven people.

In February, a 17-year-old stole a gun from the police and opened fire at a public high school in southern Thailand. The two-hour attack resulted in one death and two injuries.

In October 2023, a 14-year-old opened fire at Bangkok's popular Siam Paragon shopping mall, killing two people and wounding five others. Police said the shooter used a modified pistol, originally designed to fire blanks, that had likely been bought online.

World.title: What should Europe do about its drying rivers?
World.content:
The Rhine and Danube have reached historic lows. Dwindling water levels are affecting shipping, agriculture and ecosystems — and raising concerns about the future of drinking water supplies.

Following an intense heat wave in June and severe wildfires in southern France and Spain, Europe's summer of climate-fueled crises continues with rivers across the continent running low.

Parts of the vital Rhine, Danube and Po rivers have fallen to historically low levels, threatening freight transport, the wider economy, and agriculture, with farmers warning of increased prices due to poor harvests amid the drought.

Along the Danube, cargo and cruise ships can no longer pass in some places. In Hungary, Romania and Croatia, sunken ships and cars have reemerged as riverbeds dry out.

In German cities, including Cologne and Düsseldorf, people can now walk across parts of the Rhine where strong currents normally flow. River levels could fall even more dramatically in the coming days.

The water crisis is being intensified by global warming driven by the burning of coal, oil and gas. Low water levels are also taking a growing toll on ecosystems — and could eventually drive up the cost of clean drinking water.

The impact on nature

Parched fields, millions of hectares of lost harvests and exposed riverbeds are among the most obvious consequences of the drought. But underwater ecosystems are suffering too.

As water levels fall, rivers become warmer and contain less dissolved oxygen, increasing the risk of fish die-offs, explained Jeanette Völker, a scientist with Germany's federal environment agency, the UBA.

"Especially along the Rhine, you can see how the gravel banks are drying up. These are habitats for mussels and invertebrates, which in turn serve as food for fish. This puts enormous stress on these ecosystems. Mussels cannot move away quickly enough and die off," Völker told DW.

Drought, intense sunshine, and high nutrient loads from agricultural fertilizers also encourage algal blooms harmful to fish.

These effects were seen in 2022 on the Oder River in eastern Germany. High temperatures, low water levels and elevated salinity allowed a toxic invasive algae to spread. Around 1,000 metric tons of fish died along parts of the German-Polish border river.

Experts do not expect a repeat of the Oder disaster on the Rhine this summer because oxygen levels remain sufficiently high. But the danger to the wider freshwater ecosystem remains.

As the Danube retreats, long-submerged wreckage is resurfacing — a sign of how far the river has fallen Image: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/picture alliance

What dwindling rivers mean for drinking water costs

The Rhine and the Danube are fed by numerous tributaries that are also running low. These tributaries are crucial because their lush, reed-filled banks act as natural filters, allowing water to slowly pass through layers of soil that help remove pollutants before water reaches underground wells.

"Much of our drinking water is what's known as 'riverbank filtration,'" said Hagen Koch, a researcher specializing in climate adaptation and resilience at Germany's Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research.

In other words, Germany's drinking water comes from those wells. But drought is weakening this process. Pollutant concentrations are increasing because roughly the same volume of wastewater — largely from industry and sewage works — is discharged into rivers even as water levels fall.

"If the ecosystem is damaged — that is, the animals and plants that contribute to water purification — this results in significant additional costs. Additional treatment is needed to supply clean drinking water to millions of people," Koch told DW.

German industry groups estimate water supply costs could rise by up to 30% as a result of climate change. By 2035, additional investments of up to €14 billion could be needed for improved water treatment systems, as well as deeper mains and upgraded reservoirs designed to keep water temperatures low and limit microbial growth.

The situation has drawn attention to a broader debate over water use. While households pay for the water they consume, several industries — including mining and agriculture — are exempt from water abstraction fees in many German states.

To conserve water, authorities in some German cities are currently severely restricting withdrawal from streams and rivers by private individuals. In Cologne, residents who violate the ban face fines of up to €50,000 ($58,000).

Low water levels hitting the economy

Low water levels in Germany's rivers are already taking a significant toll on the economy. Some vessels are carrying just a fifth of their usual cargo, delaying production and driving up prices. Germany's steel, chemical and petroleum industries have been hit particularly hard.

Energy supplies are also under pressure. Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar has urged households and businesses to conserve electricity. He warned the country could face an unprecedented energy crisis after low water levels in the Danube forced the shutdown of the Paks nuclear power plant.

Rewetted peatlands like this one are the kind of restoration experts say could help rivers retain water Image: Robert B. Fishman/picture alliance

Romania blasts rocks as Europe searches for solutions

Politicians are exploring emergency measures in response to the situation. In Romania, the military blasted apart a rock formation in a branch of the Danube to secure the cooling water supply for the Cernavoda nuclear power plant and avoid a shutdown.

Germany's transport minister brought together representatives from industry, ports and inland shipping on August 6 to consider short- and long-term solutions to the crisis. One proposal under discussion was deepening parts of the Rhine's navigation channel so shipping can continue despite low water levels.

Critics warn that further dredging and deepening of shipping channels would accelerate water runoff, lower groundwater levels, and cause floodplains to dry out more quickly, ultimately do little to solve the problem in the long-term.

Exposed riverbed now stretches beneath Düsseldorf's bridges, where the Rhine once ran deep Image: Kai Kitschenberg/Funke Foto Services/IMAGO

Instead, they're calling for the expanded use of low-water vessels, as well as a shift from freight transport to rail. Koch supports the development of ships with shallower drafts, but notes such changes require significant time and investment.

For Jeanette Völker, the solution lies in restoring parts of Europe's heavily modified rivers. Reconnecting floodplains, protecting wetlands and restoring peatlands would help landscapes retain more water and improve resilience during future droughts.

Reservoirs and dams may also play a role where they are environmentally acceptable. But experts warn adaptation alone will not be enough. Without climate protection and a rapid reduction in greenhouse gas emissions, any investments are little more than a drop in a fast-flowing river.

World.title: Myanmar's Min Aung Hlaing seeks legitimacy in Thailand
World.content:
Bangkok rolled out the red carpet for the Myanmar leader, but experts say the former junta chief still faces major obstacles in his bid for regional acceptance.

Myanmar's junta chief turned president Min Aung Hlaing wrapped up a two-day visit to Thailand on Friday.

His first visit to the neighboring nation as civilian leader was aimed at recasting himself as the leader of a civilian government after years of diplomatic isolation, experts told DW.

His reception on landing in Bangkok on Thursday had all the pomp and circumstance befitting a visiting head of state — red carpet, honor guard, blaring national anthems and smiling photo ops with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul.

"Naypyidaw equates engagement with acceptance," said Moe Thuzar, head of the Myanmar Studies Program at Singapore's ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, referring to Myanmar's capital.

"Min Aung Hlaing is seeking to leverage Naypyidaw's space in bilateral relations with neighbours' specific interests to secure greater acceptance of his administration from external partners."

Min Aung Hlaing has pledged to pursue peace and improve ties with the 11-member ASEAN bloc Image: Athit Perawongmetha/REUTERS

Since the retired general seized power in a 2021 coup that toppled a democratically elected government, a brutal civil war between the military and armed resistance groups has killed an estimated 100,000 people and displaced well over 3 million.

Western countries have imposed several rounds of sanctions on Min Aung Hlaing's regime over alleged war crimes and other human rights abuses, charges the government rejects.

In 2024, the then-chief prosecutor of the International Criminal Court requested an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing himself for crimes against humanity committed against Rohingya Muslims.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), which traditionally emphasizes non-interference in another member's domestic affairs, has barred him or his foreign minister from attending its leaders' summits.

Hoping to break out of its growing isolation, Myanmar held staggered elections in December and January that were widely criticized by the United Nations and Western governments as a sham designed to legitimize continued military rule.

The military-aligned Union Solidarity and Development Party won more than 80% of seats, paving the way for parliament to elect Min Aung Hlaing president in April.

What is Thailand's role in Myanmar's reengagement?

Myanmar's government rejects criticism of the electoral process, saying the elections were part of a transition to civilian rule and a return of power to the people.

Since becoming president, Hlaing has paid official visits to India, China, Laos and now Thailand, as Bangkok pushed for peace efforts in Myanmar's civil war and its reengagement with ASEAN.

"For Min Aung Hlaing, visiting Thailand is also [about] finding legitimacy in the ASEAN region, because Thailand is a … founder of ASEAN and has [a] big voice in ASEAN," said Wai Yan Phyo Naing, a visiting scholar at Taiwan's Academia Sinica who studies Myanmar.

"He can show the [other] ASEAN members that Thailand is treating me like this, Laos already treated me like this. So, do you want to [act] based on the realistic point of view, or are you still wanting to argue I'm not the legitimate leader of Myanmar?" he said.

Moe Thuzar and Wai Yan Phyo Naing both agree that the bloc, which did not officially endorse Myanmar's last elections, like most countries, was not likely to let Min Aung Hlaing back to its leaders' summits any time soon.

Human Rights Watch's Elaine Pearson on Myanmar election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

ASEAN still insists that Myanmar first make meaningful progress on a peace plan for the country that they all agreed to a few months after the coup, a plan Hlaing has dismissed repeatedly, most recently last week.

Still, Min Aung Hlaing may be hoping that his official trips abroad as newly installed president

help convince ASEAN to accept his government "on its own terms," Moe Thuzar added.

Either way, she said, Min Aung Hlaing will use his trip to Thailand to build on the bilateral relationship between the neighbors, which share a 2,400 kilometer (1,490-mile) land border.

The visit included a business forum on Thursday for Thai and Myanmar firms.

"The focus on trade and economic deals reflects Naypyidaw's and Bangkok's interest in prioritising economic engagement and addressing concerns related to border trade," said Moe Thuzar.

The economics of legitimacy

Thailand is among Myanmar's top trade partners and foreign investors, including in energy projects vital to both. A Thai firm operates two of Myanmar's main gas fields, which supply much of Thailand's natural gas.

David Mathieson, an independent Myanmar analyst based in Thailand, says convincing those investors to stay, or new ones to come in, helps shore up support for Hlaing among a key constituency.

Regardless of the ex-general's official title, he said, "he's a military dictator, and to be a dictator you need a certain level of cooperation, and cooperation comes from economic elites."

"He's appealing to an incredibly cynical international system that's like, hey, you did this. None of us buy it, but it's good enough for us. You dressed up for the party, well done, and [it's] business as usual," Mathieson said.

"Does that help the 54 million people of Myanmar? No, it doesn't. It helps him and it helps the system that props him up."

World.title: Germany: Far-right AfD extends its lead in nationwide polls
World.content:
In the latest Sunday poll, the AfD continues to pull ahead. And more and more people are against excluding the right-wing populists from decision-making, at least on a case-by-case basis.

For the time being, there is still widespread agreement among all democratic parties in Germany: Cooperating with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) remains out of the question. However, whether this will remain the case is becoming increasingly uncertain. The established parties have so far been unable to halt the AfD's surge in the polls over recent months.

This has also been confirmed by the latest ARD-Deutschlandtrend survey conducted by the polling firm infratest-dimap. One thousand three hundred eligible voters were asked what party they would vote for if a federal election were held next Sunday, and 28% said they would vote for the AfD. This represents a one-percentage-point increase and a new record high for the AfD in the monthly polly.

In contrast, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's party, the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), and its sister party, Bavaria's Christian Social Union (CSU), have seen a slight decline compared to the last poll in early July while all other parties have maintained their previous levels.

A clear majority supports reaching out to the AfD

In September, state elections will take place in two important eastern German states: Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. In both states, the AfD leads in the polls. In Saxony-Anhalt, they are polling at 41% and might be able to govern alone, if the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) fails to cross the 5% threshhold for representation in parliament.

However, only 37% of voters across Germany are opposed to any form of cooperation with the right-wing populists while 32% believe such decisions should be made on a case-by-case basis.

A total of 27% are generally in favor of cooperating with the AfD, most of whom are AfD supporters.

What is especially interesting in the poll, however, is the contrast between East and West Germany. The AfD has its strongholds in the East, where more people than in the West are willing to fully embrace the party: 38% want to treat the party — of which several regional chapters have been categorized as far-right extremist by the domestic intelligence agency — just like any other political group. That figure roughly corresponds to the level of support for right-wing populists in the formerly socialist East Germany (GDR).

Many AfD supporters feel marginalized

This figure also reflects the continuing shift away from "mainstream" parties. A good half of those surveyed — more than ever before in the Deutschlandtrend — support a fundamental change in German politics while only four in ten prefer isolated policy adjustments.

In other words, confidence and trust in the political system continue to wane. Forty-three percent of all respondents say they constantly feel marginalized. When this question is put to AfD supporters, that figure jumps to 70%.

The past few weeks in German politics have been marked by heated debates over proposed reforms and by a rather chaotic reshuffling of the cabinet. Even before this, approval ratings for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's policies were not high; now, only 12% believe that the new cabinet appointments will lead to better policies.

One-third are afraid of terrorism

And the latest terrorist attack in Germany has also had a significant impact on people's views. On July 25, a young Islamist from Berlin drove a rental car into a crowd during the Berlin Pride celebrations, killing one woman and seriously injuring 31 people. The following day, police shot and killed the man, who had fled after carrying out the attack. This horrific event has once again drawn attention to how vulnerable Germany is to terrorist attacks.

One-third of all respondents said they are very concerned they might become victims of terrorism themselves. Now, 70% see Islamist terrorism as the greatest threat. At the end of the last decade, on the other hand, right-wing extremist terrorism was still seen by German citizens as the greatest threat.

For the ARD-Deutschlandtrend survey in August, infratest-dimap interviewed approximately 1,300 representative German citizens between August 3 and 5.

This article was translated from German.

08/07/2026 August 7, 2026 Rheinmetall says it will take years to replenish US ATACMS stockpiles

Rheinmetall CEO Armin Papperger on Friday said it would take time to ramp up planned ATACMS missile production with US partner Lockheed Martin, highlighting the difficulty of replenishing weapons stockpiles depleted by President Donald Trump's decision to launch a war against Iran.

The US has reportedly burnt through much of its stockpile of long-range precision missiles during the five-month conflict with Iran, further raising concerns about its military readiness for future crises.

Trump on Thursday played down a Reuters report this week on US weapons shortages, claiming Washington has an "almost unlimited" supply of some munitions while acknowledging stocks of others were lower.

Last month, Rheinmetall — Europe's largest ammunition maker — signed a memorandum of understanding with US arms maker Lockheed Martin — the world's largest defense contractor— to jointly produce Army Tactical ​Missile Systems (ATACMS) at Rheinmetall's Unterluess plant in northern Germany, where production facilities are scheduled to be set up next year.

"Naturally, there will also be sufficient capacity to replenish the US military arsenals depleted by the conflict involving Iran," CEO Armin Papperger told Reuters, adding the caveat: "That won't happen in two years. It will take much ‌longer."

Papperger said the ATACMS joint venture still requires approval, but noted the process was well advanced and had the backing of the US ⁠government.

Rheinmetall and Lockheed intend to target the global ATACMS market, with Papperger saying, "There will be ​a market for missiles for the next 15 years."

World.title: Italia rechaza el ultimátum del Gobierno y mantendrá los controles a los viajeros que lleguen de España al menos hasta el 15 de agosto
World.content:
La crisis diplomática entre España e Italia se recrudece: La Moncloa ha decidido elevar el tono ante Roma después de que el Ejecutivo de Giorgia Meloni introdujera la semana pasada controles en frontera a los ciudadanos provenientes de España por la entrada masiva de inmigrantes en Ceuta. El Ejecutivo español ha respondido este viernes con dureza y ha advertido al Gobierno italiano de que, si no retira estas restricciones antes de que termine el domingo 9 de agosto, “España se verá obligada a adoptar medidas proporcionales para proteger los intereses y la dignidad de sus ciudadanos”. Italia no ha tardado en responder: apenas unas horas después del comunicado de La Moncloa, el Gobierno italiano ha afirmado que no tiene intención de reconsiderar la medida al menos hasta el 15 de agosto.

“Italia no acepta ultimátums ni imposiciones del exterior en lo que respecta a la seguridad nacional y al control de las fronteras”, zanjan en otro comunicado, y defienden para justificarse que para el 15 de agosto “se prevé una nueva oleada migratoria en Ceuta, tal como han anunciado las propias autoridades españolas”. En puridad, hay movimientos en redes sociales entre marroquíes que organizan para esa fecha un nuevo asalto a la frontera, pero el Gobierno español no ha anunciado una nueva oleada. Fuentes de La Moncloa señalan a este periódico que están monitorizando la situación, pero que no ven riesgo de que se puedan repetir las imágenes del pasado jueves.

El Ejecutivo de Meloni insiste, rechazando la amenaza de España: “Solo cuando tengamos la certeza de que no hay riesgos de seguridad y de terrorismo y de que no habrá una nueva oleada y de que no haya migrantes irregulares que se dirijan a territorio europeo, nos plantearemos revisar las decisiones que hemos tomado hasta ahora”. Para tratar de conciliar posturas, el Gobierno italiano afirma que este tipo de controles fronterizos extraordinarios ya se han usado en otras ocasiones en el pasado, como por ejemplo con Eslovenia o “por parte de otros estados europeos hacia Italia o hacia la propia España”. Y añaden que, cuando “pase el peligro”, seguirán manteniendo “una relación constructiva” con Madrid.

Un cartel en un aeropuerto italiano indica a los viajeros procedentes de España que deben ir por una fila específica.

Desde Roma precisan también que las autoridades locales que están llevando a cabo los controles “harán todo lo posible” para garantizar la máxima comodidad a los ciudadanos españoles y europeos que lleguen a Italia procedentes de España. Además, recuerdan que los españoles están exentos de los controles extraordinarios, que solo van dirigidos a ciudadanos extracomunitarios. Aunque, en la práctica, estos días las largas colas y las esperas han estado a la orden del día en algunas terminales de llegada, ya que, en general —aunque depende de la gestión de cada puerto o aeropuerto—, los pasajeros procedentes de España son canalizados por una fila específica para estos controles.

En el aeropuerto de Fiumicino (Roma), que recibe entre 55 y 60 vuelos diarios desde España en la temporada de verano, varios pasajeros de un vuelo de Iberia procedente de Madrid confirman a Efe que agentes de la policía solicitaban este viernes a los viajeros su documentación en el finger que conecta la nave con la terminal. De hecho, Iberia ha enviado en la última semana a sus clientes que viajan a Italia mensajes para informarles de que las autoridades italianas “han restablecido temporalmente los controles fronterizos”. Hasta junio de este año, más de 11 millones de pasajeros se desplazaron entre Italia y España en avión, según Aena. Solo en ese mes, el último con datos, fueron más de dos millones.

Crisis diplomática

El 31 de julio, Italia anunció que suspendía el tratado de libre circulación de personas en Europa, conocido como Acuerdo Schengen. “Se trata de una medida extraordinaria para salvaguardar la seguridad nacional y prevenir posibles repercusiones para nuestra nación”, señaló entonces Meloni. En el comunicado publicado este viernes, La Moncloa señala que las medidas tomadas por Roma no tienen “precedentes en la historia reciente”, se adoptaron “sin aviso previo, de forma unilateral y con argumentos espurios que no se ajustan ni al Código de Fronteras Schengen ni a la verdad”. Italia tiene hasta “que concluya el domingo 9 de agosto” para poner fin a los controles y tratar “a los españoles como al resto de ciudadanos europeos”, concluye el Gobierno español.

El Gobierno español defiende que “ninguno de los migrantes que accedieron de forma irregular a Ceuta la semana pasada pudo ni puede entrar libremente al espacio Schengen porque la ciudad autónoma de Ceuta tiene un régimen especial en el mismo”. Y añade que “la práctica totalidad de ellos ya han retornado a Marruecos”. Según las cifras de Interior, expuestas este martes por el ministro Fernando Grande-Marlaska, en Ceuta entraron irregularmente la semana pasada unas 72.000 personas, de las cuales ya han salido unas 70.000.

Pero el mensaje no se queda ahí. La Moncloa agrava el tono, tras días de reproches moderados —sostenidos fundamentalmente por el titular de Exteriores, José Manuel Albares, que el jueves pasado convocó al embajador italiano— y señala que Italia es, según Frontex (la agencia fronteriza comunitaria), el Estado miembro que más cruces irregulares ha registrado en los últimos años, “con cifras que han llegado a duplicar las de España”.

Además, subraya que, desde 2022, Roma incumple el Reglamento de Dublín —que establece qué país es competente para las peticiones de asilo—, “generando una carga adicional de la presión migratoria al resto de Estados miembros”. “A pesar de lo anterior, España nunca ha introducido controles para Italia”, subraya el Gobierno: “De hecho, siempre se ha mostrado solidaria con ella, acogiendo parte de los migrantes que llegaron a Lampedusa en 2023 y abriendo sus puertos de forma recurrente a migrantes que son rescatados en la ruta del Mediterráneo central”.

La crisis venía fraguándose estos días. Este lunes, Albares reprochaba su actitud a Italia y a otros socios comunitarios, como Finlandia, su respuesta ante la entrada masiva en Ceuta: “Ha habido países, Estados y gobiernos que no han estado a la altura. El Gobierno italiano es uno de ellos”. El jefe de la diplomacia española recordó crisis repetitivas en la isla de Lampedusa y llegó a afirmar que Italia había estado en algún momento “absolutamente inundada de inmigrantes irregulares”, recordando que España “siempre ha sido solidaria política y en los hechos”.

El ministro de Exteriores italiano, Antonio Tajani, contestó entonces a su homólogo español —aunque afirmó que solo respondía “a los números”— en una publicación en la red social X. Tajani resaltó que la inmigración irregular ha descendido en Italia un 60% desde 2023 y presumió de que el pacto de la UE sobre asilo y migración tiene “una marcada impronta italiana, en el surco de la enseñanza de Silvio Berlusconi y de los gobiernos por él guiados”. Además, el responsable de política exterior del Ejecutivo de Giorgia Meloni defendió la suspensión del tratado Schengen, una decisión “correcta”, “respaldada por 21 países europeos” y “en línea con los tratados”.

Un día después de este cruce, el martes, el ministro de Interior italiano, Matteo Piantedosi, trató de rebajar las tensiones con Madrid tras la reunión de ministros del Interior de la Unión Europea, y aseguró que el restablecimiento temporal de los controles en las fronteras aéreas y marítimas italianas no está dirigido contra España, sino que responde a razones de seguridad y gestión de los flujos migratorios. “Se trata de una medida de carácter preventivo y organizativo, destinada a salvaguardar la seguridad nacional y la solidez de todo el sistema europeo de controles en un momento de gran presión, tal y como ha ocurrido en muchísimos otros casos”, señaló en la reunión con sus homólogos europeos. Y trasladó al Gobierno español la “sincera solidaridad de Italia”.

No ha sido suficiente para apaciguar las aguas. “Confiamos en que el europeísmo, el sentido común y la buena fe se impongan. Los gobiernos están para impulsar el entendimiento entre países y el interés general de sus poblaciones, no para crear fracturas y conflictos estériles impulsados por motivaciones electorales internas”, dicen desde Madrid; “Esta postura se adopta sin ánimo de perjudicar a un país amigo como España”, responden desde Roma, que se enroca, sin embargo, en su posición. Con las fichas así dispuestas, queda en el aire cuál será la respuesta “proporcionada” de España, que, si todo sigue igual, se aplicará a partir del lunes.

World.title: Juan Antonio González Hernández, ‘Toño’, el cronista de los astros de La Palma nos da sus mejores pistas en la isla
World.content:
Guía Starlight y del Observatorio del Roque de Los Muchachos, su pasión por los cielos nocturnos nació hace tres décadas y la ha convertido en su profesión. Una vida dedicada a la divulgación astronómica en la isla canaria, de la que recomienda los mejores miradores

En la isla de La Palma, Juan Antonio González Hernández (La Palma, 1972) es conocido como Toño. Es uno de esos tipos que ha hecho de su afición su profesión. Además de astrónomo aficionado, es divulgador, guía Starlight —parte del primer grupo de profesionales de la isla homologados como tal por el Instituto de Astrofísica de Canarias— y del Observatorio del Roque de Los Muchachos (ORM). También es promotor de productos tematizados en astroturismo, astrofotógrafo, consultor, responsable de varios proyectos del Cabildo Insular de La Palma y exgerente de la empresa Cielos-LaPalma.

Una concatenación de hechos a mediados de los ochenta le hizo mirar al cielo y hasta hoy. Primero fue la inauguración, en 1985, del ORM (en el mundo solo hay otros dos observatorios de este tipo: uno en Chile y otro en Hawái) y, un año después, la noche del 12 de abril de 1986, el paso del cometa Halley. Ese fenómeno astronómico lo dibujó a lápiz, con paciencia y con ayuda de unos prismáticos desde el balcón de su casa, en la barriada de El Pilar, en Santa Cruz de La Palma. Su hambre de galaxias, planetas, estrellas y satélites la fue saciando registrando manchas solares durante los recreos del instituto, leyendo libros de astronomía, viendo Cosmos —serie de televisión escrita y presentada por Carl Sagan— y sumándose a la Agrupación Astronómica Palmera (AAP), que llegó a presidir durante 12 años. De la mano de alguno de los miembros de dicha agrupación tuvo la oportunidad de subir al ORM y disfrutar de las vistas del cielo sobre un mar de nubes a casi 2.400 metros de altitud. Son tantas las estrellas que se pueden contemplar a simple vista desde este punto que no es fácil distinguir las constelaciones.

Cielo estrellado sobre el el Observatorio del Roque de Los Muchachos, en la isla de La Palma. Luis Davilla (GETTY IMAGES)

En 1991, con conocimiento y ya equipado con instrumentos de observación, se decantó por la carrera de Astrofísica, “pero no para viajar y hacer investigación. Yo quería enseñar, soñaba con divulgar astronomía, como Sagan”, cuenta a El Viajero de camino a un punto de observación de La Palma. En la Universidad de La Laguna en Tenerife estudió dos años; una etapa personal complicada hizo que abandonase la carrera y regresase a La Palma. De vuelta a su isla natal estudió una FP de Técnico Administrativo y empezó a trabajar como consignatario de barcos en el puerto. Se casó, tiene dos hijos y nunca se cansó ni de contemplar el cielo ni de registrarlo —ha viajado a Novosibirsk (Siberia), donde vio un eclipse total de sol, y a Coquimbo (Chile), adonde fue para conocer cómo trabajaban allí el astroturismo—. Su familia un poco sí, ahora solo le acompañan a ver grandes acontecimientos, como el eclipse solar total del próximo 12 de agosto. Como en La Palma será parcial, lo verán en la provincia de Zaragoza.

Mientras trabajaba, como miembro de la AAP y emprendedor, intensificó su afición por la divulgación de la astronomía. Hasta que llegó un momento en el que su participación en el desarrollo de proyectos, como la Red de Miradores y Senderos Astronómicos, el Taller del Astrónom@ y muchos otros trabajos divulgativos, le demandaba una jornada laboral completa. Así que dio el paso y empezó a vivir profesionalmente de lo que siempre había sido su pasión —hoy trabaja en el departamento de promoción de astroturismo de la Sociedad de Promoción y Desarrollo Económico de La Palma (SODEPAL)—.

El punto de inflexión de ese cambio profesional fue durante la primera Conferencia Internacional Starlight celebrada en La Palma en 2007, donde se habló de la necesidad de desarrollar empresas vinculadas al astroturismo. Por aquel entonces existían algunas iniciativas aisladas en otras islas del archipiélago. Toño, junto a otros miembros de la Agrupación Astronómica de La Palma, presentó un proyecto llamado La Palma y 14 cielos, con la idea de resaltar la calidad excepcional de las noches en cada uno de los 14 municipios de la isla gracias a la aplicación de la Ley de Protección del Cielo. Una ley que él apunta que permite contemplar las estrellas desde cualquier punto oscuro de la isla, incluso a nivel del mar, desde la playa, y no solo desde la alta montaña, donde está instalado el ORM.

El Observatorio Astrofísico del Roque de Los Muchachos (ORM) se encuentra a 2.396 metros de altitud. Jose A. Bernat Bacete (GETTY IMAGES)

En ese contexto, junto con Carmelo González, fundó en 2009 una empresa especializada en astroturismo de la isla. No solo fue pionera en ese campo, “también empezamos a tematizar casas, senderos y experiencias gastronómicas con el cielo”, dice mientras estaciona su vehículo en el mirador de Llano del Jable, un clásico en sus excursiones nocturnas. Detrás de toda esa labor hay una estrategia de sensibilización. No se trata únicamente de pedir a la gente que apague la luz porque interfiere en la observación astronómica, se trata de explicar que cuidar y proteger el cielo beneficia a toda la isla porque la actividad económica que genera.

Atardecer en el mirador de Llano del Jable, en La Palma. Dominic Dähncke (GETTY IMAGES)

Alrededor de La Palma, en puntos estratégicos de su volcánica orografía, hay miradores en los que hasta hace no mucho tiempo la gente se paraba para contemplar las vistas panorámicas, el amanecer y el atardecer. Ahora también lo hacen por la noche para ver las estrellas. Desde que Toño participara en el desarrollo de estos allá por 2009, y gracias al apoyo del Cabildo Insular, los miradores se han convertido en balcones astronómicos equipados con dos módulos: uno compuesto por un panel grande con planisferios (mapas del cielo según las estaciones) con un contenido específico, en algunos casos, del municipio en el que se encuentra: flora, fauna, artesanía, etcétera. Existe un segundo módulo común a todos, el formado por un palo de sendero que señala hacia la Estrella Polar, con una rueda giratoria que ayuda a distinguir las constelaciones circumpolares, junto a un pequeño panel que explica su uso.

Mirador en el inicio del sendero al volcán de San Antonio, con el poste que señala la Estrella Polar y un panel informativo. Autumn Sky (Alamy/CORDON PRESS)

Hay tres tipos de miradores: de montaña, de medianías y urbanos, como el que hay en una plaza de Los Álamos, en Breña Alta. La idea de estos miradores urbanos, desde los que se puede ver la Estrella Polar, es acercar la astronomía al público general y, sobre todo, a los niños. Que los más pequeños vean cómo se monta un telescopio y cómo funciona es sinónimo de despertar su curiosidad y el interés por la astronomía. Si le preguntan a Toño por los miradores de su isla, recomienda el mencionado del Jable (en la parte alta de El Paso), el de Llano de Las Ventas (Breña Baja), El Infinito (San Andrés), el de Buracas (Garafía), el del Molino (Barlovento) y el de las Toscas (Mazo). Enclaves en los que los aficionados y los profesionales de la astronomía instalan sus equipos para ver todos los astros que pueden.

El mirador de Buracas, en el noroeste de la isla. blickwinkel (Alamy / CORDON PRESS)

Su principal motivación es compartir su pasión por la astronomía. También facilitársela. La accesibilidad para personas ciegas y un planetario son los proyectos en los que anda enfrascado. La Palma dispone de un planetario itinerante e hinchable, pero él quiere uno fijo y con instalaciones y accesos para personas con movilidad reducida. “Desde el Cabildo y SODEPAL estamos trabajando para que la astronomía sea cada vez más inclusiva”, dice orgulloso. Un buen altavoz para contar lo que hacen es Astrofest, donde hay programadas actividades divulgativas para el público general y otras para emprendimientos astronómicos.

El color azul en la red de miradores astronómicos de La Palma identifica los puntos o paneles vinculados a la interpretación del cielo y orientación estelar. Christina Bodendorfer (GETTY IMAGES)

La asignatura pendiente de Toño es ver auroras boreales. En Groenlandia o en el norte de Noruega dice que le gustaría verlas. Él, que ya ha disfrutado de cielos del hemisferio sur, eclipses totales, anulares y parciales, eclipses de Luna y lluvias de estrellas espectaculares, anima a ir a La Palma, isla desde la que quien quiera puede ver una galaxia con sus propios ojos.

World.title: Ajax, ING and Ace & Tate hit by data breach
World.content:

Football club Ajax, bank ING and eyewear chain Ace & Tate have been caught up in the data breach at logistics firm CEVA Logistics, which came to light this week when Bol and De Bijenkorf warned customers their details may have been exposed.

CEVA handles deliveries for the companies and had access to the customer data needed to fulfil orders. The firm says it cannot rule out that personal details were leaked, although the companies affected say no payment details, usernames or passwords were taken.

Whether addresses, email addresses or phone numbers were exposed remains unclear.

At ING, the breach affects customers who ordered physical products through the bank’s rewards points scheme.

Ajax has advised supporters to be extra alert to phishing messages in the coming weeks. The club and Ace & Tate have both reported the breach to privacy watchdog AP, as Bol did earlier this week.

Ace & Tate has warned customers that current orders may be delayed, although online ordering is still running. CEVA said it would respond to the breach at a later stage.

World.title: Actor Peter Faber, star of Dutch cinema’s golden age, dies at 82
World.content:
Peter Faber, one of the best-known faces of Dutch film and theatre for half a century, has died at the age of 82.

Faber was admitted to hospital in early July with breathing difficulties related to untreatable heart problems, his family told news agency ANP.

He broke through in the 1970s, widely regarded as the golden age of Dutch cinema, with roles in Keetje Tippel and Paul Verhoeven’s wartime classic Soldaat van Oranje – the film that later spawned the long-running musical which closed last month after 16 years.

He also took the title role in the 1976 film of Max Havelaar, Multatuli’s classic novel about Dutch colonial rule, and appeared alongside Sean Connery and Anthony Hopkins in Richard Attenborough’s A Bridge Too Far.

Faber began his career as a co-founder of Het Werkteater, an Amsterdam collective set up in the early 1970s to shake up Dutch theatre with performances about ordinary people and recognisable emotions. He won the Louis d’Or, the top Dutch theatre prize for a male actor, twice.

He kept working into his eighties. His final film role came in 2023 in Sweet Dreams, the Dutch entry for the 2024 Oscars, in which he appeared alongside his son Jesse.

Faber often spoke about his difficult upbringing, part of which he spent living on the streets of Amsterdam as a teenager. In 2008 he set up the Peter Faber Foundation to help young people build confidence, and to “make the switch from destructive to creative energy”. Its motto is “I can do it, I want it, I’m doing it. Now!”

A public memorial service will be held at Het Zonnehuis in Amsterdam-Noord on Monday between 10am and midday.

World.title: Cabinet rules out compensation for drought-hit businesses
World.content:
Despite the country’s continuing water shortage, entrepreneurs feeling the squeeze won’t be receiving any help from the government any time soon.

“There are arrangements in place for the event of a natural disaster, such as the flooding in Limburg in 2021, but we are not there yet,” infrastructure and water management minister Vincent Karremans said while visiting Nijmegen on Thursday.

“We don’t have the money in the account either. We can’t help it that it isn’t raining.”

Maarten Ouboter, a technician for the Amstel, Gooi and Vecht water authority, told DutchNews: “The question is: how much is a government – the public – responsible for the weather? The minister was clear: droughts can happen.”

Low water levels are hurting everyone from inland vessels that can’t sail down dwindling rivers to houseboat owners on the Rhine who have effectively been marooned. Several locks have been closed, ferries have been cancelled and the economically important Twente Canal, reported broadcaster NOS, is also inaccessible.

And while Karremans estimates that the economic damage to businesses runs “into the tens, if not hundreds of millions of euros”, he views the water shortage as an “entrepreneurial risk, after all” – not a natural disaster.

A shortage but not a crisis

For now, the country’s water level remains at 2 – a shortage but not yet a crisis. That could change if the drought continues for another few weeks. But the government maintains its priorities are preserving the country’s dikes and ensuring enough available drinking water, not propping up businesses.

“We are now at a point that the rivers flowing into our low-lying delta have never been so low in August,” said Ouboter, who focuses on the Amsterdam area. “We are comparable to 1947, but that was in November.”

Using a football analogy, he said the drought “in June was ‘second league’; in July it was ‘first league’; in August, it’s Champions League.”

Boosting water storage

Karremans said more water must be stored for the future, including in places like the IJsselmeer and the Volkerak-Zoommeer. The cabinet is currently working on the Freshwater Delta Plan to ensure rainwater captured in the spring, for example, can be used in drier months.

In Amsterdam, an innovative system of wadis – dry water ditches – catches rainwater that can be distributed later where needed and also absorbs extra rainwater to prevent flooding.

“The way we think about water has changed,” said Ton Hilhorst, the chief garden designer at Amsterdam’s Artis zoo. “Water was always seen as the enemy, but now we must keep it in the country, not pump it out.”

Weather forecasters are predicting another warm and largely cloudless weekend, with rain unlikely in the current week.

World.title: Philip Morris rebuked over AI campaign against EU tobacco rules
World.content:
The Dutch advertising standards watchdog RCC has reprimanded tobacco behemoth Philip Morris for an AI-powered ad campaign that it says violated the country’s tobacco advertising ban.

As the EU prepares its biggest tobacco tightening rules in 15 years, the public was invited to share its views via comments.

But a recent investigation by broadcaster NOS and the journalism platform Pointer found that Philip Morris used AI to generate hundreds of fake “citizen” responses opposing tougher EU rules on vapes, which along with other cigarette alternatives like e-cigarettes and heated tobacco, now account for 40% of the company’s revenue.

Here’s how the campaign worked: Philip Morris put up yellow posters carrying QR codes in tobacco shops under the slogan “Your Voice Your Choice.” Scanning the code led to a tool that asked multiple-choice questions and then an option to write a first-person text, which users could then send to the Commission.

The investigation found that some 71% of responses from the Netherlands were written by AI, the second highest after Portugal.

The RCC had several problems with the campaign, including that the text generator was paid for and owned by Philip Morris. The company defended its actions by saying it contributed to the public debate.

“The fact that the statements are framed as a call for public consultation does not detract from their commercial character,” said the watchdog.

The written responses also portray alternative tobacco products positively, which the RCC says constitutes advertising and therefore violates the tobacco advertising ban.

Doctors

In June, a group of doctors and healthcare campaign groups made a formal complaint to the RCC, saying the “misleading” campaign used an AI tool to influence European decision-making on tobacco and nicotine products.

Lawyer Laura van Gijn, who represents the doctors, told NOS that violating the tobacco advertising ban is a criminal offence. “This decision is a clear signal to the tobacco industry that digital influence campaigns do not fall outside the scope of the advertising ban, even when packaged as citizen participation. This precedent is relevant for similar campaigns elsewhere in Europe.”

World.title: No more “shame lips”: Dutch dictionary adds new word for labia
World.content:
Women’s rights groups are applauding the latest addition to the definitive Dutch dictionary Dikke Van Dale of the word labia: vulvalippen, added alongside the word schaamlippen.

While both words mean labia, the old schaamlippen translates as “shame lips”, which the organisations say is stigmatising as compared to the more neutral “vulva lips”.

“We should just mention these parts in our education with children and young people,” artist Esther van der Valk told broadcaster NOS. “People now know that this is a normal word, and with that we can break the taboo.”

Van der Valk is a member of Dolle Mina, the women’s rights group that was founded in the Netherlands in 1969 and has been advocating for the inclusion of vulvalippen in the Dutch dictionary to counter stigmatisation. They’re joined by Schaamteloos, a more recent campaign seeking to change language and attitudes regarding female anatomy.

Body positive

While schaamlippen will remain in the dictionary, the addition of vulvalippen means the word gets official Dutch language status – proof, say the activists, that the normalisation of sexuality via language can be achieved if enough people want it.

Schaamlippen is not the only word where shame is embedded in its name. There’s schaamhaar – “shame hair” – which is the name for pubic hair, schaambeen (shame bone) for pubic bone and even schaamstreek (shame area) for pubic area.

But Schaamteloos says it had to start somewhere, so it picked schaamlippen. “Everyone has pubic hair, a pubic bone, and a pubic area,” says the group, but “only half of us have labia – or ‘shame lips’ … which adds to a disproportionately large amount of trouble due to the taboo on talking about this.”

While some doctors and even the media have taken to using vulvalippen, it’s not yet part of the everyday Dutch vernacular.

That may change when the new anatomically correct word is included in the Dikke van Dale. That’s expected to happen during its next online update, likely this Autumn.

World.title: Four arrested for death threat against Breda mayor
World.content:
Police have arrested four men suspected of threatening to kill Breda mayor Paul Depla, after a photograph found on a football supporter’s phone revealed new evidence for a case that had stalled.

A banner bearing the words “Depla Dood” (Depla dead) was hung on the front of a café in the city’s Meidoornstraat on March 8, when NAC Breda played Feyenoord. Depla reported the threat to the police, but in May prosecutors said the case had halted because the suspects could not be linked to the banner.

A breakthrough came when several NAC supporters were arrested over rioting around the club’s match against Heerenveen on May 10 and their phones were seized, police said. On one of them, officers found a photograph of the banner in which four men could be identified.

The four – three from Breda, aged 16, 32 and 34, and a 24-year-old from Oosterhout – were arrested on Thursday and will be questioned. Threatening a public official carries a maximum prison sentence of four years.

It is unclear what prompted the threat, but broadcaster NOS reported it may have followed a warning from the city council to a different café, which had planned to host a pre-match party for the club’s hardcore supporters.

When the owners called the party off, the group gathered at the Meidoornstraat café instead, where the banner was hung.

Threats and intimidation against Dutch public officials are a growing concern. Some 45% of local and regional political office holders, including mayors, told a 2024 home affairs ministry survey they had faced aggression in the preceding year.

World.title: Warm, dry weekend ahead as drought shows no sign of ending
World.content:
The Netherlands is set for another warm and largely cloudless weekend, with barely a drop of rain likely for the coming week, according to forecasters.

Friday will be calm and dry with temperatures of 21 to 25°, with morning cloud in the north east giving way to sunshine. Saturday will be sunny and slightly warmer, at 25 to 28°, before temperatures climb to around 30° inland on Sunday.

A brief cooler spell will push maximums down to around 25° on Tuesday, but forecasters expect the warmth to return later in the week – without any significant rain.

The dry spell means no let-up for the ongoing drought, which has pushed the Rhine to record low levels and prompted water use restrictions in several regions.

World.title: Childcare benefits falling short for most parents: CBS
World.content:
Almost two-thirds of parents who claim childcare benefits pay more than the government’s maximum hourly rate, leaving them with hundreds of euros in costs the benefit does not cover, according to national statistics agency CBS.

Parents claiming the benefit spent an average of €10,510 on childcare in 2025, of which 68% was covered, up from 65% in 2024. The benefit was raised in both years as a step towards the government plan for near-free childcare.

But childcare providers are free to set their own fees, and the benefit only applies to costs up to a ceiling fixed by the government each year. In 2025, 63% of parents paid more than the maximum rate for at least one child.

On average, parents paid €3,340 towards childcare themselves last year – €2,860 in regular contributions, plus an extra €480 to cover fees above the official maximum.

The share of parents paying over the ceiling varies widely. In Nunspeet, Bloemendaal, Houten and Midden-Delfland, almost 90% pay more than the maximum rate, compared with just 8% on the island of Ameland. The proportion is highest in the provinces of Utrecht and Noord-Holland and lowest in Friesland and Groningen.

Households in the lowest income group paid an average of €1,190 towards childcare, or 11% of the total cost, while the highest earners paid €5,950, just over half the bill.

In total, 719,000 parents claimed the benefit last year for nearly 1.1 million children. More children attended nurseries and after-school clubs, while the number looked after by registered childminders (gastouders) fell by 10,000 to around 95,000.

The cabinet plans to make childcare almost free for working parents from 2029, covering 96% of costs regardless of income – a scheme that has been repeatedly delayed.

In a rare clash between Poland’s two houses of parliament, in both of which the government has a majority, the Senate has rejected a candidate chosen by the Sejm to become the new head of the state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN). The nominee, Mateusz Szpytma, has served as deputy head of the IPN since 2016, including when it was under the leadership of Karol Nawrocki, who last year was elected president of Poland with the support of the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party. Szpytma’s candidacy has been opposed by most of Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, who argue he helped politicise the IPN under the former PiS government. However, some more conservative elements of the coalition joined the opposition in supporting Szpytma, giving him a majority in the Sejm but not the Senate. Senatorowie nie wyrazili zgody na powołanie Mateusza Szpytmy na Prezesa Instytutu Pamięci Narodowej – Komisji Ścigania Zbrodni przeciwko Narodowi Polskiemu — Senat RP 🇵🇱 (@PolskiSenat) August 6, 2026 The IPN is a body tasked with researching, documenting and educating about Poland’s tumultuous and tragic 20th-century history. It also has the power to prosecute crimes relating to the periods when the country was under Nazi and communist rule. The institute was led by Nawrocki from 2021 until August last year, when he became president of Poland. Since then, the IPN has been without a permanent head. Last October, the IPN’s council nominated Karol Polejowski, another of the institute’s deputy heads, to be its new president. But he was rejected by the Sejm, which, along with the Senate, must approve the choice. In April, the council instead recommended Szpytma, whose candidacy was approved by the Sejm last month. He received support mainly from opposition parties, including PiS and the far-right Confederation (Konfederacja). However, in a rare split within the ruling coalition, one of its junior members, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), also backed Szpytma, as did some MPs from the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050). That was enough to give him a majority. By contrast, the main ruling party, Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO), and The Left (Lewica) opposed his nomination, citing a letter signed earlier this year by 170 academics, who described Szpytma as “one of the faces of IPN’s politicisation” under the former PiS government. However, PSL’s leader, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, who also serves as Poland’s defence minister and deputy prime minister rejected that characterisation and said that PSL had backed Szpytma because of his work commemorating historical figures from the agrarian movement in which PSL is rooted. In a rare split in the ruling coalition, MPs from two parties, PSL and Poland 2050, voted with the opposition in the Sejm for a new head of the Institute of National Remembrance. However, PM Donald Tusk says their choice will be rejected by the Senate https://t.co/0CGmbsNp4F — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026 However, it was widely expected that Szpytma’s candidacy would be blocked by the upper-house Senate, where even the PSL and opposition combined do not have a majority in the 100-seat chamber. That was confirmed in a vote on Thursday, when 50 senators were opposed to Szyptma and only 38 were in favour, with one abstention. “We voted against further politicisation” of IPN and “against tolerating financial irregularities”, wrote the speaker of the Senate, Małgorzata Kidawa-Błonska of KO. The latter comment was likely a reference to a report by the Supreme Audit Office (NIK) last year which found that the IPN had, between 2022 and 2025, failed to properly manage tens of millions of zloty in spending, including various violations of regulations on the use of public funds. Szpytma told journalists that he was not surprised by the result of the vote, saying he believes his connection to Nawrocki, who is an ardent opponent of the current government and has vetoed a record number of laws, is the reason why he lost. Nie zgodziliśmy się w Senacie, by człowiek Karola Nawrockiego został prezesem IPN. Zagłosowaliśmy przeciw dalszemu upolitycznianiu Instytutu. Przeciw tolerowaniu nieprawidłowości finansowych. Pan Szpytma nie wprowadziłby żadnych zmian w funkcjonowaniu IPN. — Małgorzata Kidawa-Błońska (@M_K_Blonska) August 6, 2026 The IPN plays an important role in Polish public life, including in commemorating, investigating and prosecuting crimes that took place during the Nazi-German and Soviet occupations of Poland in World War Two, as well as during the decades of communist rule afterwards. Under Nawrocki’s leadership, the IPN accelerated the process of demolishing remaining Soviet monuments in Poland, often prompting criticism from Russia. It has also been closely involved in the exhumation of victims of the Volhynia massacres, in which Ukrainian nationalists killed around 100,000 Poles during World War Two. During PiS’s time in power from 2015 to 2023, the IPN was accused of becoming increasingly politicised, using its activities to support the historical narratived promoted by the government. In 2021, Israel protested after a former far-right activist was appointed to head one of the IPN’s local branches. Russia has criticised the "sacrilegious" demolition of a Soviet monument in Poland, calling it a “flagrant violation” of a bilateral agreement. But Poland's @ipngovpl says it was a "propaganda object" that had to be removed under a "decommunisation" law https://t.co/73T99ZlPqU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish state energy giant Orlen posts record half-year profit amid Middle East turmoil
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish state energy giant Orlen posted a record profit in the first half of 2026, as turmoil in the Middle East boosted earnings in the fuel sector, despite Polish government measures to cushion the rise in consumer prices. Orlen has also this year seen its highest ever proportion of revenue from foreign markets. The results come amid a political dispute over a government plan to impose a windfall tax on excess profits from fuel sales, aimed at recouping billions spent on consumer subsidies. Orlen would be the biggest target of the tax, but the plan has been obstructed by opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki. W pierwszym półroczu Orlen zarobił na czysto 15,8 miliarda złotych. Trzy razy więcej niż przed rokiem.https://t.co/qJS81csI0H — TVN24 BiS (@TVN24BiS) August 6, 2026 On Thursday, Orlen reported consolidated net profit of 15.9 billion zloty (€3.7 billion) for the first six months of the year, almost tripling from the 5.7 billion zloty recorded in the same period of 2025. Revenue rose to 152.2 billion zloty from 134.4 billion zloty. CEO Ireneusz Fąfara acknowledged that the figures came amid exceptional market conditions. Energy prices jumped globally in March, after the US and Israel began to attack Iran and Tehran responded by blocking the Strait of Hormuz, a key export route. Fąfara noted that, despite this, Poland had maintained some of Europe’s lowest fuel prices. He said that Orlen had prioritised fuel availability and competitive domestic prices while taking advantage of stronger margins abroad, where it brought in an “absolutely record level of revenue from foreign markets”. In the first half of 2026, foreign markets accounted for 35.7% of Orlen’s revenue, up from 33.8% a year earlier. The bulk came from Germany, the Czech Republic, Lithuania and Austria, where Orlen operates petrol stations, as well as from trading activities in markets such as the Netherlands and Switzerland. Pierwsze półrocze 2026 roku ORLEN zamyka rekordowym zyskiem z rynków zagranicznych. Wynik netto całej Grupy w II kwartale wyniósł 7,7 mld zł. Wypracowane wyniki finansowe pozwoliły na wypłatę rekordowej dywidendy dla akcjonariuszy oraz dalsze finansowanie największego programu… pic.twitter.com/ohcxksuv4G — ORLEN (@GrupaORLEN) August 6, 2026 Orlen has expanded rapidly in recent years, as it has swallowed up other state-owned energy firms and sought to diversify away from its traditional focus on oil towards gas, renewables and hydrogen. In March this year, Orlen’s market valuation rose to its highest ever level of €35.2 billion, up from €7 billion in early 2022. As a result, it overtook the market capitalisation of Russian energy giant Gazprom. Mateusz Czyżkowski, an analyst at brokerage XTB, attributed Orlen’s record profits this year to “skilful balancing between geopolitical conditions and local pressures”, including government-imposed fuel price caps that squeezed margins. “The global commodities market in the second quarter of 2026 was strongly buoyed by tensions between Iran and Israel and ongoing disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz…This significant geopolitical premium boosted profits in [Orlen’s] Upstream & Supply segment,” he wrote in a note. The announcement of record profits comes as Orlen finds itself at the centre of a political dispute over the government’s proposed windfall tax, which would introduce a 60% levy on excess profits from liquid fuel sales. The measure was expected to raise around 4 billion zloty, which would have offset most of the roughly 4.7 billion zloty the government spent on keeping fuel prices lower for consumers amid the crisis in the Middle East by, among other things, cutting VAT and introducing a maximum daily price. However, although the tax was approved by the government’s majority in parliament in July, President Nawrocki refused to sign it into law, instead referring it to the constitutional court for review – a process that has no time limit and can take years. President @NawrockiKn has obstructed a planned windfall tax on fuel companies by sending it to the constitutional court, where it could stay for years The tax aimed to offset fuel price protection costs after the Iran war surgehttps://t.co/UojVuYhvdV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026 According to government calculations, Orlen would account for around 60% of the tax base if the measures eventually come into force. However, at his press conference on Thursday, Fąfara emphasised that the company supports the windfall tax. “We have viewed this solution positively from the very beginning. I believe it is in the interest of the company, our customers, and the country,” he said. However, Fąfara rejected suggestions that Orlen could unilaterally reduce pump prices by sacrificing margins. “We cannot lower prices in defiance of the market and global prices…If we lowered prices below parity, there would be a shortage of fuel,” he warned, adding that artificially low prices would encourage speculative exports and fuel tourism. Prices at petrol stations jumped today in Poland after the government ended the last of the support measures introduced to cushion consumers from the energy crisis caused by the war in Iran. New Polish opposition group Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), which recently broke away from the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, has proposed the idea of paying a “parental salary” for the first three years of a child’s life. The idea is part of a package of proposals to tackle Poland’s dire demographic situation released on Friday by Development Plus in its first major policy announcement since leader Mateusz Morawiecki announced that the group would soon become a political party. 3600 zł miesięcznie na dziecko do 3. roku życia – jedna z wielu propozycji @RozwojPlus dla demografii! Pensja Rodzicielska wynosząca równowartość płacy minimalnej, czyli obecnie około 3600 zł netto miesięcznie przez pierwsze 3 lata życia dziecka. To ponad czterokrotnie więcej… pic.twitter.com/253pwcskNK — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) August 7, 2026 The proposed parental salary would amount to 3,600 zloty (€837) per month, the equivalent of the minimum wage after taxes. It is 4.5 times more than the current child benefit payment of 800 zloty per month that all Polish parents of children under 18 receive. Development Plus says that the parental salary could be combined with income from other work that parents undertake and that it would include contributions towards their pensions. It would end once a child turns three, after which parents would have access to normal child benefit payments. The group says that, for now, the idea is just a proposal, based on expert analysis of how to tackle Poland’s demographic crisis, and that it now wants to “refine it through dialogue with Poles” rather than “imposing top-down provisions”. Poland has long been grappling with a shrinking, ageing population. Last year, the number of births fell to a new post-war low of 238,000, while deaths totalled 406,000. That marked the 13th consecutive year in which more people died than were born in Poland. The country’s fertility rate – meaning the average number of children that are born to a woman over her lifetime – fell to a new record low of 1.068 in 2025. That is one of the lowest figures anywhere in the world and well below the so-called “replacement rate” – the figure needed to ensure that the population does not decline – which is generally defined as 2.1. Poland’s fertility rate, already one of the lowest in the world, fell to a new record low of 1.07 in 2025, deepening concerns over the country's shrinking and ageing population https://t.co/OMGC1MpA5l — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 28, 2026 Successive Polish governments have introduced various measures intended to boost the birth rate, though so far without clear success. The former PiS government, with Morawiecki as finance minister and later prime minister, introduced and expanded the current child benefit programme. While there was a brief bump in births after it was launched in 2016, numbers subsequently continued their downward trend. After PiS lost power in 2023, the current government, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, continued the child benefit programme and also introduced new payments to support parents who return to work and restored funding for IVF treatment, which was previously cut by PiS. When announcing the proposed parental salary on Friday, Development Plus also outlined seven other proposed new policies to ease Poland’s demographic problems. One would allow workers to have a portion of their contributions go towards their parents’ pensions. Another pledged to provide better maternity care, including access to anaesthesia, a private hospital room and dedicated midwife, prenatal testing, and infertility treatment. Other policies promised more flexible working arrangements and mortgage repayments to prevent people from having to choose between a family or a career, as well as school hours and after-school care that “adapt to the lives of families, not the other way around”. Development Plus also proposed “granting parents the right to represent the voices of their minor children”. However, they provided no details of what this would mean in practice. Dzieci to nasza przyszłość! To fundament bezpieczeństwa Polski i polska racja stanu. Jak sprawić, by Polaków rodziło się coraz więcej? Oto strategia demograficzna dla Polski Stowarzyszenia @RozwojPlus🇵🇱➕. pic.twitter.com/1hiQPNuL47 — Mateusz Morawiecki (@MorawieckiM) August 7, 2026 Development Plus was founded as an association by Morawiecki in April this year. That immediately prompted criticism from some other members of the party, who saw it as a step towards creating a breakaway group. Matters came to a head last month, when PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński demanded that all the party’s lawmakers sign a pledge of loyalty and commit to leave any political associations they are part of. Morawiecki and his allies refused to do so, prompting Kaczyński to declare that meant they had effectively resigned from the party. Last week, Development Plus announced it had formed its own separate parliamentary caucus with 40 MPs in the Sejm, the most powerful lower house of parliament. The move immediately made it the third-largest group in the parliament, while also meaning PiS was no longer the biggest. On Monday this week, Morawiecki confirmed that his group would soon form a party of its own. He laid out a vision of a more moderate, centre-right party that would focus on economic development rather than “ideological disputes”, following PiS’s shift in a more hardline direction over recent months.
